contradictions.question: Did everyone (except for Noah and his family) die in the flood?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 7:21-23 insists that every living thing outside the ark perished, yet Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33 have the Nephilim — the giant offspring of the 'sons of God' — still walking around after the flood in the days of Moses. The text cannot have both a hermetic global extinction and a post-flood population of antediluvian monsters.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists typically read Genesis 6:4 to mean the Nephilim existed 'in those days, and also after that' as a second, independent giant lineage that arose after the flood — Kenneth Mathews and Victor Hamilton both push this harmonization, treating Numbers 13:33 as a reputational echo or a later Anakim group unrelated to the pre-flood giants. The problem is that Numbers 13:33 explicitly identifies the Anakim as descended from the Nephilim, and the scouts are terrified specifically because these are the same kind of beings. The deeper issue is source-critical. Gen 6:1-4 is a J fragment that many scholars (Friedman, Speiser, Westermann) read as an etiological note about heroic beings still known in Israel's memory, appended to a Priestly flood frame that insists on total destruction. The redactor stitched two incompatible traditions together: the cosmic do-over of P and the older Yahwistic giant-lore. Ronald Hendel's work on the Nephilim traditions shows Second Temple literature (1 Enoch, Jubilees) solved the problem by inventing demonology — the flood killed the giants' bodies but their spirits became demons — precisely because readers noticed the incoherence. If you have to invent a whole demon cosmology to fix the story, the story has a problem.

contradictions.question: How long did the flood last?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 7:17 says the flood was on the earth for forty days, while Genesis 7:24 and 8:3 say the waters prevailed for a hundred and fifty days. Two different numerical frames for the same event sit side by side in the same chapter.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization, pressed by Gleason Archer and John Walton, is that the forty days refers only to the rain falling while the one hundred and fifty days refers to the total time the waters prevailed before receding. That reading is possible at the surface, but it ignores why there are two incompatible chronologies in the first place. Critical scholarship since Wellhausen has treated Genesis 6-9 as a textbook example of source stitching: the Yahwist (J) tradition uses a forty-day schema with seven clean pairs of animals and a seven-day warning (Gen 7:4, 7:10, 7:12, 8:6), while the Priestly (P) tradition operates on a precise 150-day cycle keyed to dated months and one pair of each kind (Gen 7:11, 7:24, 8:3-4, 8:13-14). Friedman's color-coded reconstruction in The Bible with Sources Revealed separates the two strands cleanly, and each reads as a coherent flood story on its own. The contradiction isn't a logical puzzle to solve — it's the literary signature of a redactor splicing two independent flood accounts. Treating the numbers as sequential rather than parallel is a harmonization move that presupposes a unity the text does not display.

contradictions.question: How long was the ark afloat?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 8:4 has the ark resting on Ararat in the seventh month, while Genesis 8:5 says the mountaintops only became visible in the tenth month. An ark cannot be resting on a mountain three months before the mountain pokes above the water.
contradictions.commentary: Mathews and Hamilton try to smooth this by arguing the ark came to rest on a submerged high peak whose summit wasn't yet visible, with the tops of lower mountains becoming visible three months later. It's physically possible as a single image, but it strains the plain sequence of the narrative, which treats 'mountains of Ararat' and 'tops of the mountains' as parallel reference points rather than one specific peak versus a range. The cleaner explanation is again source-critical. The dated notices in Genesis 8:4-5, 13-14 belong to the Priestly schema, and P's dating system operates on a liturgical calendar whose internal logic doesn't fully smooth into a naturalistic travelogue. Speiser in the Anchor Bible commentary already flagged the awkwardness of reading these dates as a continuous eyewitness log. The point isn't that a reader can't construct a physical scenario — the point is that the text is a theologically structured chronology, not an engineering report, and forcing it to behave like one generates incoherence the original authors didn't care about.

contradictions.question: When did the earth dry after the flood?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 8:13 declares the waters dried up on the first day of the first month, but Genesis 8:14 puts the earth's drying on the twenty-seventh day of the second month — almost two months later. The same narrative gives two different drying dates.
contradictions.commentary: Archer's standard move is to distinguish 'the waters were dried up from off the earth' (8:13) as referring to surface water evaporating from the mud from 'the earth was dried' (8:14) as the ground becoming firm enough to walk on. Hebrew does use different verbal forms here (charav in 8:13, yavesh in 8:14), and apologists run with that distinction. The problem is that this reads a precise technical geology into two verses that sit in the middle of the Priestly dating scheme and are otherwise formulaic date-stamps in a liturgical calendar. Friedman and Baden note that the dated notices in Gen 7-8 follow a symmetrical P calendar that is more about ritual numerology than narrative reportage. The gap between the dates probably reflects the editorial stitching of P's ceremonial timeline, not a fine-grained distinction between damp topsoil and bone-dry substrate. Treating these as two stages of a single drying process is doable — it's just not what the Priestly author was tracking.

contradictions.question: Will God curse the earth?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 8:21 has God swear in his heart never again to curse the ground because of humanity, yet Isaiah 24:1-6 announces a curse that devours the earth and Malachi 4:6 warns that Yahweh will come and smite the earth with a curse. The promise is issued and then revoked.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Archer and John Oswalt distinguish two Hebrew words — qalal in Gen 8:21 (often translated 'curse') and different terms in Isaiah 24 (alah) and Malachi 4:6 (cherem-adjacent language) — arguing the Genesis oath is narrowly about the flood-style cursing of the ground's agricultural fertility, while the prophetic curses are covenantal judgments on specific populations. That lexical point has force in the weeds, but it doesn't rescue the plain reading. Genesis 8:21 explicitly promises no more universal earth-destruction tied to human wickedness ('I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake... neither will I again smite any more every thing living'), and Isaiah 24's cosmic-scale devastation is framed in exactly those terms — the earth emptied, polluted by its inhabitants, its covenant broken. Brevard Childs and Joseph Blenkinsopp both read Isaiah 24-27 (the so-called 'Isaiah Apocalypse') as deliberately echoing and reversing Noahic themes. The author of Isaiah 24 wasn't trying to respect Gen 8:21 — he was announcing a new judgment that overrides it. That's not harmonization; that's the Bible talking back to itself.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to eat blood?
contradictions.summary: The Priestly and Deuteronomic Torah absolutely forbids eating blood as a perpetual statute (Gen 9:4; Lev 3:17; 7:26-27; 17:10-14; 19:26; Deut 12:16, 23), and the apostolic decree in Acts 15 reaffirms that prohibition for Gentile Christians. John 6:53-56, however, has Jesus commanding that his followers eat his flesh and drink his blood to have eternal life. The Torah bans blood-drinking outright; the Johannine Jesus makes it the condition of salvation.
contradictions.commentary: The standard Catholic and apologetic response is that John 6 is either symbolic (so Calvin, many Protestants) or sacramental (so Raymond Brown, in a qualified way) — either way, not a violation of the Levitical ban, since the eucharistic referent is Jesus' flesh and blood, not a prohibited animal. Craig Blomberg and D. A. Carson argue the Levitical prohibition targeted ritual slaughter of animals within Israel's purity system, not the sacramental participation in a salvific death. That defense works for internal Christian theology but collapses when you pull back. The whole point of Leviticus 17:11 is that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls' — blood is forbidden precisely because it is the site of atonement and belongs to God. John 6 presses the exact same logic in reverse: the disciples must drink the blood because it is the site of atonement. Klawans and Milgrom both note how shocking John 6 would sound to a first-century Jewish ear — John's narrator even stages that shock ('Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said, This is an hard saying'). The harmonization papers over a real theological rupture. And Acts 15:20 shows the apostolic church itself still upholding the Torah ban while presumably also practicing the eucharist, which either means they didn't read John 6 literally or they hadn't encountered it yet (John being the latest canonical gospel). Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Will God flood the earth again?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 9:11-15 gives an unqualified covenantal 'no' — God swears never again to flood the earth, with the rainbow as the binding sign. Nahum 1:8, however, describes God using 'an overrunning flood' to make an utter end of his enemies' place.
contradictions.commentary: Hamilton and Walton argue that Nahum's 'overrunning flood' is a localized judgment metaphor directed at Nineveh, not a repeat of the Genesis deluge, and that the Noachic covenant specifically pertains to a global hydrological event. That harmonization works at a technical level — Nahum is clearly poetic threat-language against Assyria — and honestly, this is one of the weaker contradictions in the SAB catalog. The critical observation is subtler: Nahum uses flood imagery precisely because it still carries divine-judgment freight in Israel's theological vocabulary, which means Gen 9:11's covenant hasn't actually retired the metaphor of God-as-flooder. More pointedly, 2 Peter 3:5-7 explicitly envisions a future cosmic destruction that parallels the flood ('the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished: but the heavens and the earth, which are now... reserved unto fire'), transposing the Noahic extinction into fire rather than respecting its finality. The theological promise of Gen 9 gets relitigated in later apocalyptic texts. Nahum isn't the sharpest edge of that tension, but it's an edge.

contradictions.question: Are we punished for the sins of others?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Romans
contradictions.summary: Romans 5:12 has Paul teach that death passed upon all humanity because of Adam's single sin — the archetypal transgenerational punishment. Deuteronomy 24:16, 2 Kings 14:6, Jeremiah 31:29-30, and Ezekiel 18:20 insist the opposite: each person dies for his own sin and no one bears the iniquity of another.
contradictions.commentary: The classical reformed harmonization, pressed by Doug Moo and John Murray, is that Romans 5 teaches federal headship — Adam sinned as humanity's representative, so we don't bear his guilt directly but inherit the corruption and death that flow from it, while Deuteronomy 24 and Ezekiel 18 govern human judicial procedures, not God's metaphysical accounting. That distinction is theologically sophisticated but it does not actually resolve the tension on the ground. Ezekiel 18:20 is explicit that 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.' It frames this as Yahweh's own judgment principle, not a human courtroom rule, and it directly contradicts the older Exodus 20:5 formula about visiting iniquity 'unto the third and fourth generation.' Joel Kaminsky's Corporate Responsibility in the Hebrew Bible traces this exact tension — the Hebrew Bible contains both corporate and individualist streams of moral accounting, and texts like Ezekiel 18 and Deuteronomy 24:16 press back against the older corporate-retribution framework visible in Exodus 20:5 (even if, as Kaminsky argues, the shift is less a clean revolution than a reweighting). Paul then inherits and radicalizes the older corporate theology via Adam, precisely the model Ezekiel was trying to bury. Romans 5:12-19 isn't a minor doctrinal gloss — it's the theological engine of original sin, and it runs directly against Ezekiel's 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.' You can privilege one stream over the other, but you cannot pretend they are saying the same thing.

answers.answer: Yes, God often punishes innocent people for the actions of others.
answers.answer_explanation: By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men. Romans 5:12

contradictions.question: Who was Sheba's father?
contradictions.summary: The Table of Nations and its parallels give three different fathers for a man named Sheba: Raamah (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9), Jokshan son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen 25:3; 1 Chr 1:32), and Joktan son of Eber (Gen 10:26-28; 1 Chr 1:20-22). Three genealogies, three fathers.
contradictions.commentary: The obvious harmonization, offered by Kidner and Mathews, is that 'Sheba' is simply a name three different ancient Near Eastern tribes independently used — the Cushite Sheba of Gen 10:7, the Abrahamic Sheba of Gen 25, and the Joktanide Sheba of Gen 10:26 are different people from different clans who share a common name. That's not crazy. The name Sheba is well attested across ancient South Arabian inscriptions as a regional ethnonym, and ethnic names getting recycled across unrelated lineages is normal. But this move only works if you treat Genesis 10 as a sober ethnographic catalog rather than what it actually is — a theological map of the known world organized into a 70-nation schema. Westermann, Cassuto, and more recently John Day have shown that Genesis 10 functions as a literary-ideological document whose genealogies are overlapping claims about the relationship of peoples to Israel, with different traditions preserving different political alignments. The three Shebas aren't three people — they're three attempts by different tradents to locate the Sabean/Arabian peoples within the genealogical imagination of Israel. Treating this as 'three different men with the same name' is a harmonization that turns a political text into a phonebook.

contradictions.question: Where was Abraham buried?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 25:8-10 has Abraham buried in the cave of Machpelah near Hebron, on a plot he purchased from Ephron the Hittite. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:15-16 relocates Abraham's tomb to Shechem and has him purchasing the plot from 'the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem' — the tomb Jacob later buys in Genesis 33:19.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleaner factual contradictions in the New Testament. Apologists like Darrell Bock and F. F. Bruce argue that Stephen's speech is a rapid-fire summary conflating two purchase stories — Abraham's at Hebron (Gen 23) and Jacob's at Shechem (Gen 33:19) — and that either Luke is accurately reporting Stephen's memory lapse in a charged speech, or Stephen is using a telescoping rhetorical device. Either version concedes the factual error; it just relocates blame. Ernst Haenchen's classic Anchor Bible-era work on Acts and more recent commentaries by Richard Pervo and Craig Keener all acknowledge the historical inaccuracy and debate only whether Luke was aware of it. The move of saying 'Luke is quoting Stephen, so Luke isn't wrong even if Stephen is' is the apologetic playbook's way of preserving inerrancy by pushing the error one level down. But that's not what inerrancy means on any robust definition — if the speech is wrong on plain historical facts that Acts presents without correction, the text transmits an error. Apologists who accept Stephen's telescoping have quietly accepted that biblical narration is not uniformly accurate; they just don't phrase it that way.

contradictions.question: Who was Dedan's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 10:7 and 1 Chronicles 1:9 list Dedan as the son of Raamah in the Cushite/Hamite line, while Genesis 25:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:32 list Dedan as the son of Jokshan in the Abrahamic/Keturite line. The genealogies give two fathers for the same ethnonym.
contradictions.commentary: Same structural problem as the Sheba contradiction in id=49, and the same harmonization is available: these are two distinct Dedanites from two distinct clans. Mathews and Kidner take exactly that route, pointing out that Dedan is attested as an important North Arabian trade center and it's plausible that two tribes with overlapping territory carried the same ethnonym. Fair enough — but the tell that this is about genealogy-as-geography, not genealogy-as-biology, is that Sheba and Dedan appear together in both lists. The same paired names get relocated from the Hamite line to the Abrahamic line across traditions. Ronald Hendel and John Day read this as the Chronicler and the Yahwist preserving competing political maps of North Arabia. When the Priestly editor compiles both into the canonical shape, he gets two contradictory patrilines side by side and doesn't bother to reconcile them. The apologetic 'two different people with the same name in the same territory doing the same trade' requires an improbable coincidence across multiple name-pairs. Parsimony favors: the tradition had multiple conflicting ethnographic catalogs and the final redactor preserved all of them.

contradictions.question: Who was the father of Uz, Hul, and Gether?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 10:23 lists Uz, Hul, and Gether as sons of Aram (making them Aram's generation, great-grandsons of Shem). 1 Chronicles 1:17, however, lists the same three names as direct sons of Shem — skipping Aram entirely.
contradictions.commentary: Kidner and Mathews note that 1 Chronicles 1 frequently collapses intermediate generations in its genealogical lists, and this is a widely acknowledged pattern in Chronicles — abbreviated genealogies that skip generations to compress lineage while preserving key nodes. Gary Knoppers' Anchor Bible commentary on 1 Chronicles makes that case at length, and honestly it is the best reading of the Chronicler's technique. The contradiction, if it's one, is mild: Chronicles is not claiming these are biological sons of Shem, he's naming them under Shem's genealogical umbrella. However, the harmonization concedes the key point: 1 Chronicles 1:17 as printed — 'the sons of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram, and Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Meshech' — reads Aram as one item in a list that continues with names that are, per Genesis 10, Aram's children. The flat-list syntax is misleading unless you already know Genesis 10. Some manuscripts of the LXX and the parallel in the MT are textually unstable here, suggesting later scribes noticed the tension. The Chronicler was working from a Genesis 10 tradition and produced a telegraphed list; the result reads as a contradiction at face value even if a sympathetic reader can reconstruct his method.

contradictions.question: How many languages were there before the Tower of Babel was built?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 11:1 declares that 'the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech' before God confounds speech at Babel. Genesis 10:5, 20, 31 — one chapter earlier — already describes the descendants of Noah as divided 'every one after his tongue' in multiple languages.
contradictions.commentary: Walton and Mathews offer the standard narrative-arrangement defense: Genesis 10 is a topical anticipation of the post-Babel diversity, and the events of Genesis 11 are chronologically prior to the linguistic dispersal described in chapter 10. In other words, Genesis 10 is written with hindsight, presenting the nations in their later diversified state, while Genesis 11 flashes back to tell you how they got that way. That ordering is coherent, and it's a common feature of ancient Near Eastern narrative to give a summary outcome before the explanatory flashback. Fine as far as it goes. But the source-critical reading is sharper. Genesis 10 (largely P, with a J insertion in 10:8-19) and the Babel narrative (Gen 11:1-9, J) are independent traditions about national origins that the Priestly compiler placed side-by-side. P's Table of Nations assumes linguistic diversity is a feature of how God structured the post-flood world, while the J narrative of Babel treats linguistic diversity as a punishment for human hubris. These are theologically incompatible origin stories for the same phenomenon. The 'narrative recapitulation' harmonization papers over that deeper conflict. Speiser, Westermann, and Friedman all read the juxtaposition as a classic redactional seam.

contradictions.question: Who was the father of Salah?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 10:24 and 11:12 both have Arphaxad directly fathering Salah. Luke 3:35-36 inserts a generation — 'Salah, which was the son of Cainan, which was the son of Arphaxad' — making Cainan an intermediate ancestor.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest textual-critical contradictions in the whole enterprise. Apologists like Archer and Glenn Morton argue Luke is following the Greek Septuagint, which does include a second Cainan at Gen 10:24 (LXX), and thus Luke's genealogy reflects a legitimate variant textual tradition. That's empirically true — the LXX of Gen 10:24 and 11:12-13 does insert Cainan. The problem is that the name appears to be a scribal expansion in the LXX tradition that has no support in the Masoretic Hebrew, the Samaritan Pentateuch, or the Qumran Genesis fragments. Emanuel Tov's textual-critical work treats the LXX Cainan as a secondary addition designed to harmonize generational counts. So the apologist either has to say (a) Luke faithfully recorded a corrupt Greek text, which means scripture transmits a genealogical error with divine authority, or (b) the MT is itself defective and the LXX preserved the original — which almost no critical textual scholar endorses and which would require rewriting every Hebrew genealogy. Either way, Luke 3:36 is in direct conflict with the Hebrew text of Genesis on a basic paternity question. The LXX defense doesn't eliminate the contradiction, it just moves which Bible contains it.

contradictions.question: How old was Terah when he died?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 11:32 states directly that Terah died in Haran at age 205. But Gen 11:26 says Terah was 70 when Abram was born, Gen 12:4 says Abram left Haran at 75, and Acts 7:4 says Abram only left after his father had died — which would put Terah's death at age 145, not 205.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization, pressed by F. F. Bruce and Darrell Bock, is that Gen 11:26 ('Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran') doesn't mean Abram was born when Terah was 70 — it means Terah began fathering sons at 70, and Abram was actually the youngest, born when Terah was 130. Then when Terah died at 205, Abram was 75 and left Haran, and Acts 7:4 fits. That reconstruction is clever but requires reading a highly specific chronological gloss into a formulaic 'X lived N years and begat Y' template that elsewhere in Genesis does indicate the age at the named son's birth (as in the Shem genealogies of Gen 11:10ff). You can't run the formula one way for the Shem list and a different way for Gen 11:26. More tellingly, the Samaritan Pentateuch actually reads Terah's lifespan as 145 years at Gen 11:32 — a textual variant that looks like an early attempt to fix exactly this contradiction. Emanuel Tov and James VanderKam both treat the Samaritan reading as a harmonizing correction. That's the diagnostic: the text was already generating contradiction-anxiety in antiquity, and the Samaritan scribes tried to patch it. Luke, writing in Greek, knew the traditional reading and went with it — creating a conflict with MT Genesis that apologists have been trying to solve for 1900 years.

contradictions.question: How old was Abraham when Ishmael was born?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 16:16 says plainly that Abraham was 86 when Ishmael was born. But if you stack Gen 11:26 (Terah was 70 when Abram was born), Acts 7:4 (Abram left Haran only after Terah died), and Gen 11:32 (Terah died at 205), then Abram was at least 135 when he left Haran — which would make Ishmael's birth even later than that, not at 86.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction is a downstream consequence of the Terah chronology problem in id=55, and the same harmonization is in play: apologists like Bock argue Gen 11:26's 'Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram' means Terah began his childbearing at 70 rather than that Abram was born when Terah was 70, so the 135-year figure dissolves. If you accept that reading, Gen 16:16's 86 is fine. But the same objection applies: the Shem genealogies in Gen 11:10-26 use the identical formula to give precise birth ages, and there is no principled reason to read it as 'age at first child' only at verse 26. Claus Westermann and Nahum Sarna both note that the formulaic pattern is consistent, and that the anomaly at Gen 11:26 is an artifact of the redactor wanting Abram listed first for theological reasons even if he wasn't the eldest. The Samaritan Pentateuch already adjusted Terah's lifespan to fix this — which tells you the contradiction was real enough to require emergency textual surgery. Acts 7:4 represents the Hellenistic Jewish tradition (Philo also reads Abram leaving Haran after Terah's death) taking the MT at face value and producing the chronology that conflicts with Gen 16:16. The apologetic fix works only by treating Gen 11:26 as uniquely non-literal in a formulaic context where every other instance is literal. That is the definition of ad hoc reasoning.

contradictions.question: Did God call Abraham before or after he moved to Haran?
contradictions.summary: Acts 7:2-3 has Stephen claim God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Haran, and commanded him to leave his country. Genesis 11:31-12:4 has the family settle in Haran first, and then Yahweh speaks to Abram there, issuing the call from Haran — not from Mesopotamia before it.
contradictions.commentary: Bock and Bruce argue that Genesis 15:7 ('I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees') and Nehemiah 9:7 ('Thou art the LORD the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur') both point to an earlier, pre-Haran call that is logically implied but not narrated in Genesis 12. On that reading, Stephen is drawing on a legitimate broader Jewish tradition and Genesis 12 just restates the call. That's a serious argument. Philo, Josephus, and Jubilees all preserve variants of a pre-Haran call, so Stephen isn't inventing it. But the Genesis 12 narrative reads naturally as a call issued at Haran: Terah's family migrates from Ur toward Canaan but settles in Haran, Terah dies there, and then Yahweh speaks to Abram. The narrator gives no indication Abram had already received a command — Genesis 12:1 introduces it as a new divine word, not as a restatement. Fitzmyer and Pervo both treat Stephen's speech as drawing on Hellenistic Jewish traditions (Philo, Jubilees) that smooth the narrative gap left by Genesis, but those traditions are interpretive expansions, not the text of Genesis itself. So the contradiction holds at the level of the Genesis narrative as written — Stephen is harmonizing with extrabiblical Jewish tradition, and his harmonization flattens a real narrative seam.

contradictions.question: Can God be seen?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Habakkuk, Baruch, Matthew, John, Acts, Colossians, 1 Timothy, 1 John
contradictions.summary: The Hebrew Bible repeatedly narrates theophanies in which God is seen face-to-face — by Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, seventy elders, Manoah, Micaiah, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Habakkuk. A parallel stream (Exod 33:20; John 1:18; 1 Tim 6:16; Col 1:15) insists God is invisible and cannot be seen, and that anyone who did see him would die. Scripture affirms both mutually exclusive positions without resolving them.
contradictions.commentary: The dominant harmonization, articulated by Kaiser, Carson, and most systematic theologians, is that the visible theophanies are either angelic mediators, the pre-incarnate Logos, or partial/accommodated manifestations — never the unmediated divine essence. That move was already underway in ancient Judaism: the Targums routinely substitute 'the Memra (Word) of the Lord' for YHWH in theophany scenes, and Philo systematically distinguishes God's essence from his visible powers. But that harmonization is a post-hoc theological grid imposed on texts that don't share it. Genesis 32:30 has Jacob explicitly say 'I have seen God face to face' and name the place Peniel ('face of God'); Exodus 24:10-11 has seventy elders 'see the God of Israel' and eat and drink in his presence without dying; Exodus 33:11 has Yahweh speak to Moses 'face to face, as a man speaketh to his friend.' These narratives are not written as guarded angelophanies — they're written as actual encounters with Yahweh. Mark Smith's The Origins of Biblical Monotheism and Benjamin Sommer's The Bodies of God both document that early Israelite religion assumed Yahweh had a visible form, and that the later invisibility tradition (especially in Deuteronomistic and Johannine theology) represents a theological development. Sommer's argument is specifically that the 'fluidity of divine embodiment' was not felt as a contradiction until later monotheizing theology made it one. The contradiction isn't within a unified theology — it's the archaeological record of a religion whose concept of God changed over a thousand years. Exodus 33:20 and Exodus 33:11 sit in the same chapter and cannot be harmonized into a single stable doctrine of divine visibility.

contradictions.question: When was the city of Dan named?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 14:14 narrates Abraham pursuing raiders 'unto Dan' — during the patriarchal age. Judges 18:29 states that the city was originally named Laish and was only renamed Dan after the Danite conquest of Laish, centuries after Abraham. The city cannot have borne the name 'Dan' during Abraham's lifetime.
contradictions.commentary: This is a textbook example of what biblical scholars call an anachronism — a later editorial insertion of a name that didn't yet exist at the narrative's chronological moment. The standard harmonization, offered by Kitchen and Archer, is that Gen 14:14's 'Dan' is either a scribal updating (a later copyist replacing an obsolete place-name with the then-current one so readers would recognize it) or a reference to a different, earlier Dan unrelated to the later Danite city. The scribal-updating explanation is actually the consensus critical view too — Alexander Rofé, Michael Fishbane, and Emanuel Tov all cite Gen 14:14 as one of the clearest examples of post-compositional onomastic updating in the Torah. That's not a harmonization that rescues inerrancy; it's an admission that the text was edited. Once you grant that later hands modernized place-names, you've conceded that the Pentateuch as we have it is not a verbatim Mosaic composition. Friedman, in Who Wrote the Bible?, uses precisely this kind of anachronism to argue for a post-Mosaic redaction layer. The apologetic move of 'it's just scribal updating' works as an explanation for the phenomenon but undermines the theological framework apologists usually want to preserve. The contradiction stands at the level of the text as a record of the patriarchal age.

contradictions.question: Who owns the earth?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, 1 Chronicles, Psalms, Matthew, Luke, 1 Corinthians
contradictions.summary: A wide set of passages (Gen 14:19, 22; Exod 9:29; 19:5; Deut 10:14; Ps 24:1; 50:12; 89:11; 1 Cor 10:26) affirm that God owns the earth absolutely. Matthew 4:8-9 and Luke 4:5-6 have Satan offer all the kingdoms of the world to Jesus — an offer only meaningful if Satan has them to give. Psalm 115:16 complicates the picture further by saying the earth has been given to 'the children of men.'
contradictions.commentary: This is a three-way contradiction and it's best handled structurally rather than as a binary. On the God-ownership side, the claim is ontological: God is creator and therefore proprietor. Apologists like Walton and Carson argue the Satan passages and Psalm 115 operate at a different register — Satan is the 'god of this age' in the sense of holding usurped influence over a fallen world (2 Cor 4:4), and Psalm 115:16 refers to divinely delegated stewardship, not ownership transfer. On that reading, God retains absolute title while humanity and Satan hold derivative or illegitimate sway. That's coherent systematic theology, but it only works if you accept the later canonical framework of usurpation-and-delegation that develops in intertestamental and New Testament thought. The temptation narrative in Matthew and Luke depends on Satan having real authority to offer — Jesus does not rebuke the offer as illegitimate, he rejects it on worship grounds, which implicitly concedes Satan could deliver. Meanwhile the Hebrew Bible's affirmations of Yahweh's ownership have no counterpart conception of a cosmic rival holding usurped title; that dualism is a Second Temple development visible in Qumran's War Scroll, Enochic literature, and then the Synoptic temptation narratives. John Collins and Paula Fredriksen both trace the evolution from Israelite Yahwism's uncontested divine sovereignty to the late-Second-Temple cosmology where Satan operates as a functional rival. So the contradiction isn't logical — it's developmental. The Bible's theology of who owns the earth changed over time, and the final canon preserves snapshots from multiple stages. Psalm 115:16 is a third data point showing that even within the Yahwist tradition there's a minor human-stewardship theme that sits uneasily with the absolute-ownership claims elsewhere.

contradictions.question: How long was the Egyptian Captivity?
contradictions.summary: The Bible gives three different answers to how long Israel was in Egypt: 400 years in Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6, four generations in Genesis 15:16, and 430 years in Exodus 12:40 and Galatians 3:17. Even inside a single chapter (Genesis 15), the numbers don't line up, and the New Testament inherits the mess.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Gleason Archer and Kenneth Kitchen try to smooth this out by treating 400 as a round number for 430, and by reading "four generations" as a generic label rather than literal fathers-to-sons counting — especially since biblical "generations" can stretch toward a century in patriarchal chronology. That works as arithmetic gymnastics, but it collapses once you track the actual genealogy. Exodus 6:16-20 gives Levi → Kohath → Amram → Moses, which is exactly four generations, and Kohath is already alive going into Egypt (Genesis 46:11), so those four generations have to cover the entire sojourn. That can't stretch to 430 years without handing Amram a lifespan that makes him a patriarch in his own right. Critical scholarship treats Genesis 15:13-16 as a composite text with two independent chronological traditions stitched together, and Exodus 12:40 itself has competing textual witnesses — the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint read the 430 years as covering Canaan AND Egypt, cutting the Egyptian stay roughly in half. Paul in Galatians 3:17 is running on that same tradition, counting 430 years from the promise to Sinai, not from the descent into Egypt. So the "contradiction" isn't a simple numerical slip — it's three overlapping sources with three incompatible chronologies, and the New Testament writers picking whichever one served the argument.

contradictions.question: What are the borders of Israel?
contradictions.summary: The Bible draws the borders of the Promised Land at least three different ways. Genesis 15:18 and Exodus 23:31 stretch from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates; Numbers 34 carves out a much smaller box basically the size of Canaan; and Ezekiel 47 draws a third map with Damascus on the northern edge and the Dead Sea region to the south. These aren't the same territory.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic move — you'll see it in Archer's *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* and Walton's *NIV Application Commentary* — is to call Genesis 15 the "ideal" or "maximal" grant that was briefly realized under David and Solomon, and to treat Numbers 34 as the practical tribal allotment. That's a clean story, except the texts don't present themselves that way. Genesis 15:18 uses the language of an unconditional covenant grant, not an aspirational maximum, and 1 Kings 4:21 only describes a sphere of tribute, not occupation to the Euphrates. Critical scholarship reads these as three different border traditions from three different eras and sources: the Genesis 15 grant reflects a Davidic-era imperial horizon, P's Numbers 34 reflects a post-exilic reconstruction of the "true" Canaan, and Ezekiel 47 is the prophet's programmatic vision for a restored, idealized Israel after the exile. Each text is coherent on its own terms; they just don't describe the same land. Treating them as three snapshots of one covenant grant is a harmonization that flattens the compositional layers. More interesting — none of these borders actually matches what Israel or Judah ever controlled archaeologically, which is a separate problem for the historicity of the promise itself.

contradictions.question: How many sons did Abraham have?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 22:2 calls Isaac Abraham's "only son" — at the moment when Ishmael is already thirteen years old and demonstrably alive, and when Genesis 25 is about to list six more sons by Keturah. So either Abraham has one son, or two, or eight, depending on the page.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization here — Hamilton in NICOT, Mathews in NAC, and Waltke in *Genesis: A Commentary* all run this play — is that "only son" in Genesis 22:2 is shorthand for "only son of the covenant promise," with Ishmael having been formally cut out by Genesis 21 and the Keturah sons chronologically later. That's a coherent theological reading, and the Hebrew *yachid* does get used elsewhere in the sense of "favored" or "unique" (Zech 12:10, Ps 22:20). But it papers over a real tension: Genesis 22:2 piles up the language — "your son, your only son, whom you love, Isaac" — in a way that reads as emphatic *literal* status, not as a covenant qualifier. James Kugel and Joel Baden point out that the Akedah (Genesis 22) in its source-critical layer almost certainly didn't know about the Ishmael material — the story reads as if Isaac is Abraham's singular child, full stop. When the redactor stitched the cycles together, the Ishmael tradition created exactly this kind of surface contradiction. Acts 7:8 and Hebrews 11:17 both inherit the "only son" framing uncritically, which tells you the tension was already baked in by the time Second Temple readers got hold of it. The apologetic reading saves the theology; it doesn't save the arithmetic.

contradictions.question: Is circumcision required?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Genesis, Leviticus, Luke, Acts, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, Colossians
contradictions.summary: Genesis 17 makes circumcision an "everlasting covenant" — every male, slave or free, on the eighth day, no exceptions. Paul in Galatians 5:2-4 says if you get circumcised, "Christ shall profit you nothing" and you are "fallen from grace." One text treats the uncircumcised as covenant-breakers; the other treats the circumcised as grace-losers.
contradictions.commentary: The standard Christian harmonization — you'll find it in Schreiner's BECNT Galatians and Moo's commentary on the same letter — is that circumcision was a provisional sign for the old covenant, fulfilled and superseded in Christ, so the Genesis 17 "everlasting" language gets read as everlasting-within-its-dispensation. That's dispensational theology doing real work. The problem is that the Hebrew *berit olam* in Genesis 17:13 is the same phrase used for the Sabbath (Exod 31:16) and for the Davidic covenant (2 Sam 23:5), and nobody argues those expired. Critical scholarship reads this exactly the way it looks: Paul is an apocalyptic Jewish reformer who decided, on the basis of his Christ experience, that the gentile mission required dropping the ethnic-identity markers — and in doing so he directly contradicted Torah. E. P. Sanders, Paula Fredriksen, and James Dunn have all documented this as a major rupture, not a smooth continuity. Acts 16:3 makes it messier, not cleaner — Paul *does* circumcise Timothy, which either means he pragmatically bent his own rule or Acts is projecting a later, more accommodating Paul backwards. Luke 2:21 is irrelevant to the contradiction; Jesus was circumcised as a Jew under Torah. The real tension is Genesis 17 vs. Galatians 5, and it's not a tension — it's a repudiation.

contradictions.question: Is incest forbidden?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 18 and 20 and Deuteronomy 27 explicitly criminalize sex between half-siblings who share a father — it's called "a wicked thing" and draws a curse. Genesis 20:12 has Abraham calmly explain that Sarah is his half-sister on his father's side and also his wife, and God blesses the marriage in Genesis 17:16. Either the Torah's incest code applies to the patriarchs or it doesn't.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Walton run two different harmonizations here, and they don't combine well. The first move is chronological: the Levitical code hadn't been given yet in Abraham's time, so he wasn't under it. The second move is textual: maybe "sister" in Genesis 20:12 means something looser, like cousin or clanswoman, and Abraham was fudging to protect himself from Pharaoh. Pick one — they pull in opposite directions. The chronological defense concedes the contradiction in principle (Abraham would have been breaking the later law if it applied) and just pushes it behind a dispensational wall. The "loose sister" defense has to explain why Genesis 20:12 goes out of its way to specify "the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother" — that level of precision is the exact half-sister relationship Leviticus 18:9 explicitly forbids. Critical scholarship treats this as obvious: the patriarchal narratives preserve older legal and social norms (sister-wife marriage is attested in ancient Near Eastern royal houses), and the Levitical and Deuteronomic codes reflect later priestly and Deuteronomic systematization. The contradiction is real; the harmonization requires you to both admit and deny that Torah applies to the patriarchs in the same breath.

contradictions.question: Did Sarah have faith that she would conceive?
contradictions.summary: Hebrews 11:11 puts Sarah in the faith hall of fame — "through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive." Genesis 18:10-15 shows Sarah laughing at the promise, getting caught laughing, and then lying about having laughed. Those are not the same Sarah.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like F. F. Bruce and Peter O'Brien's predecessors in Hebrews scholarship (and Cockerill in the current NICNT Hebrews) work hard to rescue Hebrews 11:11 by noting a textual and grammatical tangle: the Greek is awkward enough that some read the verse as actually about *Abraham* receiving power to beget, with Sarah mentioned only as the recipient — which would dodge the contradiction entirely. That's a live exegetical option, and Bruce Metzger's textual commentary flags the issue. But the majority reading, and the one Hebrews' author clearly intended within his broader rhetorical pattern, is that Sarah is the subject of faith in that verse. Under the majority reading, the contradiction is direct: Genesis paints a woman who explicitly disbelieves the promise ("after I am waxed old shall I have pleasure") and then lies to an omniscient God about her reaction. Hebrews retrofits that same woman into an exemplar of faith. Craig Koester and Luke Timothy Johnson both describe this as Hebrews doing midrashic rehabilitation of the patriarchal narratives — a common Second Temple Jewish move where flawed figures get sanitized for homiletic use. The contradiction isn't between two equally literal accounts; it's between a narrative and a later theological reframing that papers over the narrative. That's post-hoc rationalization, not harmonization.

contradictions.question: Can God do anything?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 18:14 asks the rhetorical question "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" — the obvious answer being no. Judges 1:19 then says Yahweh was with Judah and "drave out the inhabitants of the mountain; but could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron." Apparently iron chariots were too hard for the LORD.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic move — Archer pushes this one, and so does the NIV Study Bible footnote — is that the Hebrew in Judges 1:19 is ambiguous about the subject: maybe it was Judah who couldn't drive them out, not Yahweh, and the Lord's presence isn't the agent of the failure. That reading is grammatically defensible. But it runs into a bigger problem: elsewhere the text is perfectly comfortable saying God couldn't deliver on his own side of a battle. Deuteronomy 7 promises God will drive out the Canaanites entirely; Joshua 17:16-18 has Joshua telling Ephraim they'll have trouble precisely because of iron chariots; and Jeremiah 32:17 reaffirms "nothing is too hard for thee." So even if you grant the ambiguous-subject reading of Judges 1:19, the text still has to explain why the outcome — failure to conquer — matches what you'd expect from a limited deity rather than a universal covenant promise. Critical scholars like Mark Smith and Baruch Halpern read these tensions as evidence of Yahweh's evolution from a regional storm/war god with localized power to the later universal deity of Second Isaiah. The "nothing is too hard" rhetoric is the developed theology; the iron-chariot embarrassment is the older, more parochial layer leaking through. The harmonization saves the verse; it doesn't save the theology.

contradictions.question: Was Lot a righteous man?
contradictions.summary: 2 Peter 2:7-8 calls Lot "just" and "righteous" and describes his soul as vexed by the wickedness of Sodom. Genesis 19 shows the same Lot offering his virgin daughters to a rape mob and later getting drunk enough on two consecutive nights to impregnate both of them. The narrative and the endorsement don't line up.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Peter H. Davids (in the PNTC 2 Peter, which is not the withdrawn O'Brien volume) argue that 2 Peter 2 is drawing a *relative* contrast — Lot was righteous compared to the people of Sodom, not righteous in any absolute sense. That's a fair grammatical reading of the Greek *dikaios*, and it matches how Second Temple Jewish retellings (Wisdom of Solomon 10:6, Philo, Josephus) were already rehabilitating Lot's reputation before 2 Peter came along. So the harmonization works as a descriptive claim — yes, ancient readers made this move. But that's exactly the critical point: 2 Peter isn't reading Genesis 19 straight, it's inheriting a reception-history where Lot got progressively scrubbed. Genesis itself doesn't call Lot righteous. Genesis shows a man who prioritizes his male guests over his daughters' bodily safety and then passes out drunk enough to commit incest twice in a row without noticing. James Kugel catalogs the Second Temple rehabilitation machinery in detail — the same move gets run on Noah, on Jacob, on Judah. The contradiction here isn't between Genesis and 2 Peter arbitrarily; it's between what Genesis actually narrates and what later Jewish and Christian tradition needed to say about the patriarchs. Call it what it is: theological retcon.

contradictions.question: Who destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 19:13 has the two angels telling Lot, "we will destroy this place ... the LORD hath sent us to destroy it." Eleven verses later, Genesis 19:24 says "the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven." So the agent is either the angels, or Yahweh directly, or somehow both — and the text doesn't pick one.
contradictions.commentary: This one is the mildest contradiction in the batch, and honest apologists handle it easily: the standard harmonization is that the angels are God's agents, so Yahweh destroying the cities *through* the angels and Yahweh destroying them directly amount to the same act. Hamilton and Wenham both frame it that way in their Genesis commentaries. That's fine as a theological reading. The more interesting critical question is what Genesis 19:24 is actually saying with that odd doubled construction — "the LORD rained ... from the LORD out of heaven." Some rabbinic and patristic readers treated that as evidence of two divine figures, which later Christian apologists like Justin Martyr used for proto-trinitarian arguments. Critical scholars like Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer read it as a relic of older West Semitic theology where multiple manifestations of a deity could be referenced distinctly — the "fluidity of selfhood" Sommer documents in *The Bodies of God*. So the surface contradiction (angels vs. God) dissolves into agency language, but the verse underneath preserves something weirder and older than monotheism would strictly allow. That is of course a subjective opinion on which layer is doing the real work in the verse.

contradictions.question: How many generations from Abraham to Moses?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 15:16 promises Abraham's descendants will return to Canaan "in the fourth generation." But when you actually trace the genealogy Genesis and Exodus give — Abraham → Isaac → Jacob → Levi → Kohath → Amram → Moses — you get six or seven generations depending on how you count, not four.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Archer handle this by treating "generation" (Hebrew *dor*) as a long temporal unit rather than a single father-to-son step — one *dor* could be a century, they argue, so four *dorot* equals the 400 years of Genesis 15:13. That's linguistically defensible; *dor* does have semantic range. The problem is that Exodus itself seems to count the generations literally. Exodus 6:16-20 gives the Levi-Kohath-Amram-Moses chain — that's explicitly four steps from Levi (who went INTO Egypt per Gen 46:11) to Moses (who came out). So the "fourth generation" of Genesis 15:16 either matches the Levi-to-Moses count (four) or the Abraham-to-Moses count (six or seven), but you can't have it both ways with the chronology of Exodus 12:40's 430 years attached. Joel Baden and Richard Elliott Friedman both read this as a classic Documentary Hypothesis seam — the "four generations" tradition comes from one source stratum, the 400/430 year tradition from another, and the genealogical material in Exodus 6 is P's attempt to make it all fit. The numbers don't line up because they were never a unified chronology to begin with. The "dor means century" move is a rescue operation that requires ignoring what Exodus 6 is actually doing.

contradictions.question: How old was Ishmael when he was abandoned by Abraham?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 21:14-18 describes Hagar carrying Ishmael on her shoulder, laying "the child" under a shrub, and being told to lift up "the lad" — infant language. But Genesis 17:24-25 plus Genesis 21:5-9 has Ishmael at thirteen when circumcised and Isaac weaned (age 2-3) before the abandonment scene, which puts Ishmael somewhere between 14 and 17 years old. A teenager doesn't ride on the shoulder.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Mathews in NAC and Hamilton in NICOT try to resolve this by retranslating Genesis 21:14: the Hebrew may be saying Abraham placed the bread and water on Hagar's shoulder, and *then separately* gave her the child — not that the child was on her shoulder. That's grammatically plausible; the Masoretic syntax is ambiguous enough to allow it, and NRSV and NIV both render it that way. Fair enough. But that rescue only handles the shoulder detail. It doesn't explain why Hagar "casts" Ishmael under a bush (21:15), why the narrative keeps calling him *yeled* ("child") and treating him as physically helpless while Hagar weeps over him, or why the angel tells Hagar to "lift up the lad" — all language that reads naturally for a toddler and awkwardly for a mid-teen. Critical scholars like Baden, Friedman, and Westermann read Genesis 21 as coming from E, while the chronological markers in Genesis 17 and 21:5 come from P. The two sources had different pictures of Ishmael's age at this moment and the redactor didn't smooth them out. The harmonization works at the level of individual words; it doesn't work at the level of the scene's whole texture.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to swear?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 6:13, Isaiah 65:16, and Jeremiah 4:2 and 12:16 all positively command swearing by Yahweh's name. Matthew 5:34-37 has Jesus saying "swear not at all" — no heaven, no earth, just yes-yes and no-no, and anything more "cometh of evil." Torah makes oaths by God's name an act of covenantal loyalty; Jesus makes them a moral problem.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic — D. A. Carson runs this in his Matthew commentary, and Craig Blomberg takes the same line — is that Jesus isn't abolishing oaths per se, he's forbidding the casuistic abuse of oaths that first-century Jewish legal culture had developed, where you could swear by "Jerusalem" or "your head" to sound binding without actually being legally bound. Matthew 23:16-22 supports this reading: Jesus condemns the "you swear by the temple, it's nothing, but swear by the gold of the temple, you're bound" system. Fair. But the Sermon on the Mount formula is categorical — "swear not at all" — and the Epistle of James 5:12 repeats it just as categorically. Early Christian groups (the Anabaptists, the Quakers) read this as a straight prohibition for centuries, and they weren't wrong about the plain sense. Dale Allison and W. D. Davies in their ICC Matthew argue Jesus is radicalizing Torah here in the same pattern as the other antitheses in Matthew 5 — taking a Torah allowance (oaths by the Name) and canceling it under the inbreaking kingdom. That's a genuine contradiction with Deuteronomy 6:13, not a casuistic footnote. The harmonization works if you allow Jesus to be selectively overriding Torah; it just doesn't work if you need the Old Testament and Jesus to be saying the same thing.

contradictions.question: Has God ever tempted anyone?
contradictions.summary: James 1:13 draws a hard line: "God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man." Genesis 22:1 opens the Akedah by saying "God did tempt Abraham" and tells him to sacrifice Isaac. The KJV translates the same Hebrew and Greek roots consistently, which is why this reads as a contradiction in English.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Archer, Wenham, and Douglas Moo in his James commentary resolve this through translation: the Hebrew verb *nissah* in Genesis 22:1 means "test" or "prove," not "tempt" in the James 1:13 sense of luring toward evil. Modern translations (NIV, NRSV, ESV) render Genesis 22:1 as "tested" precisely to dodge the semantic collision. That's a legitimate philological point — *nissah* and the Greek *peirazō* in James 1:13 overlap but aren't identical, and James is clearly talking about enticement toward sin, while Genesis 22 is a loyalty test. So in modern translation the contradiction softens. BUT — and this is the critical wrinkle — the KJV reading isn't wrong, it's just old. The underlying theological problem doesn't go away: whether you call it "testing" or "tempting," God is in Genesis 22 deliberately commanding Abraham to commit what Torah elsewhere defines as abomination (human sacrifice, Lev 18:21, Deut 12:31). James 1:13 says God "cannot be tempted with evil" — but Genesis 22 has God commanding evil as a loyalty check. Jon Levenson's *The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son* digs into how uncomfortable this made ancient interpreters, who went to enormous lengths (LXX renderings, Jubilees 17-18 blaming Mastema/Satan for the prompt) to get God out of directly initiating the test. The translation fix saves the verses; it doesn't save the theological problem.

contradictions.question: Does God approve of human sacrifice?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 18:21, Deuteronomy 12:31, and 2 Kings 21:6 condemn making your child pass through the fire as abomination. Genesis 22:2 has Yahweh himself commanding Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on a mountain. Torah says human sacrifice is what the nations do that Yahweh hates; Genesis has Yahweh ordering it.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic move — Walton, Archer, and Copan in *Is God a Moral Monster?* all run this one — is that the Akedah is a test God never intended to let go through; the ram is provided, Isaac lives, and the episode actually functions as a *polemic against* human sacrifice, demonstrating that Yahweh is different from the Molech-worshipers because he stops the knife. That's a real reading and it's theologically useful. But it's not watertight. First, the command itself is unambiguous — "offer him there for a burnt offering" — and Abraham's willingness, not his refusal, is what the text praises. Second, Jephthah's daughter in Judges 11 gets actually sacrificed with no narrative condemnation and with the text straightforwardly reporting that Jephthah "did with her according to his vow." Third, critical scholars like Jon Levenson and Francesca Stavrakopoulou have documented substantial evidence that child sacrifice was practiced in pre-exilic Israelite religion (the *molek* offerings, the Hinnom valley cult), and that the Torah's repeated prohibitions are polemics against a practice that was demonstrably internal to Israel, not just foreign. Ezekiel 20:25-26 even has Yahweh admitting to giving Israel "statutes that were not good" involving the offering of firstborns as a punishment. The Akedah either sits awkwardly with that history or reflects an earlier theological layer where the question of whether Yahweh wanted human sacrifice wasn't as settled as Leviticus wants it to be. Take your pick; neither option lets the apologetic "polemic against sacrifice" reading stand unchallenged.

contradictions.question: Was Keturah Abraham's wife or concubine?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 25:1 says "then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah." 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her "Abraham's concubine." In biblical Hebrew those are two different legal statuses, and the Chronicler is demoting what Genesis promoted.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Mathews typically handle this by noting that ancient Hebrew status terminology isn't as rigid as modern legal categories — a *pilegesh* (concubine) could be a secondary wife with limited inheritance rights, and the same woman could be called both "wife" (*ishshah*) and "concubine" depending on context and genealogical purpose. Genesis 25:6 actually speaks of Abraham's "concubines" in the plural when sending away the sons of Keturah with gifts, while keeping Isaac as the heir, so even Genesis itself flickers on her status. That softens the contradiction. But the critical point Sara Japhet makes in her I & II Chronicles commentary is that the Chronicler is doing *deliberate* editorial work on the patriarchal genealogies — cleaning up lineage status, consolidating tribes, making succession lines explicit. Calling Keturah a concubine rather than a wife is part of the Chronicler's systematic move to elevate Isaac's Sarah-descent as the exclusive legitimate line and downgrade Abraham's other wives and their sons to lower-status branches. So the "contradiction" is real at the lexical level, and it's not an accident. It's the Chronicler rewriting the Genesis record to match a later theological hierarchy. That's a small contradiction with a big implication about how scripture edits itself.

contradictions.question: What is the human life span?
contradictions.summary: Psalm 90:10 puts the human lifespan at seventy years. Genesis 6:3 has Yahweh cap it at 120 years. The patriarchal genealogies then list people who live 950 (Noah), 600 (Shem), 464 (Eber), and 175 (Abraham) — blowing past both numbers by orders of magnitude. The Bible gives you three incompatible answers.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists handle this three different ways depending on which tradition they're defending. Young-earth creationists like Henry Morris argue the antediluvian lifespans were literal and the post-flood drop reflects environmental collapse (the vapor canopy theory — which has no scientific support). Archer and Walton take the softer line: the Genesis 6:3 "120 years" is a promise of impending judgment (the flood comes in 120 years), not a cap on human lifespan, and Psalm 90:10 is poetic observation, not a decree. That's a coherent reading of Genesis 6:3 in context, and it's probably the best apologetic option. But it still leaves the core issue that the patriarchal numbers sit in their own chronological universe. Critical scholarship — John Walton's own *Ancient Near Eastern Thought* included — recognizes the Genesis 5 and 11 lifespan lists as stylized, theologically freighted numbers paralleling the Sumerian King List, where antediluvian kings reigned tens of thousands of years before the numbers shrink post-flood. They're doing genre work, not biology. Psalm 90 is doing something else — wisdom literature reflecting on human finitude. The "contradiction" is real when you treat all three as modern-style factual claims about the same topic; it dissolves when you recognize they're three different genres doing three different rhetorical jobs. But that recognition is itself a concession that the Bible doesn't speak univocally on human lifespan.

contradictions.question: Will there be many Jews?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 22:17-18 and 26:4 promise Abraham's and Isaac's descendants will be as numerous as the stars of heaven and the sand on the shore. Deuteronomy 4:23-27 threatens that if they make a graven image, Yahweh will scatter them and leave them "few in number among the heathen." One promise is unconditional multiplication; the other is conditional reduction.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic move here is straightforward and pretty solid: the two verses operate at different covenant levels. Genesis 22 is the Abrahamic covenant, which scripture treats as unconditional; Deuteronomy 4 is the Mosaic covenant, which is explicitly conditional on obedience. Paul even makes this distinction load-bearing in Galatians 3. That's a coherent distinction and it holds. But the critical question is whether the two covenants really sit together the way the apologetic framework claims. Deuteronomy 4:31 immediately pulls back from the scattering threat by invoking the Abrahamic covenant ("he will not forget the covenant of thy fathers"), which means the Deuteronomist himself thought the two promises needed reconciliation — and he did it by having the Abrahamic one eventually override the Mosaic threat. That's not a clean two-covenant system; that's a post-exilic theologian trying to explain why the exile happened while preserving the "many descendants" promise. Critical scholars like Moshe Weinfeld and Bernard Levinson read Deuteronomy as a deliberate revision of earlier covenant theology — updating the unconditional patriarchal promises to include conditional threats as a response to the actual historical catastrophe of the northern kingdom's fall. So the "contradiction" is also a record of theology evolving in real time to handle real events. Calling it a simple two-covenant system papers over what the text is doing historically.

contradictions.question: Who named Beersheba?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 21:31 has Abraham naming Beersheba after his well-treaty with Abimelech. Genesis 26:33 has Isaac naming the same place, after his own well-treaty with a Philistine king also named Abimelech, with the narrator noting "therefore the name of the city is Beersheba unto this day" — as if the name originated there.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Hamilton and Waltke handle this with the "re-naming" or "re-digging" solution: both Abraham and Isaac had well disputes with Abimelech at the same site, Isaac's wells were re-dug over his father's (explicit in Gen 26:18), and he re-applied the existing name in a commemorative ceremony. That's workable as narrative logic. But it doesn't handle the problem that both accounts use "therefore" / etiological-origin language — each text presents itself as the *first* explanation for the name. And the two stories are suspiciously parallel beyond the naming: Abraham pretends Sarah is his sister to Abimelech (Gen 20), Isaac pretends Rebekah is his sister to Abimelech (Gen 26), both cut a treaty at Beersheba with officials named Phicol, both dig or claim wells. Critical scholarship — Gunkel long ago, and more recently Friedman, Baden, and Ronald Hendel — reads these as two variants of a single traditional legend attached to both patriarchs independently in the oral tradition and then preserved as two separate narratives when the sources were written down and combined. That's the classic "doublet" phenomenon. Treating them as two distinct historical events at the same spot with the same kind of king is possible, but the odds of that much coincidence are what the Documentary Hypothesis was designed to explain. The harmonization technically works; it just costs more than the source-critical explanation.

contradictions.question: Who was Laban's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 28:5 explicitly identifies Laban as "the son of Bethuel the Syrian." Genesis 29:5 has Jacob asking shepherds, "Know ye Laban the son of Nahor?" Bethuel and Nahor are not the same person — Nahor is Bethuel's father and Laban's grandfather in Genesis 22:20-23.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists like Archer and Mathews handle this with the ancient Near Eastern "son of" convention: *ben* in Hebrew can mean son, grandson, or descendant generally, and Genesis 29:5's "son of Nahor" just means Laban belongs to the Nahorite family line, with Nahor as the identifiable clan patriarch. That's philologically defensible — Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus "son of David, son of Abraham" in exactly the same extended sense. The apologetic reading works. What it doesn't quite handle is why the narrator switches conventions between Genesis 28:5 (strict biological "son of Bethuel") and Genesis 29:5 (loose genealogical "son of Nahor") within the space of a few verses, with no narrative signal that a different sense is in play. Critical scholars like Friedman and Westermann note that this is one of many small signs of source-combination in the Jacob cycle: the patriarchal narratives preserve multiple oral traditions about the same figures, and the grandfather-vs-father variation reflects genuinely different genealogical traditions rather than a consistent use of "son" as "descendant." So the apologetic explanation is live — "son of" really can mean descendant — it just has to assume the narrator is inconsistent within a single pericope for no rhetorical reason. The source-critical explanation accounts for the inconsistency without requiring that assumption. Parsimony favors the latter.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to marry your wife's sister, while your wife is still alive?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 29:24-28 has Jacob married to Leah and Rachel simultaneously, and the narrative treats it as legitimate — these two sister-wives become the mothers of the twelve tribes. Leviticus 18:18 explicitly forbids marrying "a wife to her sister" during her lifetime. Either the foundational marriage of the nation was Torah-illegal, or Torah is retroactively criminalizing patriarchal practice.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic — Archer, Wenham, Mathews — runs the chronological rescue: the Leviticus prohibition hadn't been given yet in Jacob's time, so he wasn't bound by it, and Laban's deception adds a special-case wrinkle since Jacob was tricked into the first marriage. That handles the legal-technical question. But there's a deeper issue. The Karaite Jewish tradition, and some modern Jewish scholars like Adele Berlin, have argued that Leviticus 18:18 was written *precisely* with the Jacob-Leah-Rachel marriage in mind — as a post-facto critique of the patriarchal practice, telling later Israelites "don't do what Jacob did." Under that reading, the Levitical author is consciously legislating against a story the priestly tradition had received from the patriarchal narratives. Calum Carmichael's *Law and Narrative in the Bible* argues this across multiple Levitical prohibitions: they're responses to specific bad-behavior narratives in Genesis. That reading makes the "contradiction" the point of Leviticus — a deliberate course correction on patriarchal precedent, not an oversight. Either way, the apologetic "Torah hadn't been given yet" move concedes that if Torah had been given, Jacob would have been breaking it, which is the whole tension. And it doesn't explain why the Genesis narrator shows zero awareness that the arrangement is problematic — Jacob's only complaint is being tricked, not being in a forbidden union.

contradictions.question: Is it always wrong to steal?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Matthew, Mark, Luke, Romans, Ephesians, 1 Thessalonians
contradictions.summary: The Decalogue and its echoes across the Torah, Gospels, and Epistles absolutize the prohibition on stealing, yet Genesis 31:19 reports without condemnation that Rachel stole her father's household gods on her way out of Laban's territory. The law says never; the narrative says sometimes you get away with it.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist move here is predictable — Archer and Kaiser will tell you Rachel's theft isn't approved, it's merely reported, and that descriptive passages don't overturn prescriptive ones. Fine, that's a real distinction. But the narrator of Genesis 31 never censures Rachel, never has Yahweh punish her, and in fact lets her clever deception (sitting on the teraphim while menstruating) carry the scene as a kind of trickster victory. That's not neutral reportage. The Jacob cycle is saturated with sanctioned trickery — Jacob stealing Esau's blessing, Jacob outmaneuvering Laban's flocks — and the text treats these episodes as covenant-aligned rather than covenant-violating. Friedman and Alter both read the ancestral narratives as working from a different moral grammar than the Sinai code: the patriarchs are shrewd operators whose victories get ratified by Yahweh regardless of the means. Layer Exodus 1 on top — the Hebrew midwives lie to Pharaoh and God "deals well with them" — and you have a Hebrew Bible that treats absolute moral commands and narrative ethics as running on different tracks. The contradiction isn't that someone broke a rule; it's that the text doesn't seem to notice a rule was broken.

contradictions.question: Who did Jacob wrestle with?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 32 has Jacob wrestling "a man" at the Jabbok, after which Jacob insists he has "seen God face to face" and names the place Peniel. Hosea 12:4 reaches back to the same episode and calls the opponent an angel. Man, God, or angel — the tradition couldn't make up its mind.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization is that "angel of Yahweh" functions as a circumlocution for God himself, so "angel" and "God" are two names for one encounter. Walton and Hamilton both push this line. It's not crazy — angelophanies and theophanies do blur in the Hebrew Bible. But the tradition history here is messier than the harmonization admits. Benjamin Sommer has mapped the mal'akh YHWH across the Hebrew Bible and argued it reflects a "fluidity model" in which the angel is a small-scale embodiment of Yahweh himself — which salvages the harmonization at one level but concedes the text is operating with a notion of divine multiplicity that later monotheism had to work hard to domesticate. Hosea 12 shows that domestication already underway: the Jabbok story in its Genesis form has Jacob grappling with a divine being close enough to touch and strong enough to dislocate his hip, and Jacob names the place "face of God." By Hosea's time the opponent is named an angel. Friedman reads Genesis 32 as J material preserving an older, more physical conception of the deity that Hosea's Ephraimite tradition was actively reworking. The contradiction isn't a narrator slipping up — it's a fossil record of Israel's evolving discomfort with a God who could lose a wrestling match until sunrise.

contradictions.question: When did Jacob rename Luz to Bethel?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 28 has Jacob naming Luz "Bethel" on his way out of Canaan, before he ever meets Rachel. Genesis 35 has God telling him to rename the same place Bethel after he's come back from Paddan-Aram with a full household — "And Jacob called the name of the place where God spake with him, Bethel." Same town, same name, two different founding moments.
contradictions.commentary: The traditional fix, pressed by Kidner and Mathews, is that Genesis 35 is a re-dedication rather than an original naming — Jacob is simply ratifying the name he already gave the place in chapter 28. The text strains against that reading. Genesis 35:15 uses the same naming formula ("wa-yiqra" plus the place name) that Genesis 28:19 used, with no hint that this is a commemoration of a previous act. The Documentary Hypothesis explanation is cleaner: Friedman, Baden, and Carr all assign Genesis 28 and Genesis 35 to different source strands (typically E in 28, with 35 showing Elohist and Priestly material layered together), each of which preserved an independent tradition about how Bethel got its name. The redactor who stitched Genesis together didn't bother reconciling them because the cult site at Bethel was foundational to both traditions and each source claimed the etiology. This is the same pattern you see with the double naming of Israel (Gen 32 vs. Gen 35), the double covenant with Abraham, and the double promise to Hagar. The contradiction isn't that Jacob forgot he already named it — it's that two separate storytellers each gave Bethel its origin story, and both made it into the final text.

contradictions.question: Who was Bashemath's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 26:34 names Esau's wife Bashemath as the daughter of Elon the Hittite. Genesis 36:2-3 names Esau's wife Bashemath as the daughter of Ishmael. Same Esau, same wife-name, two incompatible fathers-in-law.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist workaround — Archer runs it, so does Kaiser — is that Esau had multiple wives and Bashemath was simply a common name, so Genesis 26 and Genesis 36 are talking about two different women who happened to share it. The problem is that Genesis 36:3 also lists "Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite" as Esau's wife, whereas Genesis 26:34 named that same daughter-of-Elon as Bashemath. The names have been swapped between the two passages, not just duplicated. Sarna and Westermann both treat this as a clear case of conflicting wife-lists preserved in different ancestral traditions. The Priestly genealogist in Genesis 36 was working from a different source than the J/E material in Genesis 26, and the editor who combined them didn't iron out the names. Friedman's source-critical breakdown shows Genesis 36 as largely Priestly toledot material organizing Edomite lineage for a post-exilic audience, whereas Genesis 26:34 sits in an older narrative stratum. Trying to rescue both lists as historically accurate requires positing that Esau had a confusingly redundant naming practice where wives got renamed every few chapters. That's not harmonization — that's damage control.

contradictions.question: Who was Anah?
contradictions.summary: Three statements inside Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles can't all be true of the same person: Anah is Zibeon's daughter (Gen 36:2, 14), Anah is Seir's son and Zibeon's brother (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38), and Anah is Zibeon's son (Gen 36:24; 1 Chr 1:40). The Edomite genealogy preserves three mutually exclusive identities for Anah.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonizing tradition — Keil and Delitzsch, later picked up by Archer — runs a "two-Anahs" play: there's Anah-the-Hivite-woman (Esau's mother-in-law) and Anah-the-Horite-man (Seir's son), and the repetition is just the genealogist tracking different people with the same name. Fine as far as it goes, but it doesn't resolve the Genesis 36:24 problem, where Anah is "son of Zibeon" and Zibeon is the one who found hot springs — and that's immediately adjacent to Gen 36:20, where the same Anah is Zibeon's brother. Westermann and Sarna both treat Genesis 36 as a patchwork of Edomite king lists and clan genealogies assembled from multiple sources, each using "Anah" slightly differently. The Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch both try to smooth Genesis 36:2 by reading "son of Zibeon" instead of "daughter," which is exactly what a scribe would do if the contradiction was already showing in the received text. Textual critics like Tov treat this as evidence of early scribal discomfort with the passage. The apologist position requires you to assume a genealogist who repeatedly reused the same name in the same chapter without clarifying which Anah he meant. The critical reading is simpler: the compiler had incompatible source traditions and preserved them all.
