contradictions.question: Who was Korah's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 36:5, 14, and 18 all make Korah a son of Esau by Aholibamah. Genesis 36:15-16 just a few verses later lists Korah as one of the clan-chiefs ("dukes") descended from Eliphaz, who was Esau's firstborn — making Korah Esau's grandson, not son.
contradictions.commentary: The favorite apologist escape here — run by Archer and by various evangelical study Bibles — is that there are simply two different Korahs, one an Esau-son and one an Eliphaz-son, and the genealogist just tracked both. This is possible but thin: Genesis 36:16 reads awkwardly in the Masoretic Text precisely because "duke Korah" is parenthetically inserted into the Eliphaz line, and the Samaritan Pentateuch along with some LXX witnesses drops it. Tov treats this kind of localized disagreement as evidence of a scribal gloss — somebody early in the transmission added Korah to the Eliphaz list to match a different tradition, and the Masoretic Text preserved the gloss. Friedman's source analysis places the Esau toledot as Priestly material that incorporated Edomite king-list traditions from multiple hands, and the duplications are exactly what you'd expect when multiple sources are spliced without full harmonization. The text-critical picture is clearer than the "two Korahs" gambit admits: the contradiction has been visible since antiquity, the manuscripts disagree, and the smoothest reading is that a scribe inserted Korah where he didn't originally belong.

contradictions.question: Who was Dishon's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 36:20-21 and 1 Chronicles 1:38 list Dishon as one of Seir's sons, making Seir the father. A few verses later, Genesis 36:24-25 and 1 Chronicles 1:40-41 say Dishon is Anah's son — and since Anah is Seir's son in 36:20, that makes Dishon Seir's grandson, not son.
contradictions.commentary: This is the same pattern as the Korah contradiction and the apologist response is the same — Keil, Delitzsch, Archer all argue for two different Dishons in the Horite genealogy. The problem is that the Seir genealogy in Genesis 36:20-30 lists only one Dishon (verse 21) and one Dishan, and when it expands the Anah line in verse 25 it names Dishon again without any indication that this is a different person. The repetition with the Aholibamah line ("Anah's daughter Aholibamah") makes the identity explicit — it's the same Anah, therefore the same Dishon. Westermann and Sarna both treat the Horite list as an independent tribal genealogy that the Priestly compiler spliced into the Esau toledot, and the splice produced generational inconsistencies the editor didn't smooth. Friedman's source-critical work on the Esau material shows the same pattern across Genesis 36: two competing systems of organizing the Edomite/Horite clans, combined without harmonization. The "two Dishons" defense requires assuming the genealogist gave identical fathers and sisters to two separate men and never noted it. The critical reading — compiled from incompatible sources — explains the doubling without the acrobatics.

contradictions.question: Who brought Joseph into Egypt?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 37:28 says the Midianite merchants drew Joseph out of the pit, sold him to the Ishmaelites, and the Ishmaelites brought him to Egypt — a position Genesis 39:1 reinforces. Genesis 37:36, in the very same chapter, says "the Midianites sold him into Egypt." The narrative can't decide which caravan delivered Joseph.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization treats "Midianite" and "Ishmaelite" as overlapping ethnonyms — Judges 8:24 does link the two groups — so Keil, Archer, and Mathews all argue it's one caravan being described two ways. That's not nothing. But Friedman, Baden, and Carr all see this as one of the cleanest fingerprints of source-critical seams in Genesis: the J source has Judah proposing to sell Joseph to Ishmaelites who then carry him to Egypt, while the E source has Reuben wanting to rescue Joseph and Midianite traders pulling him out of the pit unbeknownst to the brothers. The redactor wove them together and produced Genesis 37 as we have it, where Joseph gets "sold" multiple times to different groups in the same paragraph. Speiser's Anchor Bible commentary on Genesis made this case decades ago and the critical consensus has barely moved since. The "overlapping ethnonym" answer doesn't explain why Genesis 37:28 has the Midianites drawing Joseph out and selling him to the Ishmaelites — they're clearly two distinct groups in that verse. Reuben never finds out in the E source, and the brothers' subsequent lie to Jacob makes more sense if they sold Joseph rather than had him stolen. The doublet is the data; the sources are the explanation.

contradictions.question: Where did Joseph's brothers find the missing money?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 42:27 says one brother opened his sack at the lodging place ("the inn") and found the returned money right there. Genesis 43:21 has Judah retelling the story and saying all the brothers found their money at the inn. But Genesis 42:35 shows them emptying their sacks at home in Canaan and being terrified when every bundle of money appears. Money discovery at two different locations.
contradictions.commentary: Keil, Delitzsch, and Archer argue the simplest harmonization: one brother found his money at the inn (42:27), they all got home, emptied the sacks, and discovered the rest (42:35). The retelling in 43:21 collapses the stages. That's plausible on a charitable reading — but it can't be that simple, because Genesis 42:28 has all the brothers reacting with fear to the discovery at the inn ("their heart failed them, and they were afraid"), implying they all knew at the inn. Then they're shown freshly afraid in 42:35 at home, as if discovering it for the first time. Speiser's Anchor commentary and Friedman's source-critical breakdown both treat this as another Joseph-narrative doublet, with J and E each having their own version of the money-discovery scene and the redactor preserving both. In the Yahwist telling, discovery happens at the inn; in the Elohist, discovery happens at home. Stitched together, the brothers seem to discover the same money twice and react to it as a fresh shock each time. The harmonization works only if you accept that the narrative accidentally records the same reaction twice — which is exactly what happens when two sources are combined without full smoothing.

contradictions.question: How old was Benjamin when his clan migrated to Egypt?
contradictions.summary: Judah tells Joseph in Genesis 44:20 that Benjamin is "a little one," "a child of his old age" who "cannot leave his father." Two chapters later, Genesis 46:21 lists Benjamin as the father of ten sons among those who went down to Egypt. Infant on one page, patriarch-of-ten on the next.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist solution — Archer, Sailhamer, Mathews — is that "little one" (na'ar / yeled) is used flexibly in Hebrew and Judah is just emphasizing Benjamin's status as the youngest, not his literal age. That works up to a point. Na'ar does have semantic range. But the contradiction isn't only about the word — it's about the whole scene in Genesis 44 being built on Benjamin being young, fragile, and irreplaceable. Judah's entire speech assumes a child who would die away from home. Now do the chronology: Joseph is 17 when sold (Gen 37:2), 30 when he interprets Pharaoh's dream (41:46), and roughly 39 when the family migrates (seven good years plus two famine years). Benjamin is younger but not by much — probably mid-to-late twenties at the migration, already old enough to have fathered the ten sons Genesis 46 attributes to him. The numbers make Judah's "he is but a little one" speech narratively effective but chronologically implausible. Westermann and Speiser both treat the tension as a narrative-source issue: the Joseph novella preserves its own internal chronology emphasizing Benjamin's youth, while the Priestly genealogy in Genesis 46 is working from a different list with ten pre-migration sons. Combining them produces a Benjamin who can't possibly be both.

contradictions.question: Was Mahli the son of Levi?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 8:18 calls Mahli "the son of Levi, the son of Israel" — a direct father-son claim. But every Torah and Chronicles list of Levi's sons (Gen 46:11; Exod 6:16; 1 Chr 6:1, 16; 23:6) names only Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Mahli isn't Levi's son; he's Merari's son (Exod 6:19), making him Levi's grandson.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonizing fix — offered in Keil-Delitzsch and by Archer — is to read "son of Levi" loosely as "descendant of Levi," which Hebrew ben regularly does. Fair. Ben can mean descendant across several generations, and that usage is well-attested. The issue is that Ezra 8:18 isn't just giving a loose tribal affiliation — it's a genealogical chain: "Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel." In that formula, each link is a direct generation elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible. Compare the Levitical genealogies in 1 Chronicles 6, which carefully preserve the three-generation structure Levi → Merari → Mahli. Williamson's commentary on Ezra and Blenkinsopp's both read Ezra 8:18 as a telescoping genealogy in the Chronicler's style — skipping Merari and treating Mahli as representative of the Merarite clan. That's a real scribal convention. But calling it a "convention" doesn't erase that the chain as written is historically incorrect. Telescoping genealogies were a flexible ancient Near Eastern device specifically because writers felt free to compress the record — the existence of the convention is itself evidence that genealogies in the Hebrew Bible shouldn't be taken as literal father-son successions. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but the harmonization concedes the critical point while insisting no contradiction exists.

contradictions.question: How many descendants of Jacob and Leah went to Egypt with Jacob?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 46:9-15a enumerates 32 Leah-descendants by name — Reuben and his four sons, Simeon and his six sons, Levi and his three sons, Judah plus his sons and two grandsons, Issachar and his four sons, Zebulun and his three sons, plus Dinah. That's 32. Genesis 46:15b then totals them at 33.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist answer — Archer's, and you see it in Keil-Delitzsch — is that the count includes Jacob himself, or Leah, or some other extra person the enumerator quietly added. The LXX preserves "thirty-three" and various commentators have juggled whether Dinah counts once or twice, whether Er and Onan (who died in Canaan) belong in the tally, or whether Jacob is implicitly included. Speiser and Westermann both treat the numerical mismatches in Genesis 46 as classic Priestly genealogical arithmetic that doesn't actually add up — the numbers were rounded or symbolic, not computed. The broader pattern confirms this: Genesis 46 totals 70 persons entering Egypt, the Septuagint and Acts 7:14 total 75, and the Masoretic 46:26 gives 66. These numbers all fail to cohere with each other in any arithmetic sense. Friedman treats the 70-count as schematic — it matches the 70 nations of Genesis 10 — rather than literal. The off-by-one in Genesis 46:15 is a small instance of a larger pattern: Priestly genealogies are built for theological symmetry, not arithmetic accuracy. The harmonizations that rescue each individual discrepancy end up conceding that the text wasn't trying to pass a counting test in the first place.

contradictions.question: Will God destroy those that intermarry?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 7:3-4 bans intermarriage with the Canaanite nations on pain of God's anger destroying the offender "suddenly." Genesis 46:20 records Joseph's marriage to Asenath, the daughter of Potipherah, priest of the Egyptian sun-god at On/Heliopolis — a foreign priestess-daughter — with no divine pushback. The law says destruction; the narrative shows endorsement.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologist move, run by Kaiser and Archer, is that Deuteronomy 7 targets specifically the seven Canaanite nations and their idolatry, not all foreign unions, and that Joseph's Egyptian marriage falls outside that list. Narrow the category, shrink the problem. That works partially — Deuteronomy 7:1 does name specific peoples. But Ezra 9-10 and Nehemiah 13 extend the prohibition much wider, treating any marriage to non-Israelites as a defilement, and they explicitly appeal to the Deuteronomic law as their warrant. So by the post-exilic period, the principle had clearly generalized. Christine Hayes and Shaye Cohen have both mapped how intermarriage theology hardened from the monarchic period through the Second Temple era — the J and E sources are comfortable with Joseph marrying an Egyptian priest's daughter, Moses marrying Zipporah the Midianite, Boaz marrying Ruth the Moabite (who is specifically one of the prohibited nations under Deut 23:3), while Deuteronomic and Priestly writers get increasingly anxious about foreign wives. The contradiction isn't within a single author's work; it's between different theological generations that produced incompatible ethics and then got bound together. Joseph's marriage stands in the text as a patriarchal-era artifact that the later Deuteronomic editors never scrubbed.

contradictions.question: Were Naaman and Ard the sons or the grandsons of Benjamin?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 46:21 lists Naaman and Ard as sons of Benjamin who migrated to Egypt. Numbers 26:40 lists Ard and Naaman as sons of Bela — making them Benjamin's grandsons, not his sons. Same names, different generational slots.
contradictions.commentary: The go-to apologist solution is telescoping: Archer and Kaiser both argue that Genesis 46:21 lumps descendants without strict generational markers and that Numbers 26 gives the more precise family tree. Possible, but it runs into the same problem we saw with Benjamin's age — if Benjamin was young enough in Genesis 44 to be called a "little one," the presence of ten sons and multiple grandsons at the migration becomes chronologically impossible. Friedman, Baden, and Carr place Genesis 46:8-27 in the Priestly tribal-list tradition and note that the Priestly census lists in Numbers are working from overlapping but not identical genealogical data. The Samaritan Pentateuch and LXX preserve variant readings in both passages that smooth some of the tension — another indication that ancient copyists were already trying to reconcile the lists and failing. Knoppers' work on Chronicles shows that the Chronicler's parallel list in 1 Chronicles 7:6-12 doesn't match either Genesis or Numbers cleanly, giving three distinct Benjaminite genealogies that disagree on generation counts and names. Three independent list-traditions, three incompatible family trees. The "telescoping" answer papers over a real data problem: the tribal censuses don't agree with each other, full stop.

contradictions.question: How many were in Jacob's family when they came into Egypt?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 46:27, Exodus 1:5, and Deuteronomy 10:22 all put the migration number at 70. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:14 puts it at 75. Two counts, five people apart.
contradictions.commentary: This one has a textual solution that apologists and critics actually agree on at the front end — the 75-count comes from the Septuagint, which adds five of Joseph's Egyptian-born grandsons to the tally in Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5. The Dead Sea Scrolls fragments 4QGen-Exod-a and 4QExod-b both agree with the LXX reading of 75. So Luke (writing Acts) was working from the Greek Old Testament, which is why his Stephen speech says 75 while the Masoretic-based English translations say 70. That's the textual fix, and it's real. But notice what the harmonization concedes: the New Testament author is quoting a version of the Hebrew Bible that differs from the version Christians and Jews eventually canonized, and the two versions don't agree on basic numerical facts. Emanuel Tov's work on the Pentateuch textual history shows that the 70/75 discrepancy is part of a broader pattern where the LXX, MT, and Samaritan Pentateuch preserve three different editorial layers of Genesis-Exodus, each with its own numbers. Calling this "not a contradiction" requires you to pick which Hebrew Bible is the real one and ignore that the New Testament author picked a different one. The text of Acts is internally consistent with the text Luke had. The contradiction is between Luke's Bible and the Bible most of his later readers inherited. That is of course a text-critical observation, not a doctrinal one.

contradictions.question: What were the twelve tribes of Israel (Jacob)?
contradictions.summary: The Hebrew Bible and New Testament preserve six different lists of the "twelve tribes" of Israel — Gen 49, Num 1, Num 13, Deut 33, Ezek 48, Rev 7 — and no two lists match. Across the six, fourteen different tribal names appear. Only eight tribes appear on every list. Simeon, Levi, Dan, Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh each get dropped somewhere.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist explanation — Archer, Wenham, LaSor — is that the "twelve tribes" is a flexible theological schema rather than a strict roster. Levi gets counted or not depending on whether you're listing land-allotment tribes or worship-officiant tribes; Joseph gets split into Ephraim and Manasseh when you need to replace Levi; the number twelve is preserved even when the individual names shift. That's accurate as description. The problem is what this concedes: the "twelve tribes" is a theological scaffold, not a historical memory. Mark Smith and Daniel Fleming both argue that Israel's tribal structure was fluid, politically contingent, and differently remembered by different sources at different times — Ephraim dominates northern lists, Judah dominates southern lists, the Levitical priesthood had its own interests in how tribes got counted. The Revelation 7 list drops Dan and Ephraim, which makes sense if you're a late first-century Christian writer working from a tradition that associated those tribes with apostasy (a trope visible in rabbinic literature). Ezekiel 48 reorganizes tribal land allotments around a future-ideal geography rather than historical facts. The number twelve is preserved across all six lists precisely because twelve is the theologically loaded number — three tribes per compass point around the tabernacle, twelve apostles, twelve foundation stones in the New Jerusalem. When the names change but the total doesn't, the scaffold is doing the work, not the memory. A historical twelve-tribe confederation may have existed in Israel's past, but the biblical lists are theological projections, not archives.

contradictions.question: Where was Jacob buried?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 50:13 has Jacob's sons carrying him into Canaan and burying him in the cave of Machpelah near Hebron, the family tomb purchased by Abraham. Stephen in Acts 7:15-16 says Jacob was "carried over into Shechem, and laid in the sepulchre that Abraham bought" — which is fifty miles north of Machpelah, and which Abraham never bought. The speech in Acts gets both the location and the buyer wrong.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist strategy — Bruce, Marshall, Archer, Bock — is that Stephen is telescoping two different burials: Jacob at Machpelah and Joseph and his brothers at Shechem (Joshua 24:32 has Joseph's bones reburied there). The speech conflates the two for rhetorical compression, and the "Abraham bought" reference is a slip for Jacob's purchase of the Shechem plot in Genesis 33:19. That's one way to read it. But even with the most generous telescoping, Acts 7:16 explicitly says Jacob and the fathers were buried in Shechem and that Abraham bought the tomb. Genesis is unambiguous on both points — Jacob was not buried at Shechem and Abraham did not buy the Shechem plot. Pervo's Hermeneia commentary on Acts treats this as a historical error in the Lucan source rather than a compression technique, and Fitzmyer's Anchor commentary at least concedes the tension without resolving it. The deeper issue: Stephen's speech has multiple demonstrable factual errors against the Hebrew Bible (Abraham's departure timing, the 400 vs. 430 years, the Shechem burial) and the pattern suggests Luke is drawing on a tradition whose details don't line up with canonical Genesis. Either Stephen is wrong, Luke is wrong, or the speech is reflecting a non-canonical Samaritan-influenced tradition that located the patriarchal tombs at Shechem. Take your pick — none of those options rescue inerrancy.

contradictions.question: Is it wrong to lie?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Ephesians, Colossians, James, Revelation
contradictions.summary: The Decalogue and a long chorus of prophetic, wisdom, and epistolary texts prohibit lying absolutely — false witness, false reports, deception are abominations. Revelation 21:8 and 21:27 even send liars to the lake of fire. But Exodus 1:18-20 has the Hebrew midwives lying to Pharaoh about why they didn't kill the newborn boys, and God explicitly "deals well" with them for it. Lying merits hellfire in one place and divine reward in another.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist scaffolding — Kaiser, Geisler, Copan — is "graded absolutism": moral commands form a hierarchy, and when commands conflict (don't lie vs. don't let babies die), obeying the higher one absolves you for violating the lower one. Fine as ethical theory. But watch what happens to the text. Exodus 1:20 doesn't say "God understood they had to lie" or "God forgave them for lying" — it says God blessed them and gave them households because of it. The Rahab case in Joshua 2 runs the same pattern: she lies to the Jericho authorities about the spies and is rewarded with survival, property, and ancestry in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5). James 2:25 explicitly praises Rahab's deception as righteous works. Meanwhile, Proverbs and Revelation treat lying as categorically disqualifying. Dale Allison's work on ethics in early Judaism and Christianity shows this tension wasn't resolved within the biblical corpus — different writers operated with different ethical grammars. The Holiness Code and prophetic tradition were absolutist; the narrative traditions were consequentialist when it suited them. The graded-absolutism defense works as a philosophical overlay but requires admitting that the Bible itself doesn't articulate the hierarchy. That framework was imposed later to reconcile texts that were already in conflict.

contradictions.question: Did Moses fear the king?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 2:14-15 says Moses feared when he learned his killing of the Egyptian was known, and he fled from Pharaoh's face. Hebrews 11:27 retells the same departure: "By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king." The Torah says he feared and fled; Hebrews says he didn't fear at all.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist workaround, pressed by Lane, Cockerill, and Bruce, is that Hebrews 11:27 isn't describing Moses' flight to Midian in Exodus 2 but rather the later Exodus-from-Egypt event when Moses led the people out — which puts a different framing on the "faith" and "not fearing" language. That reading has real merit: Hebrews 11:28 immediately describes the Passover, so the sequence favors the Exodus departure over the Midian flight. Problem: Hebrews 11:27 says "he forsook Egypt" in the singular, Moses-as-individual sense, and in the plain narrative order of Exodus 2, Moses' individual flight is exactly what's being described. Attridge's Hermeneia commentary lays out the ambiguity and concedes that the author of Hebrews is working from a typologically reworked memory of Moses rather than a strict reading of Exodus. Koester's Anchor Yale commentary on Hebrews treats the verse as a theological gloss on Moses' character that smooths over Exodus 2's "fear" language in service of the faith-catalog structure of Hebrews 11. Either Hebrews is referring to the Exodus (which wasn't "by faith" alone — it was after a year of plagues and divine coercion) or it's referring to Moses' Midian flight (which Exodus explicitly says was motivated by fear). Either reading generates a conflict with some piece of the Torah narrative. Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Who appeared to Moses in the burning bush?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 3:2 says "the angel of the LORD" appeared to Moses in the flame, and Acts 7:35 confirms it was an angel. But Exodus 3:4 in the same passage shifts and says "God called unto him out of the midst of the bush," and Mark 12:26 has Jesus himself affirm that God spoke to Moses at the bush. Same encounter, two different speakers.
contradictions.commentary: The traditional solution — endorsed by Calvin, carried by Kaiser, Walton, and Stuart — is that "the angel of Yahweh" is a functional stand-in for Yahweh himself throughout the Hebrew Bible, so "angel" and "God" can name the same being without contradiction. Some apologists go further and read the angel as a pre-incarnate Christophany. The pre-incarnate-Christ reading is a dogmatic overlay, not anything the text suggests. But even the broader "angel as God-surrogate" claim is doing heavy lifting. Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer have mapped the mal'akh YHWH formula across Hebrew Bible texts and shown it functions inconsistently — sometimes as Yahweh himself in disguise (Gen 16, Gen 22), sometimes as a genuinely separate emissary (Num 22, 2 Sam 24). In Exodus 3 the narrative oscillates: verse 2 has the angel appearing in the flame, verse 4 has Yahweh and Elohim both speaking. Friedman's source analysis splits the passage between J and E, each using different terms for the divine speaker. Carr, Baden, and Propp all treat the angel/God alternation in Exodus 3 as a redactor's seam rather than a unified theology — the E source tends to use "angel" or "God" circumlocutions while J uses "Yahweh" directly. The harmonization works at the level of mature second-temple theology (where "angel of Yahweh" got systematized as an avatar doctrine), but the Exodus 3 text itself preserves two source-strands with different names for who showed up at the bush.

contradictions.question: What is God's name?
contradictions.summary: The Hebrew Bible gives God several different "names" and in some cases insists that a particular one is THE name. Exodus 6:3 says God's name is Jehovah (YHWH), Exodus 3:14 gives "I AM THAT I AM," Isaiah 42:8 flatly claims "the LORD" is his name, Exodus 34:14 says his name is Jealous, Amos 5:27 says his name is the God of hosts, and Psalm 68:4 says his name is JAH. The contradiction is that multiple passages each claim to be stating THE divine name, and the names don't match.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist move here is predictable — these aren't different names, they're different titles or epithets for the same deity, like calling someone "Dad," "Mr. Smith," and "Bob" depending on context. Archer runs this line in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and Kaiser does the same thing. Fine. That harmonization partially works for the epithets. "Lord of hosts" (YHWH tseva'ot) is clearly a title describing YHWH's military role, and "I AM THAT I AM" (ehyeh asher ehyeh) is widely read as a folk-etymology explaining the tetragrammaton. But the harmonization collapses on Exodus 6:3, which is the structural load-bearing verse in the Priestly source. P is doing something specific here: he's claiming YHWH was NOT known by that name to the patriarchs. That is flatly incompatible with the J source in Genesis, where YHWH is invoked by name as early as Genesis 4:26 ("then began men to call upon the name of the LORD") and where Abraham builds altars to YHWH in Genesis 12:8. This is one of the foundational data points for the Documentary Hypothesis — Friedman covers it at length in Who Wrote the Bible and The Bible with Sources Revealed. The J source uses YHWH from the beginning. The E and P sources use Elohim or El Shaddai until Exodus 3 (E) or Exodus 6 (P), where the name is revealed for the first time. So "what is God's name" has a real answer from critical scholarship: different sources had different theologies about when and how the divine name was revealed, and the redactor stitched them together without smoothing out the contradiction. The apologist "multiple titles" move doesn't touch that.

contradictions.question: Was Moses a good speaker?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 4:10 has Moses himself telling YHWH he is not eloquent and is "slow of speech, and of a slow tongue" — the whole reason Aaron gets attached to the mission. Acts 7:22, by contrast, has Stephen claiming Moses was "mighty in words and in deeds." The two verses assign Moses opposite verbal abilities.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists have a standard three-move playbook here. Archer runs all three. Move one: Moses was just being humble or suffering a confidence crisis in Exodus 4, not making a factual claim about his oratorical ability. Move two: Stephen is describing the young, Egyptian-trained Moses, while Exodus 4 is describing the older, self-doubting, forty-years-shepherding-sheep Moses. Move three: "mighty in words" means powerful in content, not fluent in delivery — so the two can both be true. These are not zero moves. Move two has genuine narrative texture to it — there IS a forty-year gap. But here's what the apologist has to do to make this work: reject Moses' own self-report as unreliable, accept Stephen's summary (delivered in a hostile trial setting, in Acts, a text written ~80 years after Paul by Luke, who is retelling a speech he did not witness) as the accurate biographical data, and then paper over the fact that YHWH doesn't respond to Moses in Exodus 4 by saying "no, you're actually a great speaker, I know your past." YHWH's response is to provide Aaron as a mouthpiece (Exod 4:14-16). The narrative itself treats Moses' speech impediment as a real limitation, not a confidence problem. Stephen's speech, on the other hand, is doing something different — it's a sweeping rhetorical summary of Israelite history designed to condemn his accusers, and it lionizes Moses for rhetorical effect. Luke is not writing biography; he's writing theological history. Pervo and Haenchen both treat Stephen's speech as a Lukan composition, not a verbatim transcript. So the contradiction is real at the level of the narrator's framing: one tradition has Moses as verbally inadequate (a detail the E-source narrator uses to elevate Aaron), the other has him as a rhetorical powerhouse (a detail that serves Stephen's argument). You can harmonize these if you work for it. You can't harmonize them cleanly.

contradictions.question: Who hardened the Pharaoh's heart?
contradictions.summary: Exodus gives contradictory agency for Pharaoh's heart. In Exod 4:21, 7:3, 9:12, 10:1, 10:20, 10:27, 11:10, 14:4, 14:8, and 14:18 YHWH explicitly hardens Pharaoh's heart. In Exod 8:15, 8:32, and 9:34 Pharaoh hardens his own heart. 1 Samuel 6:6 looking back attributes the hardening to Pharaoh and the Egyptians. The contradiction is over who is morally responsible for the hardening that triggers the plagues — God or Pharaoh.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologist harmonization here is from Archer, Kaiser, and Stuart in his NAC on Exodus: Pharaoh hardens his own heart first (chapters 7-8), and God only ratifies or intensifies that hardening later (chapters 9-14). On this reading, Pharaoh is morally responsible because he initiates the hardening, and God's hardening is judicial — the Romans 1:24-26 "God gives them over" pattern. That is a clever reading and it picks up on a real narrative progression. The plain text does have self-hardening appearing in the early plagues and divine hardening concentrated later. But here's where it breaks down. Exodus 4:21 and 7:3 — BEFORE Pharaoh has done a single thing — already have YHWH declaring "I will harden his heart" and "I will harden Pharaoh's heart." This is programmatic, announced from the outset, and framed as the whole point of the plague sequence ("that I might shew these my signs before him," 10:1). Fretheim reads this correctly in his Interpretation commentary: the divine hardening is not a late-sequence judicial response; it's the theological engine that drives the whole narrative, because YHWH wants maximum display of power against the Egyptian gods. Source-critical scholars (Baden, Propp) note that the hardening vocabulary actually differs between sources — the P source uses חזק (strengthen), J uses כבד (make heavy), E uses קשה (make hard) — and the blending produces the inconsistency we see. So the apologist harmonization can squint and read a chronological escalation, but it has to ignore that the hardening is divinely pre-announced and theologically pre-committed. You can call that "God hardening Pharaoh who was going to harden himself anyway," but that's Calvinist compatibilism, not textual harmony. The text itself contradicts itself on the agency of the hardening.

contradictions.question: Did Abraham know God's name?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 22:14 has Abraham naming a place "Jehovahjireh" (YHWH-yir'eh, "YHWH will provide") — he knows and uses the name YHWH. Exodus 6:3 has YHWH telling Moses that he appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai (God Almighty), "but by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them." The two verses are flatly incompatible.
contradictions.commentary: This is the cleanest single-verse contradiction in the Hebrew Bible, and it's a structural load-bearing verse in the case for the Documentary Hypothesis. The apologist moves are exhausting but they exist. Archer and Kaiser claim Exodus 6:3 doesn't mean the patriarchs didn't know the name YHWH, it means they didn't know the full meaning or full character represented by the name — a kind of "experiential knowing" versus "propositional knowing" distinction. Motyer tried this move too. That is an enormous amount of theological freight to hang on a single verb. The niphal of yada (to be known) in Exodus 6:3 is contrastive with "I appeared... by the name of God Almighty" — the syntax is specifically naming one name that WAS known and another name that WAS NOT known. The plain reading is that the name YHWH itself was not revealed before Moses. Kugel lays this out in How to Read the Bible: Genesis is riddled with uses of YHWH by the patriarchs (Gen 12:8, 13:4, 15:7, 22:14, 26:25, 28:13), and Exodus 6:3 has YHWH declaring that his name wasn't known to them. Friedman in Who Wrote the Bible identifies this as one of the fingerprints of source division — J uses YHWH from Genesis 4:26 onward, while P (Exodus 6:3) and E (Exodus 3:14-15) both treat the name as a Mosaic revelation. This isn't a contradiction that the apologist "experiential knowing" dodge can paper over, because the verses aren't saying "Abraham didn't grok YHWH's character," they're saying Abraham did and didn't know the name itself. Two authors with two different theologies of how the divine name entered history got stitched together. That's the parsimonious reading.

contradictions.question: Who was Libni's father?
contradictions.summary: Three Levitical genealogies in Exodus 6:17, Numbers 3:18, and 1 Chronicles 6:17 list Libni as a son of Gershon (Levi's firstborn). But 1 Chronicles 6:29, tracing a completely different Levitical line, has Libni as son of Mahli and grandson of Merari (Levi's third son). Same name, two different fathers, two different Levitical branches.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist move here is cheap and it sometimes actually works: two different men named Libni. Archer goes for this in Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and Keil-Delitzsch did it before him. Harmonizers point out that Hebrew genealogies reuse names constantly — there are multiple Zechariahs, multiple Azariahs, multiple Jonathans. On that logic, one Libni is Gershonite and the other is Merarite, end of story. That move is available and we should take it seriously. But here's the textual problem. Look at 1 Chronicles 6 as a literary unit. The chapter is systematically listing Levi's descendants by branch. Verses 16-19 lay out the three Levitical branches (Gershon, Kohath, Merari) and verse 17 explicitly identifies Libni as Gershon's son. Then verse 29, in the SAME chapter, reassigns Libni to the Merari line. Knoppers in his AB commentary on 1 Chronicles flags this as a likely corruption or textual transmission error — the parallel list in Merari's line should probably read a different name, and the LXX tradition preserves some variation. The apologist "two different Libnis" defense requires that the Chronicler, writing a unified genealogical treatise, inserted two identically-named figures in two different branches without comment. That's possible. It's also the least parsimonious reading. The simpler explanation is textual corruption in the Masoretic tradition, which is what Noth, Japhet, and Knoppers all argue. Either way, as the text stands the two verses contradict each other.

contradictions.question: How many days is unleavened bread to be eaten during the Passover?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 12:15, 13:6-7, 23:15, Leviticus 23:6, and Deuteronomy 16:3 all require seven days of unleavened bread. But Deuteronomy 16:8, three verses after Deut 16:3 says seven, specifies six days of unleavened bread followed by a solemn assembly on the seventh. Even internally within Deuteronomy 16, the count flips between six and seven.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist harmonization here is mathematically creative. Keil-Delitzsch and Craigie both try versions of it. The argument: Deut 16:3 says seven days, Deut 16:8 says six days, and the reconciliation is that the seventh day is a "solemn assembly" (atzeret) on which you ALSO eat unleavened bread, just in a different liturgical frame, so the total is still seven days of unleavened bread with six ordinary days plus one sacred assembly day. That actually could work grammatically if you're willing to read "six days" as "six ordinary days" with the seventh being counted separately. Tigay takes this line in his JPS Torah Commentary on Deuteronomy. But here's the textual problem. The Exodus and Leviticus texts never split the count. They say "seven days" cleanly. Only Deuteronomy 16:8 introduces "six days" language. Levinson and Bernard Levinson specifically (different scholars, same surname — I mean Bernard M. Levinson, the Deuteronomy/hermeneutics guy) argues in Deuteronomy and the Hermeneutics of Legal Innovation that Deuteronomy is deliberately reworking the older festival calendar — combining Pesach with Chag Matzot and centralizing the festival at the chosen place. The six-day count in Deut 16:8 is a vestige of that redactional reworking. So the apologist can technically reconcile the numbers by reading the seventh day as a separate category, but that reading requires accepting that Deuteronomy has a different festival structure than Exodus-Leviticus — which is exactly what critical scholars are saying when they call this a contradiction. Harmonization and source criticism are pointing at the same thing; only the framing differs.

contradictions.question: Did God kill all the Egyptian cattle in the sixth plague?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 9:3-6 (the fifth plague, the murrain — the question's "sixth" is wrong) says "all the cattle of Egypt died." Three verses later at Exodus 9:19, God is warning Egyptians to bring their cattle and servants indoors because hail is coming and what's left in the field will die. So either "all" didn't mean all, or there's a narrative continuity problem between the fifth and seventh plagues.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist standard move on this one is the "all" hyperbole defense. Archer, Stuart, and Kaiser all run it. The argument: biblical Hebrew routinely uses kol ("all") hyperbolically — think of "all the world went out to be taxed" in Luke 2:1, or "all Judea went out to John the Baptist." On this reading, "all the cattle of Egypt died" means "all the cattle that were in the field as specified in Exodus 9:3" — the murrain only struck field cattle, not sheltered cattle, so there are cattle left for Exodus 9:19's hail plague. Keil-Delitzsch formulated this harmonization and every conservative commentary since has leaned on it. Here's where it gets interesting. Exodus 9:3 does in fact specify that the murrain is "upon thy cattle which is in the field, upon the horses, upon the asses, upon the camels, upon the oxen, and upon the sheep." So the harmonization isn't invented from thin air — it's scaffolded on the actual text. BUT. Exodus 9:6 explicitly says "all the cattle of Egypt died" without repeating the "in the field" qualifier, and then 9:7 says Pharaoh sent messengers and found "there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead." The contrast is between all-dead-Egyptian and all-alive-Israelite, which is how the plague gets its rhetorical punch. Propp in the Anchor Bible commentary on Exodus notes the tension and suggests the plagues are composite — the "all cattle died" is from one stratum and the hail's cattle survivors are from another, stitched together by the redactor without smoothing out the death count. Friedman assigns the murrain primarily to E and the hail primarily to J, which helps explain why the cattle count doesn't add up across plagues. The apologist hyperbole defense works if you're willing to let "all" mean "some" whenever the narrative gets trapped, but then "all the cattle died" is just a rhetorical flourish, not an actual datum about what happened. Flag: the question text incorrectly calls this the sixth plague — it's the fifth (murrain). The sixth plague is boils (Exod 9:8-12).

contradictions.question: Is God warlike or peaceful?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Exodus, Psalms, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, 2 Thessalonians, Hebrews
contradictions.summary: Exodus 15:3 calls YHWH "a man of war" and Psalms 18:34 and 144:1 describe YHWH as the one who teaches hands to war and fingers to fight. The New Testament, by contrast, repeatedly titles God "the God of peace" (Rom 15:33, 16:20, 2 Cor 13:11, 1 Thess 5:23, Heb 13:20) and declares God is "not the author of confusion but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33). The contradiction is between a martial YHWH who trains warriors and a peaceful God who authors shalom.
contradictions.commentary: This is a category the apologist usually wins the surface skirmish on and loses the deep argument. The surface move is easy: God is both. He is peaceful toward his people and warlike toward his enemies. War and peace aren't contradictory attributes; they're contextual expressions of righteousness. Copan runs this line in Is God a Moral Monster?, Wright in The God I Don't Understand, and Longman in Reading the Bible with Heart and Mind. Fine. That move has textual support — there's plenty of material in both Testaments where God's peace toward Israel requires martial action against Israel's enemies. Psalm 46 has "he maketh wars to cease" as proof of divine peace. Here's where the critical scholarship lands. Mark S. Smith in The Early History of God documents that early Israelite YHWH was indistinguishable from Canaanite and Mesopotamian warrior gods — the divine warrior motif ("man of war" — ish milkhamah) is stock ANE storm-god imagery, closely paralleled by Baal, Marduk, Ashur. Patrick D. Miller in The Divine Warrior in Early Israel catalogs how deeply this warlike portrayal saturates pre-exilic material. The shift to "God of peace" framing in the New Testament is not a contradiction in the apologist's sense; it's a theological development across centuries, as Israelite religion moved through the exile, the Hellenistic period, and emergent Christianity, progressively reframing God's character. Jon Levenson covers this in Creation and the Persistence of Evil. So the apologist harmonization "he's peaceful to his people and warlike to enemies" flattens a real theological evolution into a single timeless attribute. The text DOES present two different models of God — one from Bronze Age divine-warrior theology, the other from a later peace theology. The apologist is reading both through a single systematic-theology filter. Critical scholarship reads them as evidence of genuine theological development over time.

contradictions.question: Is dancing a sin?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 32:19-28 has Moses kill 3,000 Israelites after catching them dancing around the golden calf, treating the dancing as part of the capital offense. Exodus 15:20-21, just seventeen chapters earlier, has Miriam and the women dancing with timbrels to celebrate YHWH's defeat of Pharaoh's army — treated as praise, not sin. Same book, dancing gets you killed in chapter 32 and praised in chapter 15.
contradictions.commentary: This is a weak contradiction on its face and the apologist is right to push back. Dancing is not intrinsically sinful in biblical thought — it's how the dancing is directed that matters. Miriam's dance in Exodus 15 is praise to YHWH after the Red Sea crossing. The golden calf dance in Exodus 32 is idolatrous worship of a forbidden image. 2 Samuel 6 has David dancing before the ark as worship. Ecclesiastes 3:4 has "a time to dance." Psalm 149:3 and 150:4 commend dancing as praise. So on the context-matters framing, the contradiction dissolves — and that's what Archer, Mathews, and Kaiser argue. I don't think the apologist is wrong on this one. What's actually being punished in Exodus 32 is the worship of the calf, which was the breach of the first and second commandments. The dancing is incidental coloring of the idolatrous scene, not the offense itself. The text supports that reading — Moses' anger in 32:19-20 is directed at the calf, not at the dancing per se. Fretheim, Propp, and Sarna (JPS Exodus commentary) all read the dance as part of the idolatrous cultic scene rather than as the sin-in-itself. That said, the SAB framing isn't entirely empty — it does capture a surface-level oddity: the same physical act (group dance with musical instruments) triggers opposite narrative valences in the same book, and the distinction between "sacred dance" and "idolatrous dance" is nowhere explicitly defined by the text. A naive reader getting the Ten Commandments as their filter might reasonably wonder what the difference is. But as contradictions go, this is low-grade. The verdict: context-sensitive ritual categories are doing the work, and the text is internally coherent once you read the cult context. Flagging as a weak contradiction without recommending delete.

contradictions.question: What was in the Ark of the Covenant?
contradictions.summary: 1 Kings 8:9 and 2 Chronicles 5:10 both state flatly that when Solomon brought the ark into the temple, "there was nothing in the ark save the two tables of stone." Hebrews 9:4, describing the same ark, says it contained "the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant" — three items, not one. Either the ark had three things in it or it had only one. The two texts contradict.
contradictions.commentary: This is a hard one for apologists and the standard harmonization shows the strain. Archer, Ellingworth (NIGTC Hebrews), and Lane (WBC Hebrews) all try variants of the same move: at the original construction of the tabernacle (Exodus 16:33-34 for the manna jar, Numbers 17:10 for Aaron's rod), those items were placed "before the Testimony" or "before the ark" — which may have meant beside or in front of rather than strictly inside. The apologist argument is that Hebrews 9:4 is using "in" loosely to mean "associated with the ark," and that by Solomon's time the pot and rod had been removed, so 1 Kings 8:9 is historically accurate for Solomon's era. That is a multi-layer rescue. It requires (1) Hebrews using a preposition loosely, (2) a tradition about items being associated-but-not-inside, and (3) an undocumented removal of items between the wilderness and Solomon's temple. Attridge in his Hermeneia commentary on Hebrews reads the text straightforwardly — the Greek en he ("in which") means what it says: the author of Hebrews is describing the ark as containing all three items. Attridge notes that the author is drawing on a priestly-traditional picture of the ark, not on actual Solomonic practice, and that there is a genuine inconsistency with 1 Kings / 2 Chronicles. Koester (AB Hebrews) and deSilva (Perseverance in Gratitude) come to similar conclusions. The Numbers 17 and Exodus 16 texts specifically say the manna jar and Aaron's rod were placed "before the Testimony" — which in context is language for being in the most holy place, near the ark, but the author of Hebrews has apparently conflated that with being inside the ark. The apologist's loose-preposition defense is technically possible but it's post-hoc rationalization. The parsimonious reading is that Hebrews, writing in the late first century to a Diaspora audience, drew on an extracanonical or liturgical tradition about the ark's contents that differed from the Kings/Chronicles historical record. Two traditions, stitched together, don't match.

contradictions.question: Where did Moses get water from a rock?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 17:1-7 locates the water-from-rock miracle at Rephidim in the wilderness of Sin ("the rock in Horeb"), with Moses naming the place Massah and Meribah. Numbers 20:1-8 (with Num 27:14 and Deut 32:51 confirming) locates it at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, at the waters of "Meribah-Kadesh." Two different wildernesses, two different locations, same miracle (or so it appears).
contradictions.commentary: The apologist harmonization on this one is clean and well-established: there are two separate water-from-rock miracles. Archer, Kaiser, and Ashley (NICOT Numbers) all make this move. The evidence supports it. Exodus 17 happens early in the wilderness wanderings, shortly after the Red Sea crossing, at Rephidim. Numbers 20 happens in the fortieth year, at Kadesh, where Miriam has just died and where Moses will be punished for striking the rock instead of speaking to it. Different locations, different timeframes, different outcomes (Moses is faithful in Exodus 17, disobedient in Numbers 20). On the surface, this resolves the contradiction: the two stories are two distinct events with the coincidental shared name "Meribah" attached because both involved water disputes. That is a reasonable reading and in harmonization terms, it works. But the critical scholarly read complicates it. Budd in his WBC commentary on Numbers, Levine in the AB commentary, and Friedman in The Bible with Sources Revealed all argue that Exodus 17 (JE) and Numbers 20 (P) are variant traditions of the same underlying event, redactionally separated and placed at different points in the wilderness narrative. The clues: both miracles are named Meribah (strife), both involve a rock being struck, both involve water for a rebellious congregation, and the Deuteronomy 33:8 blessing of Levi refers to a SINGLE event ("thou didst prove at Massah, and... at the waters of Meribah"). The most parsimonious source-critical reading is that P retold the J/E Rephidim story to relocate it to Kadesh and to add Moses' disobedience as the etiological explanation for why Moses wouldn't enter the promised land. So the apologist "two separate miracles" defense reconciles the surface contradiction at the cost of ignoring the structural parallels that suggest one underlying tradition doubled by the redactor. Both readings are defensible, but the critical one has stronger source-critical warrants.

contradictions.question: Can God be tempted?
contradictions.summary: James 1:13 declares God "cannot be tempted with evil" — a flat denial of divine temptability. Deuteronomy 6:16 (and Jesus citing it at Matt 4:7 / Luke 4:12) commands "Ye shall not tempt the Lord your God" — a command that presupposes God CAN be tempted, otherwise why forbid it? The verses contradict on whether God is subject to temptation at all.
contradictions.commentary: This one actually turns on a translation and semantic range problem, and the apologist is partially right. The Greek peirazo and Hebrew nasah cover a semantic range from "tempt (to sin)" to "test" to "put to the proof." James 1:13 uses peirazo in the moral-solicitation sense — God cannot be seduced into evil. Deuteronomy 6:16 and Jesus' citation of it use the same verb family but in a different sense: don't put God on trial, don't demand that God prove himself, don't treat God like a subject of experiment. Blomberg and Carson run this argument and they're not wrong about the semantic difference. So in English the word "tempt" looks like the same concept, but the underlying Hebrew and Greek are deploying different senses. The harmonization wins the surface skirmish. Here's where it gets interesting. Even granting the semantic distinction, the theological problem doesn't fully disappear. James 1:13 isn't just saying "God can't be morally solicited," it's making a broader claim about divine impassibility — that God is not subject to internal disruption by external stimuli. But the Hebrew Bible has YHWH regularly being "tested" by Israel (Exod 17:2, Num 14:22, Ps 78:18, 41, 56, 95:9) and responding with anger, disappointment, and changed plans. That's not temptation-to-sin, but it IS being moved by external provocation, which is in tension with James' absolute framing. Kugel notes in How to Read the Bible that the Hebrew Bible's God is profoundly responsive — he grieves (Gen 6:6), relents (Exod 32:14, Jonah 3:10), and changes his mind (1 Sam 15:11). The James 1:13 framing reflects a later Hellenistic-Jewish and early Christian theology of divine impassibility, influenced by Greek philosophical categories, that is at tension with older Hebraic portrayals. So while the narrow "tempt = solicit to evil" harmonization works for the lexical contradiction, there's a deeper theological tension between the two portrayals of divine susceptibility. The SAB is raising a real issue even if the specific verse pairing is semantically sloppy.

contradictions.question: How did God tell Moses to get water from a rock?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 17:5-7 has God instructing Moses to strike (smite) the rock with his rod. Numbers 20:7-8 has God instructing Moses to SPEAK to the rock — and the whole point of Numbers 20's narrative is that Moses' striking (instead of speaking) is the transgression that bars him from the promised land. Deuteronomy 33:8 adds a third element: the Urim and Thummim (mistyped in the scrape as "Umim and Thumim") "proved" Moses at Massah and Meribah, hinting at a divinatory element in the tradition. The three texts describe three different divine instructions for the same category of miracle.
contradictions.commentary: This is a structurally richer version of contradiction 111, and the harmonization moves are similar but the stakes are higher because the method matters for the narrative. The apologist move is the same two-miracles defense: Exodus 17 is one event where striking was commanded; Numbers 20 is a second event forty years later where speaking was commanded and Moses disobeyed by striking anyway. Archer runs this straightforwardly. Deuteronomy 33:8's Urim-and-Thummim reference is a Mosaic blessing on Levi that poetically references the Massah/Meribah events without explicitly specifying a divinatory method for producing water — the apologist reads it as referring to Levi's priestly role having been validated at these events, not as a separate method for water production. Craigie, Merrill (NAC), and Tigay (JPS) all handle it this way. That's a reasonable reading of Deut 33:8. Where the apologist defense strains is Numbers 20 itself. Granted the two-miracles framing, the critical reader still has to reckon with the source-critical evidence that Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 are doublets from different sources — Friedman, Baden, Budd, and Levine all make this case. The repetition of Meribah, the near-identical plot structure, the water shortage, the rock, the rod — these are literary parallels too close to be coincidental. Milgrom in his JPS Numbers commentary explicitly argues Numbers 20 is P's retelling of the older JE Rephidim tradition, relocated to Kadesh and modified to include Moses' disqualifying sin (striking instead of speaking). So the methodology disagreement between Exodus 17 (strike) and Numbers 20 (speak) isn't evidence of two separate events where Moses got different instructions — it's evidence that the P author deliberately reframed the JE striking-miracle as a disobedience narrative to explain Moses' exclusion from the land. The Deuteronomy 33:8 allusion to Massah/Meribah isn't a third method; it's a Deuteronomic echo of the older tradition. Three variant traditions, one underlying event, different theological purposes.

contradictions.question: Who was Moses' father-in-law?
contradictions.summary: Three different names are given for Moses' father-in-law. Exodus 3:1, 4:18, 18:1, 18:5 all call him Jethro (the priest of Midian). Numbers 10:29 and Judges 4:11 call him Hobab. Exodus 2:18-21 calls him Reuel. The verses directly identify different men by different names in the same narrative role.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the classic Pentateuch contradictions, and the apologist moves are creative but strained. Archer, Kaiser, and Cole (TOTC Exodus) all run versions of two reconciliation strategies. Strategy one: Reuel is the clan-name or grandfather, Jethro is the given name, Hobab is a separate individual (Moses' brother-in-law, not father-in-law). The Numbers 10:29 reference to "Hobab, the son of Raguel" (Raguel being Reuel) is then read as Moses addressing his brother-in-law — Hobab — calling Reuel the father-in-law. Strategy two: the same man had multiple names, as was common in the ANE — Reuel was his given name, Jethro ("excellency") was his priestly title, Hobab was a nickname or additional name. That harmonization is not zero. ANE figures did often have multiple names — think Abram/Abraham, Jacob/Israel, Gideon/Jerubbaal. And the Hebrew word translated "father in law" (חֹתֵן, choten) can mean broader in-law relation, including brother-in-law. So the apologist defense is available. Here's the source-critical reading. Propp in the AB Exodus commentary and Friedman in Who Wrote the Bible argue that the J source uses Reuel (Exod 2:18), the E source uses Jethro (Exod 3:1, 4:18, 18), and Numbers 10:29 (also J in Friedman's analysis) uses "Hobab son of Reuel." Judges 4:11, which has Hobab as father-in-law, is a separate tradition, likely deuteronomistic, that diverges from the Pentateuchal accounts. The simplest reading: multiple sources had different names for Moses' father-in-law, reflecting different oral traditions about this peripheral Midianite figure, and the redactor harmonized them incompletely. The apologist "three names for one man" defense is possible but requires a complex reading of choten in Numbers 10:29 and an unexplained why-would-he-have-three-names scenario. The source-critical explanation is parsimonious. Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to make images?
contradictions.summary: The Second Commandment in Exodus 20:4 and Deuteronomy 5:8 prohibits making "any graven image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath." Deuteronomy 4:16-18, 4:23, and 27:15 reinforce this as an absolute ban. But Exodus 25:18-20 has God himself commanding Moses to make two gold cherubim (winged images of heavenly beings) to cover the mercy seat, and Exodus 26:1 adds cherubim woven into the tabernacle curtains. God forbids images of heavenly beings and simultaneously commands images of heavenly beings.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist harmonization here is elegant and partially works. The argument, run by Archer, Mathews, Sarna (JPS Exodus), and Propp: the prohibition in Exodus 20:4 is not against image-making per se but against image-making for worship (the next clause, 20:5, is "thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them"). Cherubim on the mercy seat and woven into curtains are images — but they're not worshipped. They're decorative or theologically functional, not cultic objects of devotion. On this reading, the commandment is about idolatry, not about iconography. This is a solid reading and the apologist has internal biblical warrant for it. The bronze serpent in Numbers 21:8-9 fits the same pattern — God commands a serpent image for healing purposes; Hezekiah later destroys it (2 Kings 18:4) precisely because people started worshipping it. Solomon's temple had cherubim, lions, oxen, and pomegranates as decorative elements (1 Kings 7) without apparent violation. So the apologist is right that the Second Commandment is about cultic use, not image-making as such. Where it gets interesting is that this interpretation is not unanimous within the biblical tradition. The strictest deuteronomic strand (Deut 4:16-18 especially) reads like a near-absolute ban on any likenesses of creatures, and second-temple Judaism inherited this more rigorous reading — leading to the aniconic coin tradition under the Hasmoneans, the destruction of the Roman eagle over the temple under Herod, and the eventual rabbinic discomfort with figural art (though the Dura-Europos synagogue in the 3rd century CE shows the rule wasn't absolute even then). Moberly in Old Testament Theology and Halbertal-Margalit in Idolatry both note that the Hebrew Bible contains at least two distinct iconic theologies: a cherubim-are-fine strand (P, priestly) and a no-images-at-all strand (strict Deuteronomic). The apologist "it's about worship, not making" reading is the P-strand reading. It works for resolving Exodus 20 vs Exodus 25, but it glosses over the genuine tension between the priestly iconic tradition and the stricter deuteronomic anti-iconic tradition. The biblical text contains both theological strands, and the SAB contradiction is pointing at that internal diversity even if clumsily.

contradictions.question: How should parents be treated?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Exodus, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Matthew, Luke, John, Ephesians
contradictions.summary: The Torah and the wisdom literature hand down an unambiguous rule: honor your father and mother. It is one of the Ten Commandments, repeated in Deuteronomy, echoed in Proverbs, and reaffirmed by Paul as "the first commandment with promise." Then the Gospels put words in Jesus' mouth that run the other way — disciples must "hate" father and mother, leave a father unburied, and call no man on earth their father. One stream demands you honor your parents; the other demands you subordinate or reject them for the sake of the kingdom. They cannot both be the operative standard at the same time.
contradictions.commentary:
Here's the thing — the honor side isn't ambiguous. Exodus 20:12 makes parental honor a Decalogue obligation, Deuteronomy 5:16 attaches a long-life reward to it, and Ephesians 6:2 calls it "the first commandment with promise." That's the baseline the Gospel sayings collide with.

Apologists have three main escape routes, and the strongest version of each deserves a fair hearing. First, the Semitic-idiom move: the Greek μισέω (miseo, "hate") in Luke 14:26 renders a Hebrew idiom of preference, so "hate" just means "love less." Genesis 29:31 (Leah "hated") and the Matthew 10:37 parallel ("loveth father or mother more than me") give that reading real support. Second, the life-stages move: honor binds you as a child, while the discipleship sayings address adults choosing a vocation — different situations, no conflict. Third, the radicalizing move: Jesus isn't abolishing the commandment, he's relativizing all earthly loyalties under the kingdom, the way Mark 7:9-13 actually defends parental support against the corban dodge.

The idiom argument is the best of the bunch — Matthew clearly softened Luke's wording for exactly this reason, which tells you the early church already felt the friction. But softening "hate" to "love less" doesn't dissolve the problem; it relocates it. A commandment that says honor your parents is hard to square with a teacher who makes loving them less than him the entry ticket to discipleship. And Luke 9:59-60 won't bend to the idiom defense at all: refusing to let a man bury his own father isn't "loving him less," it's overriding one of the most sacred filial duties in Second Temple Judaism. The harmonizations require you to read each hard saying through the softest available lens while ignoring that the texts themselves are pulling in opposite directions. The tension is real, and the church's own editorial fingerprints prove it felt real to them too.

contradictions.question: Is it wrong to have sex outside of marriage?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Exodus, Deuteronomy, Hosea, Acts, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, Hebrews, Jude
contradictions.summary: The Torah (Exod 20:14, Deut 5:18) and the New Testament (Acts 15:20, 1 Cor 5:1, 6:13, 6:18, 10:8, 2 Cor 12:21, Gal 5:19-21, Eph 5:3, Col 3:5-6, 1 Thess 4:3, Heb 13:4, Jude 7) repeatedly condemn fornication and adultery. But Hosea 1:2 and 3:1 have YHWH commanding the prophet Hosea to take a "wife of whoredoms" and later to love an adulteress — God explicitly commanding the act his own law forbids.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist harmonization here is clean and widely held: Hosea 1 and 3 are prophetic symbolic actions, not endorsements of fornication. The marriage of Hosea to Gomer is a divinely commanded object lesson about Israel's infidelity to YHWH, not a general license for sexual immorality. Stuart (WBC Hosea), Garrett (NAC Hosea), and Dearman (NICOT Hosea) all take this line. The apologist argument: Hosea's marriage operates in a special category of prophetic sign-act, parallel to Ezekiel lying on his side for 390 days, Isaiah walking naked for three years, or Jeremiah wearing a yoke — these are symbolic acts that would be problematic if done for their own sake but are meaningful as embodied prophecy. On this reading, Hosea is not committing adultery himself; he is MARRYING a woman with an immoral past or promiscuous character as a living metaphor for YHWH's covenant with unfaithful Israel. That harmonization works. The sign-act genre is well-documented in ANE prophetic literature, and the context of Hosea makes the symbolic purpose explicit. Andersen and Freedman's AB commentary lays this out exhaustively. Here's where it gets complicated. Even granting the sign-act reading, the contradiction doesn't fully dissolve. The command in Hosea 1:2 isn't "marry a woman who WAS promiscuous and is now repentant" — it's "take a wife of whoredoms AND children of whoredoms, for the land hath committed great whoredom." Hosea 3:1 explicitly commands love for an adulteress, and the prophet pays silver and barley as if purchasing her (3:2). The moral category of the act is messy. Hebrew Bible scholars like Heschel (The Prophets) and Brueggemann (Prophetic Imagination) point out that the prophetic sign-acts DO involve the prophet in morally complex behavior that stretches or contravenes normal ethical categories — that's part of their rhetorical force. So the apologist is right that it's not a simple endorsement of fornication, but the contradiction is real at the level of divine command: God is commanding behavior that his law elsewhere condemns, and he's doing so for a higher pedagogical purpose. The SAB framing is a bit blunt but the underlying tension is genuine. This is a case where "God is above his own law when he has a reason" is the actual apologist answer, which is itself a theologically interesting concession.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to covet?
contradictions.summary: The Tenth Commandment as quoted by Paul in Romans 7:7 and 13:9 prohibits coveting, and Ephesians 5:3 and Colossians 3:5 reinforce that covetousness is idolatry and should not even be named among believers. But 1 Corinthians 14:39 has Paul himself saying "covet to prophesy" — using the same Greek verb (zeloo, in some manuscripts; KJV renders zelote as "covet") in a positive sense. Paul is simultaneously condemning covetousness and commanding it.
contradictions.commentary: This is a translation contradiction, and the apologist is right on it. The KJV "covet to prophesy" is translating zeloute (from zeloo, to be zealous, to strive after, to earnestly desire) — the SAME root that gives us "jealous" and "zealot." The prohibitions on coveting in Romans 7:7 and 13:9 translate the Greek epithymeo (to desire, lust after) — a different verb. Ephesians 5:3 and Colossians 3:5 use pleonexia (greed, grasping for more) — also a different word. Three different Greek words all rendered "covet" in the KJV because Jacobean English had a narrower vocabulary. Modern translations handle this cleanly: ESV has "earnestly desire" for 1 Cor 14:39, "covet" for the prohibitions. NIV has "eagerly desire" for 1 Cor 14:39. This is a pure translation artifact, not a substantive contradiction. Archer notes this correctly, and Fee (NICNT 1 Corinthians) and Thiselton (NIGTC) both handle the Greek precisely. The contradiction only exists in the KJV and in readers who don't check the underlying Greek. That said, the SAB is using a King James-centric framing that wouldn't register the contradiction in any modern translation. If the question is "is there a genuine contradiction in the New Testament Greek," the answer is no. If the question is "does the KJV contradict itself with the same English word," the answer is yes, but that's a translation issue, not a textual one. Flag: this is a weak contradiction that dissolves under minimal exegesis. The underlying Greek distinguishes what the English conflates. Verdict: the text does not contradict itself; the translation does.

contradictions.question: Who gave the law to Moses?
contradictions.summary: The Exodus narrative (Exod 19:20, 20:22) has YHWH descending on Sinai and speaking the law directly to Moses — no intermediaries. But Galatians 3:19 explicitly says the law "was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator" — Paul is telling his Gentile converts that the Torah came through angels and a human mediator (Moses), not directly from God. Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2 echo the angel-mediation tradition. Two different models of Sinai revelation.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist harmonization here actually has solid second-temple texture behind it, but it still leaves the contradiction largely intact. The argument: Exodus 19-20 says God descended on Sinai and spoke with Moses, but it doesn't explicitly deny angelic involvement. Second-temple Jewish tradition — Jubilees, Philo, Josephus, and the LXX translation of Deut 33:2 — developed a theology in which angels were present at Sinai and served as intermediaries in the law's transmission. Paul is drawing on this established tradition, not inventing it. Bruce (NICNT Galatians), Longenecker (WBC Galatians), and Moo (BECNT Galatians) all make this point, and Dunn's Galatians commentary goes further. On this reading, Galatians 3:19 isn't contradicting Exodus; it's drawing on a Jewish interpretive tradition that filled in Sinai with angelic mediators. That IS historically accurate. Philo's De Somniis and Josephus's Antiquities 15.136 both reference angelic involvement at Sinai. The LXX of Deuteronomy 33:2 reads "at his right hand were angels" where the Hebrew has "from his right hand was a fiery law." So Paul is working within an existing interpretive framework. Here's where the critical read lands. The Exodus narrative itself, in its plain reading, does NOT include angelic mediators. YHWH speaks, Moses hears, the people tremble and refuse direct revelation (20:18-21), and Moses becomes the mediator. But the mediator in Exodus is Moses, not angels plus Moses. The angelic-mediator tradition is a second-temple development, not an exegetical entailment of the Pentateuchal text. Paul in Galatians 3 is using this tradition for a specific polemical purpose — he's diminishing the Torah's ontological status to make room for Christ as a superior mediator. The more direct the law's origin, the harder for Paul to relativize it; the more layers of mediation (angels, then human mediator), the easier. Martyn in the AB Galatians commentary argues Paul is deliberately minimizing the law's divine directness. So Paul isn't just reporting a tradition; he's weaponizing it theologically. The contradiction between Exodus and Galatians is real, and the second-temple angelic-mediation tradition is interesting context but doesn't erase the difference in how Sinai is described.

contradictions.question: How should strangers be treated?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 19:34 and Deuteronomy 10:19 command Israel to love the stranger (ger) as themselves, remembering that they were strangers in Egypt. Deuteronomy 7:2, however, commands utter destruction and no mercy for the Canaanite nations Israel is displacing. The contradiction is between two opposite imperatives toward outsiders — welcome/love vs. exterminate.
contradictions.commentary: This is a case where the apologist harmonization has lexical and historical precision but doesn't fully resolve the moral tension. The argument: the word translated "stranger" in Leviticus 19:34 and Deuteronomy 10:19 is ger, which means resident alien — a foreigner living among Israel under Israelite authority, who has accepted the covenantal framework. The "strangers" marked for destruction in Deuteronomy 7:2 are the specific Canaanite nations (Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites) who must be cleared from the land to prevent idolatrous contamination. Different Hebrew category, different theological function. Copan runs this line in Is God a Moral Monster?, as do Merrill (NAC Deuteronomy) and Tigay (JPS). The lexical distinction is genuine — ger (resident alien) and nokri (foreigner) do mark different statuses in biblical law, and the herem (devoted destruction) of Deuteronomy 7 is specifically targeted at Canaanite nations, not at individual travelers or immigrants. Good. So the apologist can correctly say these commands are about different populations with different statuses under Israelite law. Here's what the harmonization doesn't resolve. The Canaanite herem in Deuteronomy 7:2 and 20:16-18 is not just "displacement" — it's total extermination of men, women, children, and livestock, with the stated theological justification being to prevent religious contamination. Critical scholars including John J. Collins, Susan Niditch, and Walter Brueggemann have extensively engaged with the moral and historical problems posed by these texts. Niditch in War in the Hebrew Bible categorizes this as a "ban ideology" that is theologically coherent within ANE warfare categories but morally toxic by modern standards. Collins in Does the Bible Justify Violence? argues that even if you grant the lexical distinction between ger and Canaanite, the Deuteronomic command to slaughter entire populations functions as a biblical warrant for violent xenophobia that later readers have repeatedly invoked. The apologist is right that "stranger" in Lev 19:34 and "stranger" in Deut 7:2 map to different Hebrew categories with different statuses — the SAB oversimplifies. But the deeper contradiction between an ethic of hospitality to outsiders and an ethic of total extermination of specified outsiders is real, textually embedded, and not dissolved by showing that two different Hebrew words are involved.

contradictions.question: Is only God holy?
contradictions.summary: Revelation 15:4 declares that God alone is holy, framing holiness as an exclusive divine attribute. The Torah and 1 Peter tell Israel and the church that they must be holy because God is holy, making holiness something creatures are commanded to possess. One passage reserves holiness for God; the other insists humans share it.
contradictions.commentary:
The apologist move here is predictable — page one of the playbook. Archer and Köstenberger will argue that Revelation 15:4 means God is holy in a unique ontological sense, while Leviticus 11:44, 19:2, and 1 Peter 1:16 speak of derivative, covenantal holiness. Different categories of holiness, no contradiction. That harmonization has real exegetical weight. The Hebrew qadosh and the Greek hagios both carry a primary sense of "set apart," and the Priestly call to "be holy" (Lev 19:2) is structurally a mimetic command — imitate the set-apartness of YHWH.

Here's where it falls apart. Revelation 15:4 is drawing on Septuagintal language (hosios, not hagios) and functions as a doxology echoing Psalm 86 and Jeremiah 10. The writer of Revelation is not carving out an ontological category that excludes creaturely holiness — he is praising God in liturgical absolutes. The contradiction only appears if you force both passages to be flat propositional statements about the distribution of the attribute "holy." That is a bad reading of both. The SAB framing atomizes the verses from their liturgical and ethical contexts.

Critical scholarship has been clear on this for decades. Jacob Milgrom's work on the Holiness Code shows that P and H deliberately extend holiness from the sanctuary outward to the people and the land — holiness is scalar and relational, not a zero-sum property. Baruch Schwartz and Israel Knohl develop this further. The "contradiction" here is really a genre collision between doxological hyperbole and covenantal ethics. That is of course a subjective read on the rhetorical genre, but the literary evidence is lopsided. Verdict: a weak contradiction at the surface level, strong only if you refuse to read either passage on its own terms.
