contradictions.question: How did David kill Goliath?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 17:49-50 says David killed Goliath with a sling and a stone and that "there was no sword in the hand of David." The very next verse, 1 Samuel 17:51, has David running over, drawing Goliath's own sword, and killing him with it. Within two verses Goliath dies twice by two different weapons.
contradictions.commentary:
Read the verses back to back and the tension is right there on the page. Verse 50 closes with an emphatic editorial summary: "David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and smote the Philistine, and slew him; but there was no sword in the hand of David." That's a definitive statement of cause of death. Then verse 51 immediately has David running up, taking Goliath's sword out of its sheath, "and slew him." The root in both verses is the same — mwt, "to die/kill" — though the stems differ (hiphil wayemitehu in v. 50, polel waymotetehu in v. 51), and both verbs translate as "and he killed him."

The standard harmonization treats verse 50 as a summary statement and verse 51 as the detail. Archer, Kaiser, and Tsumura in the NICOT volume all argue that the stone knocked Goliath unconscious or wounded him fatally, and the sword stroke was the coup de grace. Tsumura specifically argues that the Hebrew narrative regularly uses summary-then-detail structure and verse 51's "slew him" should be read as "finished him off." That is at least a coherent reading of the Hebrew syntax.

The problem with the harmonization is verse 50's explicit clause "there was no sword in the hand of David" — that is the narrator inserting a comment for emphasis, not a summary of stage-one of a two-stage kill. The narrator is signaling that the manner of death matters theologically: the LORD saves not by sword but by sling. Then verse 51 walks that back. McCarter notes again that the doublet problem is at work here too — verses 12-31, 50, and 55-18:5 are all in the MT "plus" material relative to LXX-B. The shorter Septuagint reading drops verse 50 entirely. If you take LXX-B as primary, the contradiction disappears because verse 50 was added later and clashed with the original verse 51.

So the apologist has to either accept that one of the two kill-statements is a redactional gloss (which makes the canonical text a stitched document), or insist that "there was no sword in the hand of David" was a stylistic flourish the narrator immediately undermined. Take your pick. The textual data strongly favors the redactional explanation. The harmonization is grammatically possible but it requires the narrator to mean the opposite of what he just emphatically said.

contradictions.question: Who killed Goliath?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 17 credits David with killing Goliath of Gath. 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim killed Goliath the Gittite, identifying Goliath specifically by the same weapon-description ("the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam") used for Goliath in 1 Samuel 17:7. The Chronicler in 1 Chronicles 20:5 "fixes" the problem by inserting "the brother of" before Goliath's name — a transparent harmonization.
contradictions.commentary:
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19 is the smoking gun. It reads, without ambiguity, that Elhanan ben Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite slew et-golyat hag-gitti — Goliath the Gittite — and the spear description matches 1 Samuel 17:7 word for word. The Chronicler, writing centuries later and aware that this clashes with the famous David-vs-Goliath story, rewrites the verse to read "Elhanan son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite." Look at the Hebrew: the Chronicler took beit-ha-lakhmi ("the Bethlehemite") from 2 Samuel and reparsed it as et-lakhmi akhi ("Lahmi the brother of"). It's a literal letter-shuffle harmonization in the Chronicler's source text.

The apologetic response is the standard appeal to textual corruption: 2 Samuel 21:19 is scribally damaged and 1 Chronicles 20:5 preserves the original reading. Archer takes this line, so does the NIV Study Bible footnote, so does Tsumura in NICOT. The textual argument is that a scribe miscopied the original "Lahmi the brother of Goliath" as "Bethlehemite Goliath," creating a phantom contradiction.

The critical scholarship reverses the direction of dependence. McCarter, Anderson in the WBC volume on 2 Samuel, and Auld in the OTL volume on Samuel all argue 2 Samuel 21:19 is the older, harder reading and 1 Chronicles 20:5 is the smoothing. The principle is lectio difficilior potior — the more difficult reading is more likely original, because scribes harmonize toward coherence, not toward awkward contradictions. The Elhanan-killed-Goliath reading is theologically embarrassing; nobody would invent it. The Chronicler's fix is theologically convenient; that's exactly what a later editor would produce. Add to that the parallel verse in 2 Samuel 23:24 listing "Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem" as one of David's mighty men — possibly the same Elhanan, possibly a doublet — and the original tradition starts to look like Elhanan was the actual Goliath-killer and David inherited the feat in a later legendary expansion.

The parsimonious account is the one almost every critical scholar offers: Elhanan killed Goliath in the older tradition, the David-Goliath story is a secondary literary development (or transferred legend), and the Chronicler did exactly the kind of harmonization that betrays awareness of the underlying problem. The apologetic "scribal error" defense reverses the textual-critical principles it claims to apply, and it requires the Chronicler to have access to a manuscript reading nobody else had — except, conveniently, the one that resolves the embarrassment.

contradictions.question: When did Saul meet David?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 16:21-23 has David enter Saul's court as a beloved armor-bearer and harpist whom Saul personally requests from Jesse. One chapter later, 1 Samuel 17:55-58 has Saul not knowing who David is after the Goliath fight, asking Abner whose son this youth is, and then asking David himself. The same king either knows David well or has never seen him.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the same doublet problem as entry 223, viewed from Saul's angle. 1 Samuel 16:21-23 is unambiguous: David comes to Saul, stands before him, Saul loves him "greatly," makes him armor-bearer, sends a formal note to Jesse asking that David stay in court, and David is the personal music therapist who calms Saul's evil-spirit episodes. That is a deep working relationship. Then in 17:55 Saul watches David go out against Goliath and asks Abner, "whose son is this youth?" Abner — captain of Saul's entire army, who would have known the king's armor-bearer — also has no idea. After the fight, Saul asks David personally: "whose son art thou, thou young man?"

The apologetic harmonization runs in two flavors. Flavor one (Archer, Kaiser): Saul wasn't asking who David was, he was asking about David's family for the purpose of the reward in 17:25 (whoever kills Goliath gets the king's daughter and tax exemption for the father's house). Flavor two (Youngblood, Tsumura): Saul's mental deterioration was such that he genuinely didn't recognize his own armor-bearer, plus David had visibly aged or changed appearance during the gap.

Flavor one fights the text. Saul's question to Abner — "whose son is this youth?" — uses ben-mi zeh ha-na'ar, the phrasing for personal identification, and Abner's answer is "as thy soul liveth, O king, I cannot tell." That is not bureaucratic genealogy-gathering; that is Abner saying he doesn't know who the kid is. If David were Saul's armor-bearer, Abner's response is impossible. Flavor two requires Saul's mental deterioration to extend to Abner as well, and to all of Saul's court, which is a stretch.

The critical-scholarship answer is the same as the Goliath-doublet case. McCarter, Auld, and Hertzberg all argue 1 Samuel 16:14-23 and 1 Samuel 17 reflect two originally independent David-court-entry traditions that the redactor placed side by side. LXX-B omits the verses that create the worst contradictions (17:55-18:5). The MT preserves the conflation; LXX-B preserves an earlier shorter tradition. That is not an apologetic-friendly explanation, but it is the one that fits the manuscript evidence and the seam analysis. Saying Saul had two completely different first encounters with David is exactly what you would expect if the text is two stitched traditions, and it is exactly what you would not expect if a single coherent history was being told.

contradictions.question: How many Philistine foreskins did David buy his first wife with?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 18:27 says David killed 200 Philistines and brought back their foreskins to Saul as the bride-price for Michal. 2 Samuel 3:14 quotes David himself claiming he paid 100 foreskins. The text disagrees with itself, and David's own retrospective is half the original number.
contradictions.commentary:
Saul originally asked for 100 (1 Samuel 18:25). David delivered 200. Years later, asking for Michal to be returned to him after Saul's death, David says in 2 Samuel 3:14, "deliver me my wife Michal, which I espoused to me for an hundred foreskins of the Philistines." He cites the original demand, not the actual delivery.

The apologetic move here is straightforward and not crazy: David is referencing the contractual price Saul set, not the bonus he threw in. Archer and Youngblood both run this line. McCarter actually concedes it has some force — David's framing in 2 Samuel 3 is legal-formal, referring to the bride-price as covenanted rather than as delivered.

But there is a textual wrinkle that complicates the harmonization. The Septuagint and 4QSam-a both read 100 in 1 Samuel 18:27 as well, not 200. So one branch of the Hebrew tradition has David delivering exactly what was asked, and the contradiction simply doesn't exist there. The MT preserves the inflated 200 — possibly an early scribal enhancement of David's prowess, possibly the original. McCarter argues 100 is original and 200 is a glorifying expansion. Auld and Anderson lean the same way.

This one is a soft contradiction. If you accept MT as primary, you get a real number-clash that requires the "legal price vs. delivered amount" harmonization to resolve. If you accept the Qumran/LXX reading at 100, the numbers match and there is no contradiction. Either way you concede something — either the text has internal inconsistency or the text has manuscript variation. The apologetic move that wants both MT inerrancy and harmonized numbers needs to do work on both fronts. That is of course a textual-critical judgment call, but the manuscript evidence is what it is.

answers.answer_explanation: And David sent messengers to Ishbosheth Saul's son, saying, Deliver me my wife Michal, which I espoused to me for an hundred foreskins of the Philistines. 2 Samuel 3:14

Wherefore David arose and went, he and his men, and slew of the Philistines two hundred men; and David brought their foreskins, and they gave them in full tale to the king, that he might be the king's son in law. And Saul gave him Michal his daughter to wife. 1 Samuel 18:27

contradictions.question: When did Saul become David's enemy?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 18:8-9 says Saul began to eye David with suspicion immediately after the women's song crediting David with greater slaughter than Saul — "Saul has slain his thousands and David his ten thousands." 1 Samuel 18:27-29 marks the turn after the foreskin bride-price, when "Saul became David's enemy continually." The text gives two different ignition points for the rivalry within the same chapter.
contradictions.commentary:
1 Samuel 18 is a notorious chapter for narrative ordering. The women's song happens in verse 8, Saul "eyed David from that day and forward" in verse 9, and Saul's first attempt to kill David with a spear comes in verse 11. Then verses 12-16 narrate ongoing fear of David, the Merab-then-Michal marriage plot to use Philistines to kill David is verses 17-25, the foreskins are delivered in verse 27, and the chapter's summary in verse 29 says Saul "became David's enemy continually."

The apologist read here is the easiest of the bunch — the chapter is describing escalation. Saul's initial suspicion in verse 8 evolves into ongoing fear in verses 12-16 and finally hardens into continual enmity in verse 29. Tsumura and Youngblood both argue the contradiction is the SAB reading too much into a literary-summary phrase. There's some force to that. The word "continually" in verse 29 reasonably reads as the endpoint of the escalation, not a fresh beginning.

Where it gets interesting is the manuscript evidence again. LXX-B is significantly shorter through 1 Samuel 18 than the MT, omitting verses 10-11 (the first spear-throw), verses 17-19 (the Merab episode), and parts of verses 21, 26-27, and 29-30. The shorter LXX preserves a cleaner narrative: song-in-18:7, Saul's suspicion, Michal plot, foreskins delivered, full enmity. McCarter argues again that LXX-B is more original and MT is conflation. If you read the MT as primary you get a chapter that escalates messily across multiple ignition points; if you read LXX-B as primary the escalation is single-tracked.

This one is a soft contradiction. If the contradiction is just "the chapter has two summary statements about when the enmity started," the apologetic escalation read works fine. If the contradiction is "the chapter is internally chaotic because it conflates source material," the critical-scholarship account is more parsimonious. I lean toward calling this a poorly-formed contradiction question — the chapter is messy, but "messy" is not the same as "contradictory." That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. The SAB framing overstates a real seam problem as a binary contradiction.

contradictions.question: When did "Is Saul among the prophets?" become a proverb?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 10:11-12 gives the origin of the proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?" when Saul prophesies among Samuel's prophet band shortly after his anointing. 1 Samuel 19:24 gives a second, independent origin story for the same proverb — Saul stripping naked and prophesying before Samuel while pursuing David. Two different etiologies for the same saying.
contradictions.commentary:
These are classic etiological doublets. Both passages explicitly say "wherefore they say" or "it became a proverb" — the narrator is anchoring a folk-saying to a specific event. The problem is they anchor it to two different events. In 1 Samuel 10, Saul is freshly anointed, has a positive spirit-experience among the prophets at Gibeah, and the saying captures public surprise that the new king has a prophetic streak. In 1 Samuel 19, Saul has gone full antagonist, his messengers all get caught in prophetic ecstasy when sent to grab David, Saul himself comes and strips naked and prophesies for a day and a night, and the same saying is again given as the etiology.

The apologist line is that both episodes contributed to the proverb's currency — the saying became proverbial in chapter 10 and got reinforced in chapter 19. Archer and Walter Kaiser run this. It's not implausible on its face, but it ignores the textual signal. Both passages use the etiological formula "therefore it became a proverb" or "wherefore they say," which is Hebrew narrative shorthand for "this is the event that produced the saying." Doing that twice for the same saying is textbook source-doublet behavior.

The critical reading is that 1 Samuel preserves two independent traditions about Saul and ecstatic prophecy, one positive (chapter 10) and one humiliating (chapter 19), and the redactor included both with their separate etiologies intact. McCarter, Hertzberg, and Auld all treat these as parallel traditions rather than sequential events. The two stories serve opposite theological functions — chapter 10 legitimates Saul through prophetic experience, chapter 19 delegitimates him by showing his prophetic frenzy as pathetic and out of control. The Deuteronomist had both traditions in his sources and kept both, even though the etiological formulas can only really work once.

The "both events contributed" defense is functionally an admission that one of the two narrators is wrong about being the origin. Either chapter 10 "originated" the saying and chapter 19 is a later application, or chapter 19 originated it and chapter 10 is anachronistic, or both narrators are independently claiming to be the origin and at least one is wrong. The text won't let you have one neat answer. That is exactly the signature of compiled source material rather than unified composition.

contradictions.question: When was the last time that Samuel saw Saul?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 15:35 states emphatically that "Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death." 1 Samuel 19:24 then has Saul stripping naked and prophesying before Samuel during the David-pursuit episode. The narrator first closes the door on Samuel/Saul contact, then opens it again four chapters later.
contradictions.commentary:
1 Samuel 15:35 is unambiguous. After Samuel hews Agag to pieces and rebukes Saul over the Amalek incident, the chapter closes: "And Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul." That is a categorical end-of-relationship statement. Then in 1 Samuel 19:24, Saul shows up at Naioth in Ramah where Samuel is staying with the prophet band, gets overwhelmed by the spirit, strips, and prophesies in Samuel's presence. The text says explicitly that Saul "prophesied before Samuel" — Samuel is right there.

The apologetic harmonization reads 1 Samuel 15:35 as "Samuel did not visit Saul socially" or "in his official prophetic capacity" — meaning the chance encounter in chapter 19 doesn't violate it because Saul came to Samuel, not the other way around. Archer takes this line, and Tsumura defends a version of it. Hebrew lo' yasaf shemu'el lir'ot et-sha'ul, literally "Samuel did not continue to see Saul," can grammatically support "did not seek out" rather than "did not see at all."

The Hebrew can technically bear that, but the verse explicitly extends the no-seeing "until the day of his death," and the parallel verse in 1 Samuel 28 has the witch of Endor summoning Samuel's ghost specifically because Saul has no living prophet to consult — Samuel will not deal with him. The narrative logic of 1 Samuel as a whole is that Samuel withdrew from Saul permanently after Amalek. Hertzberg, McCarter, and Auld all treat 19:24 as an originally independent tradition spliced into the David-flight narrative, originally unconnected to 1 Samuel 15:35. The redactor put them together without resolving the contradiction. The witch-of-Endor episode in chapter 28 effectively re-confirms 15:35 — Samuel and Saul have not seen each other in life since chapter 15.

There is also a reading where 19:24 is actually a doublet of 10:11-12 with the same proverb-etiology (see entry 229) and so the entire scene is a literary repetition rather than a separate event. If that is right, the "meeting" in 19:24 is a doublet artifact, not a chronological problem. Either way — splicing of independent traditions or doublet of chapter 10 — the parsimonious explanation is compositional, not historical. The apologetic "Samuel didn't initiate the visit" reading is grammatically possible but theologically forced and ignores the rest of the Samuel cycle.

contradictions.question: When David fled to Nob, what was the priest's name?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 21:1 names Ahimelech as the priest at Nob who feeds David the showbread. Jesus in Mark 2:25-26 references the same incident and attributes it to "Abiathar the high priest." The Synoptic parallels in Matthew 12 and Luke 6 quietly drop the name.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the contradiction that has launched a thousand harmonization attempts because it sits in the mouth of Jesus himself. 1 Samuel 21:1 is unambiguous — David came to Nob, the priest was Ahimelech, Ahimelech gave him the showbread. Abiathar was Ahimelech's son (1 Samuel 22:20) and only became high priest after his father was butchered by Doeg at Saul's order. So at the time of the showbread incident, Abiathar was not the high priest. Mark has Jesus saying he was.

The apologetic moves here are extensive. Move one: the Greek epi Abiathar archiereos can be translated "in the passage about Abiathar the high priest" (using epi as a textual reference marker like 12:26's "in the passage about the bush"). This is the favored move of D. A. Carson in his Matthew commentary and is endorsed by Craig Blomberg. Move two: Abiathar was high priest at the time of the writing of the narrative and so Mark uses his more famous title proleptically. Move three (Archer): Ahimelech is Abiathar's father in some texts and his son in others (cf. 2 Samuel 8:17), so there may be two priests named Ahimelech and Abiathar functioning together, and Jesus is right.

The textual data is brutal on these defenses. Matthew 12:3-4 and Luke 6:3-4 both repeat the Mark story and both drop the name Abiathar entirely. The Synoptic-redaction inference is obvious: Matthew and Luke noticed the error and silently fixed it. Bart Ehrman in Jesus, Interrupted explicitly walks through this case, as does Joel Marcus in the Anchor Bible Mark commentary. Marcus rejects the "in the passage about" reading because epi with a genitive proper name in this construction in Mark almost universally means "during the time of" or "in the lifetime of" — Marcus cites Mark 12:26 itself, where epi tou batou ("in the passage about the bush") uses a different construction with a definite article that 2:26 lacks. Move three (two priest pairs) requires assuming the narrative is genealogically chaotic precisely where Jesus speaks, which is unfalsifiable special pleading.

The most parsimonious account: Mark made a mistake, or Mark's source made a mistake, or the historical Jesus made a mistake about an Old Testament detail. Matthew and Luke noticed and silently corrected. The harmonization industry depends on a grammatical reading of epi that the Markan Greek does not naturally support, and it requires both later evangelists to have independently dropped the name without comment, which is itself evidence they saw the problem.

contradictions.question: Was David alone when asking for the holy bread at Nob?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 21:1 has Ahimelech ask David "why art thou alone, and no man with thee?" — implying David arrived solo. Jesus in the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew 12:3-4, Mark 2:25-26, Luke 6:3-4) explicitly says David's companions ate the showbread with him. The Old Testament source says David came alone; Jesus says he had companions.
contradictions.commentary:
Reading 1 Samuel 21 in context, the loneliness is the point of the scene. Ahimelech is afraid when David arrives without an entourage — "why art thou alone, and no man with thee?" David lies in response, claiming the king sent him on a secret mission and that he has "appointed his servants to such and such a place." So David is concealing his fugitive status by pretending his men are stationed elsewhere; the men are not present at the showbread transaction. Then David asks for "five loaves of bread" specifically — which all three Synoptics latch onto as evidence that David had companions.

The apologetic harmonization runs like this: David's men were nearby but not at the moment of the bread request, and David collected the bread to bring back to them. Archer, Blomberg, and Carson all take this line. The five-loaves request supports the idea that David was provisioning multiple people. So Jesus's framing — "David and they that were with him" — is technically accurate in context even though the actual scene at Nob has David appearing alone.

The critical reading is more complicated. The companions in 1 Samuel 21 are a fiction David invents to cover his solo flight; the text does not actually confirm they exist. When David next appears in 22:1 he goes to the cave of Adullam alone and his family then "and every one that was in distress" rallies to him there. So the companions whose existence Jesus presupposes either (a) were already with David at Nob (contradicting 21:1's solitude) or (b) joined him afterward at Adullam (in which case Jesus is wrong that they ate the showbread). The five-loaves request can be read as part of David's cover story rather than a real-need-for-companions inventory.

This is a softer contradiction than the Abiathar one because the Synoptic gospel writers had a hand in framing the incident to support their Sabbath-violation argument — Jesus needs the showbread story to feature multiple people eating in violation of priestly law so it parallels his disciples plucking grain. Mark's framing of David "and they that were with him" may be loose with the source text precisely because Mark needs the parallel to hold. Ehrman, Marcus, and Collins all note this redactional pressure on the showbread tradition. The simpler reading is that the Synoptic Jesus is shaping the David story to fit his argument, and the original 1 Samuel narrative has David functionally alone.

contradictions.question: Was Abiathar the father or the son of Ahimelech?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 22:20, 23:6, and 30:7 consistently identify Abiathar as the son of Ahimelech. 2 Samuel 8:17, 1 Chronicles 18:16, and 1 Chronicles 24:6 reverse the relationship and call Ahimelech the son of Abiathar. The genealogy contradicts itself across the two main historical books.
contradictions.commentary:
The 1 Samuel data is consistent and detailed: Abiathar escapes the massacre at Nob in 22:20 as "one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub." He shows up with the ephod at 23:6 as "Abiathar the son of Ahimelech." In 30:7 David addresses him as "Abiathar the priest, Ahimelech's son." This is a sustained, multi-attestation identification.

Then 2 Samuel 8:17 lists David's court officials: "Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests." 1 Chronicles 18:16 repeats this — "Abimelech the son of Abiathar" (textual variant). 1 Chronicles 24:6 again has "Ahimelech the son of Abiathar." Three witnesses for the reversed relationship in the Chronicler's tradition and one in 2 Samuel.

The apologetic harmonization is that there were two pairs of Ahimelech/Abiathar — that Abiathar named his son after his father, which was common Israelite practice. So in 1 Samuel we meet Abiathar son of the elder Ahimelech, and in 2 Samuel 8:17 and Chronicles we meet a younger Ahimelech who is Abiathar's son. Archer runs this, as does Keil-Delitzsch in their commentary on Samuel.

The critical-scholarship account is that 2 Samuel 8:17 contains a textual corruption — McCarter, Anderson, and Wellhausen all argue the original read "Abiathar son of Ahimelech, son of Ahitub" and a scribe swapped the names. Wellhausen's emendation has been widely accepted; the Lucianic recension of the LXX may preserve the corrected form. This is one of the rare cases where the apologetic two-pairs solution and the critical scribal-error solution converge on the same outcome — the relationship really is Abiathar-son-of-Ahimelech — but they disagree on whether the MT of 2 Samuel/Chronicles is reliable. The apologetic move keeps the MT inerrant and posits a second priest pair the text never explicitly identifies. The critical move admits a scribal error preserved in the MT.

Either way, the surface text contradicts itself. The harmonization either invents undocumented family duplicates or concedes textual corruption. Take your pick — but you can't have both an inerrant MT and a consistent genealogy.

contradictions.question: Did Saul inquire of the Lord?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 28:6 says explicitly that Saul inquired of the Lord and the Lord refused to answer. 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 says Saul died because he "inquired not of the Lord." The two texts disagree about whether Saul's failure was that he tried and got no answer, or that he never tried.
contradictions.commentary:
1 Samuel 28:6 is unambiguous: "And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets." Saul tried every legitimate channel of revelation. The text frames the witch-of-Endor consultation as a desperate last resort after Yahweh ghosted him. 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 retells Saul's death and offers this theological summary: "So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD ... and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to inquire of it; and inquired not of the LORD: therefore he slew him." The Chronicler's verdict is that Saul did not inquire of Yahweh at all.

The standard apologetic harmonization is that the Chronicler means Saul did not inquire properly or did not inquire with a faithful heart. Archer, Eugene Merrill in his Kregel Chronicles commentary, and Andrew Hill in NIVAC Chronicles all run versions of this. The Hebrew verb darash means both "to inquire" and "to seek with proper devotion," and so the Chronicler is supposedly emphasizing the quality of Saul's seeking rather than its existence.

The critical reading rejects that as semantic overreading. The Chronicler is doing what the Chronicler routinely does — rewriting the Deuteronomistic History to underline a theological point. The Deuteronomist in 1 Samuel 28 tells a complicated story: Saul did the right thing first (inquired of Yahweh, got nothing), then did the wrong thing (consulted a necromancer). The Chronicler simplifies and moralizes: Saul died because he was a covenant-breaker who went to a medium instead of Yahweh. The Chronicler erases the inconvenient detail that Saul actually tried Yahweh first, because that detail complicates the theology.

Sara Japhet, Ralph Klein, and Gary Knoppers all treat this as a paradigmatic case of the Chronicler's theological revisionism. Japhet specifically notes that the Chronicler's account of Saul's death (in his single chapter on Saul before pivoting to David) is calibrated to make Saul a pure foil for David, and any mitigating circumstances in Samuel are dropped. The harmonization that wants both 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles to be precisely accurate has to twist darash to mean two different things in two texts. The simpler reading is the Chronicler is doing redaction-with-an-agenda, and it shows.

answers.answer: Saul did not inquire of the Lord.

contradictions.question: Was Jesus the first to rise from the dead?
contradictions.summary: Acts 26:23 and 1 Corinthians 15:20 call Jesus the firstfruits of the resurrection and the first to rise from the dead. But the witch of Endor in 1 Samuel 28:11-14 raises Samuel from the dead centuries earlier, and the Hebrew Bible has Elijah and Elisha raising others (1 Kings 17, 2 Kings 4, 2 Kings 13), as does Jesus himself in the Gospels (Lazarus, Jairus's daughter, the widow of Nain's son). Jesus is not chronologically first.
contradictions.commentary:
Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Christ "the firstfruits of them that slept," and Acts 26:23 has Paul before Festus claiming Christ would be "the first that should rise from the dead." These are theological claims. The Hebrew Bible has the witch of Endor explicitly raising Samuel — "an old man cometh up; and he is covered with a mantle. And Saul perceived that it was Samuel" — and Samuel speaks at length to Saul before predicting Saul's death. Elijah resuscitates the widow's son in 1 Kings 17, Elisha resuscitates the Shunammite's son in 2 Kings 4, and 2 Kings 13:21 has a corpse revive on contact with Elisha's bones. In the Gospels, Jesus himself raises Lazarus, Jairus's daughter, and the Nain widow's son — all chronologically before Jesus's own resurrection.

The standard apologetic distinction is between resuscitation (returning to mortal life, eventually dying again) and resurrection (immortal eschatological body, never dying again). Paul's claim is that Jesus is the first to undergo the latter. N. T. Wright in The Resurrection of the Son of God makes this argument at length — Samuel, Lazarus, et al. were resuscitated to mortal life and died again, while Jesus rose with a glorified body that does not die. Acts 26:23's "first that should rise from the dead" is read as eschatological-resurrection-specific.

This distinction works for Paul but has a problem for the Samuel case. Samuel in 1 Samuel 28 is not resuscitated to mortal life — he's brought up from Sheol in a spectral form, speaks, and presumably returns. If the apologist wants "resuscitation vs. resurrection" to do the work, then Samuel's appearance is neither, and the verse can be discarded as not really being a "rising from the dead." But that just means the SAB has picked a weak example. The Lazarus and Jairus's-daughter examples are tighter — Jesus does explicitly raise people from the dead before his own resurrection, and those resurrections happen in the same Gospel narrative.

The Wright distinction is theologically coherent but it is post-hoc to Paul's text. Paul does not say "Christ is the first to rise with a glorified body" — he says Christ is the firstfruits. The apologist read requires reading "firstfruits" as a technical eschatological-body marker rather than a chronological one. That is plausible but it is exegesis-by-need. The simpler reading is that Paul is making a theological claim that doesn't bother to harmonize with the pre-Christian Jewish revival traditions. The Hebrew Bible writers and the synoptic gospel writers did not share Paul's framework, and the texts disagree on whose resurrection counts as the first.

contradictions.question: Did Saul and Samuel kill all the Amalekites?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 15:7-8 says Saul utterly destroyed all the Amalekites with the edge of the sword. The same chapter lets Agag's mother survive (15:33), David is still slaughtering Amalekites years later in 1 Samuel 27:8 and 30:1-17 (with 400 escaping), and an Amalekite kills Saul in 2 Samuel 1:8-10. The text contradicts its own "utterly destroyed all" claim multiple times within a few chapters.
contradictions.commentary:
1 Samuel 15 is the herem chapter — total annihilation, every man, woman, infant, suckling, and livestock except what Saul illicitly spared. Verses 7-8: "Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, that is over against Egypt. And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword." Then in the very same chapter, verse 33: Samuel tells Agag "as the sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women." Agag's mother is alive, which means the "all the people" of verse 8 was not actually all the people.

It gets worse. 1 Samuel 27:8-9 has David raiding the Amalekites ("David and his men went up, and invaded the Geshurites, and the Gezrites, and the Amalekites: for those nations were of old the inhabitants of the land"). 1 Samuel 30:1 has Amalekites still numerous enough to sack Ziklag, and David's revenge slaughter in 30:17 explicitly lets 400 escape. Then 2 Samuel 1:8-10 has an Amalekite present at Saul's death — the very people Saul allegedly exterminated produce his executioner. And in Esther, centuries later, an Agagite is grand vizier of Persia (see entry 221).

The apologetic position is that "utterly destroyed all" is ancient Near Eastern war-rhetoric hyperbole, not a literal claim. Paul Copan in Is God a Moral Monster?, Nicholas Wolterstorff, and Richard Hess all argue this from the comparative ANE evidence — Egyptian, Assyrian, and Moabite (Mesha Stele) royal inscriptions routinely claim total annihilation that was demonstrably not literal. The point of the rhetoric is decisive victory, not census-accurate body count. Lawson Stone defended a version of this for the Joshua conquest narratives.

The hyperbole reading is genuinely well-supported by comparative epigraphy. The Mesha Stele's claim that Omri "utterly destroyed" Israel is a useful parallel — Israel demonstrably persisted. So the rhetorical-hyperbole defense has real evidentiary backing. But it cuts both ways. If you concede 1 Samuel 15:8 is hyperbolic, you are conceding the text reports things that did not literally happen — and the same standard then has to apply to Joshua, Judges, and elsewhere. The herem texts cannot be both literal divine commands and convention-bound rhetoric. The apologist who wants Yahweh's command to be a real moral act AND the report to be hyperbolic ANE convention has a tension to resolve. Most critical scholars (McCarter, Hertzberg, Klein, Niditch) just call it what it is: the chapter is a stylized theological narrative in which the literal claims do not have to harmonize with later chapters because the genre does not demand it.

contradictions.question: How did Saul die?
contradictions.summary: 1 Samuel 31:4-6 and 1 Chronicles 10:4 say Saul committed suicide by falling on his sword. 2 Samuel 1:8-10 has an Amalekite claim he killed Saul at Saul's request. 2 Samuel 21:12 says the Philistines killed Saul. 1 Chronicles 10:14 says Yahweh personally killed him. Four different causes of death across four different texts.
contradictions.commentary:
1 Samuel 31:4 has Saul, gravely wounded, ask his armor-bearer to finish him off. The armor-bearer refuses out of fear, so Saul falls on his own sword. The armor-bearer then falls on his own sword too. 1 Chronicles 10:4 repeats this account essentially verbatim. So far, suicide.

2 Samuel 1:8-10 then has an Amalekite show up to David after the battle, claim he found Saul leaning on his spear, and that Saul personally asked the Amalekite to kill him because Saul was sure to die anyway. The Amalekite says he killed Saul and took the crown to David. 2 Samuel 21:12 says "the Philistines had slain Saul." 1 Chronicles 10:14 wraps up the death narrative with "the LORD ... slew him."

The traditional apologetic harmonization works through each claim. Suicide is the literal physical cause (1 Samuel 31, 1 Chronicles 10:4). The Amalekite is lying in 2 Samuel 1 to curry favor with David — David executes him anyway, but his story is fabricated. The Philistines "slew Saul" in 2 Samuel 21:12 in the sense that they put him in the situation that led to suicide; the Hebrew makah can mean "struck" in a broader sense. And Yahweh "slew him" in 1 Chronicles 10:14 theologically — every death is ultimately God's doing in the Deuteronomistic-Chronistic worldview. Archer, Youngblood, and Walter Kaiser all run versions of this stacked harmonization.

The Amalekite-was-lying answer is the strongest of the apologetic moves and is genuinely defensible — David's reaction (executing the Amalekite as if for regicide) only makes sense if the Amalekite's story is taken at face value within the narrative even if the narrator implicitly doubts it. McCarter and Anderson both note this is possible. The other harmonizations work but only by allowing the verb "to kill" to do progressively more metaphorical work across the texts. The Philistines did not literally kill Saul; they were the proximate threat. Yahweh did not literally kill Saul; he is the theological cause behind the historical event. Stack enough of those reinterpretations and you can harmonize any death account — but only by treating the texts as if they were all answering different questions.

The critical reading is that these are independent traditions about Saul's death, each making a different theological point. The Deuteronomist in 1 Samuel 31 wants Saul as the tragic suicide. The court history in 2 Samuel 1 wants the David-clears-his-conscience-of-Saul's-blood story, which requires a non-David killer. The Chronicler wants Saul's death as divine judgment for covenant breach. Each tradition foregrounds a different cause. They don't synthesize into one historical account — they reflect different theological agendas applied to a shared event. The apologetic synthesis works on paper but it requires four different definitions of "killed" to function.

contradictions.question: Did Saul's family die with him?
contradictions.summary: 1 Chronicles 10:6 says "Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together." 2 Samuel 2:1-7 then has Ishbosheth — Saul's son — made king of Israel after Saul's death. 2 Samuel 21 has David later handing over seven of Saul's descendants to be hanged. The "all his house died together" claim is contradicted by surviving family members appearing throughout 2 Samuel.
contradictions.commentary:
1 Chronicles 10:6 is sweeping: "So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together." The parallel in 1 Samuel 31:6 is narrower — "so Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together." The Chronicler globalizes "all his men" into "all his house."

The rest of Samuel demolishes the Chronicler's globalization. Ishbosheth, Saul's son, is made king over Israel by Abner in 2 Samuel 2:8-11. He reigns two years. Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, survives and ends up at David's table (2 Samuel 9). Rizpah, Saul's concubine, is alive in 2 Samuel 3 and 2 Samuel 21. And 2 Samuel 21:1-14 has David hand over seven of Saul's male descendants — Rizpah's two sons Armoni and Mephibosheth, plus the five sons of Saul's daughter Merab — to be hanged by the Gibeonites to end a famine. That is at minimum nine living members of Saul's house after the events of 1 Samuel 31.

The apologetic harmonization is the standard Chronicler-summary defense: the Chronicler is making a theological point about the end of Saul's dynastic legitimacy, not a literal census claim. Archer and Hill both argue "all his house" means "the rest of his fighting men with him at Gilboa" rather than every blood relative. Eugene Merrill in his Kregel Chronicles commentary takes a similar line, reading "house" as the military household rather than the family.

This reading has Hebrew lexical support — bayit ("house") can mean dynasty, family, or fighting unit depending on context. But the Chronicler's redactional move is doing more work than the apologist concedes. The Chronicler's account of Saul is a single chapter, structured to terminate Saul completely so David's kingship has no genealogical competition. Japhet, Klein, and Knoppers all argue the Chronicler deliberately compresses and exaggerates the end of Saul's house to underscore the theological discontinuity. The Chronicler knows about Ishbosheth — he just doesn't include him because Ishbosheth complicates the narrative. The contradiction is real at the surface level, but it is a deliberate Chronistic literary decision, not a factual error in the modern sense. Either way, the bare-text claim of 1 Chronicles 10:6 — that Saul's whole house died at Gilboa — is contradicted by the narrative of 2 Samuel that the Chronicler is supposedly summarizing.

contradictions.question: Who was David's second son?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 3:3 names David's second son born in Hebron as Chileab, son of Abigail. 1 Chronicles 3:1 names David's second son born in Hebron as Daniel, son of Abigail. Same mother, same birth-order slot, different name.
contradictions.commentary:
Both texts give the same list of David's first six sons born in Hebron in the same order, with the same mothers — except the second name. 2 Samuel 3:3 has "his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite." 1 Chronicles 3:1 has "the second Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess." Position matches, mother matches, name doesn't.

The apologetic harmonization is that this person had two names — Chileab and Daniel — and each text preferred one. Archer takes this line. Keil-Delitzsch and Youngblood agree. Multi-naming is well-attested in the Hebrew Bible (Jacob/Israel, Solomon/Jedidiah), and it's not unreasonable on the surface.

The textual-critical reading is messier. Some manuscripts of 2 Samuel and Chronicles show further variation: certain LXX manuscripts of 2 Samuel 3:3 read Daluyah or Daluiah, and the Lucianic recension preserves still other forms. McCarter argues the original name was probably Daniel ("God is my judge"), Chileab is a Hebrew variant or corruption, and the Daluyah readings reflect intermediate confusion. Anderson in WBC and Auld in OTL note the same textual messiness. Sara Japhet on Chronicles also flags the variant tradition.

The double-name hypothesis is possible but undocumented — neither text actually says "also called." The textual-variation hypothesis is documented — we have manuscript witnesses with different readings, suggesting scribal evolution of the name across transmission. Either way, the contradiction is at the textual surface. The apologist can save the inerrancy of both names only by positing an unmentioned dual identity; the critical scholar treats it as ordinary textual variation. This is a relatively minor contradiction — names are easy to corrupt in transmission — but it is real on the canonical surface, and the harmonization is post-hoc.

answers.answer_explanation: And unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. 2 Samuel 3:3
Now these were the sons of David, which were born unto him in Hebron; the firstborn Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; the second Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess. 1 Chronicles 3:1

contradictions.question: Who were the sons of David born in Hebron?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 3:2-5 lists David's six sons born in Hebron as Amnon, Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, and Ithream. 1 Chronicles 3:1-4 lists them as Amnon, Daniel, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, and Ithream. The lists agree on five of six, but the second son's name differs.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the same contradiction as entry 239, expanded to the full list. The two lists agree completely on first, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth — Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah, Ithream — and on the mothers. They diverge only on the second son's name (Chileab vs. Daniel). The mother (Abigail of Nabal/Carmelite) and the birth-order position match.

The apologetic move and the critical move are the same as in entry 239. Dual-name (Archer, Keil-Delitzsch) vs. textual variation (McCarter, Anderson, Japhet, Klein). The LXX manuscript tradition for 2 Samuel 3:3 preserves multiple readings (Daluyah, Daluiah, Chileab), which McCarter takes as evidence that the name was unstable in early transmission.

Where this entry adds something over the previous one is the comparative scope. The fact that the two lists agree on five of six entries shows they share a common source — they are not independent attestations. The Chronicler is using Samuel as a source and reproducing the list. The single point of divergence is therefore not two independent traditions disagreeing but a transmission variant at one point in a shared list. That actually strengthens the textual-corruption explanation: if the Chronicler had Samuel in front of him and reproduced the list with one name change, the change is either deliberate harmonization-of-an-unfamiliar-name or a copyist substitution. Neither one supports the dual-name hypothesis. Why would the Chronicler change a name but keep everything else identical, unless his Samuel manuscript already read "Daniel" or unless he is deliberately substituting?

The parsimonious account is that early transmission of the name varied (Chileab and Daniel both attested in different manuscript streams), the MT of Samuel preserved one form, the MT of Chronicles preserved the other, and there is no underlying historical fact about a dual name. Take your pick — but the dual-name hypothesis requires an unattested cultural detail (David's son had two names) while the textual variation hypothesis is supported by actual surviving manuscript variants.

contradictions.question: Was Solomon David's second or fourth son by Bathsheba?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 12 narrates the birth of Solomon as the immediate replacement child after the death of Bathsheba's first son, implying Solomon is her second son. 1 Chronicles 3:5 lists four sons born to David by Bathshua/Bathsheba in Jerusalem — Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon — making Solomon her fourth, not her second.
contradictions.commentary:
The Samuel narrative is built as a tight moral parable. Nathan confronts David, the first child of the adultery dies, David comforts Bathsheba, and she immediately bears Solomon. The text doesn't pause to insert two intermediate brothers between the dead infant and Solomon. That's the whole rhetorical point — the LORD took one child and gave back another, and the one He gave back is the heir. 2 Samuel 12 is a theodicy story, not a birth registry.

The Chronicler then comes along centuries later, working from his own genealogical sources, and gives a flat list of four Jerusalem sons by Bathshua daughter of Ammiel: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon. That's not a casual aside — Chronicles is obsessed with genealogies, and the order is deliberate. Solomon is listed fourth. The Chronicler is not telling the Bathsheba-Uriah story (he scrubs the adultery entirely), so he has no narrative reason to compress.

The harmonization apologists reach for is the standard one: 2 Samuel 12 never explicitly says Solomon was the second-born, it just narrates his birth without mentioning siblings. Technically true. But that requires reading 2 Samuel as a deliberately incomplete birth notice, with Shimea, Shobab, and Nathan slotted in silently between verses 24 and 25 — and it requires explaining why the narrator would say "she bare a son, and he called his name Solomon" right after the comfort scene if three other sons had already been born in between. The plain reading of Samuel and the genealogy in Chronicles point in different directions.

The parsimonious explanation is that the two authors are working from different traditions with different purposes. Samuel is a court narrative reshaped around David's sin and restoration. Chronicles is a post-exilic priestly recalculation of the royal line. Neither author was trying to coordinate with the other.

answers.answer_explanation: And Nathan departed unto his house. And the LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife bare unto David, and it was very sick. ... And David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in unto her, and lay with her: and she bare a son, and he called his name Solomon.
And these were born unto him in Jerusalem; Shimea, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon, four, of Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel.

contradictions.question: Where did God kill Uzza?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 6:6 locates Uzzah's death at "Nachon's threshingfloor." 1 Chronicles 13:9 locates the same event at "the threshingfloor of Chidon." Both texts describe the identical incident — Uzzah steadying the ark, the oxen stumbling, God striking him dead — but they name the location differently.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the most transparent Samuel-Chronicles divergences in the text. Same scene, same actor, same outcome, two different threshing-floor names. The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 6:6 reads Nodab/Nodan, and the textual apparatus shows scribes were already struggling with this name in antiquity. The Hebrew of Samuel has Nachon (nakon, which can also be read as a participle meaning "prepared"); Chronicles has Chidon (kidon, which can mean "javelin" or "destruction"). Either both are corrupted forms of a lost original, or the Chronicler is working from a different tradition entirely.

The standard apologetic move is to claim the threshing-floor had two names — owned by Nachon, sometimes called Chidon — or that one is a personal name and the other is a place-feature. Keil and Delitzsch made exactly this move in the nineteenth century. The problem is that nothing in either text supports this. Neither narrator hints at a dual name. The text in Samuel says "Nachon's threshingfloor." The text in Chronicles says "the threshingfloor of Chidon." The harmonizer is inventing a tradition neither author preserved to rescue a contradiction neither author noticed.

The critical reading is simpler. The Chronicler is working from Samuel as a base text but had access to variant traditions, or he is correcting what he found in his Vorlage. The textual history of Samuel is notoriously messy — the Qumran fragments (4QSam-a) show that the MT of Samuel has suffered significant corruption, and McCarter's Anchor Bible volume documents dozens of cases where Chronicles preserves an older or different reading. This is a name-variant, not a divinely-coordinated travel itinerary.

Nothing theologically heavy rides on the location. But "Where did this happen?" is exactly the kind of question two reliable witnesses should agree on, and these two don't.

contradictions.question: How many horsemen did David take?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 8:4 says David captured from Hadadezer a thousand chariots and seven hundred horsemen. 1 Chronicles 18:4 reports the identical event as a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen — a tenfold discrepancy in the cavalry count.
contradictions.commentary:
These are parallel reports of the same campaign against Hadadezer king of Zobah. Same king defeated, same chariot count, but the horsemen number jumps from 700 in Samuel to 7,000 in Chronicles. That's not a rounding difference. That's an order of magnitude.

The textual data here actually helps narrow the problem. The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 8:4 reads seven thousand, agreeing with Chronicles against the Hebrew MT. The Dead Sea Scrolls fragment 4QSam-a, while damaged at this verse, generally aligns with the LXX tradition in similar cases. The most parsimonious reading is that the Hebrew text of 2 Samuel has suffered a scribal omission of an "alep" (the abbreviation for "thousand") and the original number was 7,000, which Chronicles and the LXX preserve. That makes this a textual corruption in MT Samuel rather than a doctrinal contradiction.

This is the move apologists generally also make — Gleason Archer goes there in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and so do most evangelical commentators. Fine. But notice what the apologist concession amounts to: the received Hebrew Bible, the text presented as inerrant in countless pulpits, contains a transmission error that changes the number by a factor of ten. The "contradiction" gets resolved by admitting that one of the canonical texts is wrong. That's a perfectly reasonable historical-critical conclusion. It's also a problem for any doctrine of preserved inerrancy.

The contradiction is real at the level of the received canonical text. The resolution requires either accepting textual corruption (which undermines inerrancy in the form most lay believers hold it) or doing the harmonization gymnastics where the 700 are some elite subset of the 7,000, which neither text actually says.

answers.answer_explanation:
And David took from him a thousand chariots and seven
			          hundred horsemen. 2 Samuel 8:4

And David took from him a thousand chariots and seven
			          thousand horsemen. 1 Chronicles 18:4

contradictions.question: How many men did David kill?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 10:18 reports David killed 700 men in chariots and 40,000 horsemen of the Arameans/Syrians. 1 Chronicles 19:18 reports the same battle as 7,000 men in chariots and 40,000 footmen — both the chariot men and the type of the 40,000 troops differ.
contradictions.commentary:
Two discrepancies, same battle. First, the chariot-men jump from 700 in Samuel to 7,000 in Chronicles — same kind of factor-of-ten variance as the 2 Samuel 8 / 1 Chronicles 18 horsemen number. Second, and more interesting, the 40,000 are horsemen in Samuel but footmen in Chronicles. Cavalry versus infantry is not a rounding error; that's a different kind of force.

On the 700 versus 7,000 question, the same textual-corruption analysis applies as in entry 243. The MT of 2 Samuel is unstable, the LXX often agrees with Chronicles, and the most economical explanation is a missing "alep" in Samuel. The horsemen-versus-footmen swap is harder. The Hebrew words are different — parashim (horsemen) versus raglim (footmen) — so this isn't a simple letter-confusion. Either the Chronicler had a different source, or he is deliberately editing the type of troop to fit his theological picture of Davidic warfare, or one of the manuscripts has corruption at the word level rather than just the number.

The harmonization attempts here get strained. Keil and Delitzsch suggest the 40,000 were mixed forces and the two authors counted them differently — Samuel emphasized the cavalry component, Chronicles the infantry component. That's possible in principle but unsupported by either text. Neither narrator says "of these, some were cavalry and some infantry." Each gives a single number with a single descriptor. The harmonization requires importing information neither text contains.

The critical reading: parallel battle reports from two different post-exilic compositions working with overlapping but non-identical source traditions, plus textual corruption in MT Samuel. Some Bible Difficulties authors (Archer) acknowledge the textual problem; the broader inerrancy claim then requires defending the autographs while admitting the received text is corrupt.

answers.answer_explanation:
And David slew the men of seven hundred chariots of the
				          Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen. 2 Samuel 10:18

David slew of the Syrians seven thousand men which
				          fought in chariots, and forty thousand footmen. 1 Chronicles 19:18

contradictions.question: When did Absalom rebel against David?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 15:7 reports Absalom's rebellion begins "after forty years." 2 Samuel 5:4 states David reigned only forty years total. If 15:7 is read as forty years into David's reign, the rebellion comes at the very end of his life — but the rebellion narrative is followed by years of additional reign and the eventual succession of Solomon, which is internally inconsistent.
contradictions.commentary:
This one is an internal Samuel problem, not a Samuel-versus-Chronicles problem. 2 Samuel 5:4 sets David's total reign at 40 years. 2 Samuel 15:7 then says "after forty years" Absalom hatched his Hebron coup. If "forty years" counts from the start of David's reign, then Absalom rebelled in the last year, which leaves no room for everything 2 Samuel 16-24 and 1 Kings 1-2 describes happening afterward — David's flight, the Mahanaim period, the return, the Sheba revolt, the census, the threshing-floor purchase, the succession struggle.

The Septuagint and the Syriac Peshitta and a few Hebrew manuscripts read "after four years" rather than "after forty" at 2 Samuel 15:7. Most critical scholars, including McCarter in the Anchor Bible volume, take "four" as the original reading and "forty" as a textual corruption — probably a scribe assimilating to the round number forty that appears so often in Samuel. Even Josephus, in Antiquities 7.196, knows the tradition as "four years."

So the apologetic move here is actually the same as the critical one: the MT "forty" is a textual error and the original was "four." Where critic and apologist part ways is what to do with that admission. The critic says: this is normal for ancient texts, MT Samuel is full of these corruptions, the Bible is a human document. The apologist says: the autographs were inerrant, the transmission introduced errors, but the underlying text is recoverable. Either way, you can't get out of this contradiction without conceding that one of the canonical texts has an error.

There is also a harmonization that tries to read "forty years" as counting from David's anointing by Samuel rather than from the start of his Hebron reign, but the chronology still doesn't work out cleanly, and nothing in the text signals such a counting scheme.

And it came to pass after forty years, that Absalom said unto the king, I

				    As soon as ye hear the sound of the trumpet, then ye shall say, 
				    Absalom reigneth in Hebron. 2 Samuel 15:7-10

contradictions.question: Who was Amasa's father?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 17:25 identifies Amasa's father as Ithra "an Israelite." 1 Chronicles 2:17 identifies him as Jether "the Ishmaelite." The discrepancy is both in the form of the name and, more importantly, in the ethnicity.
contradictions.commentary:
Two questions here. First, is the name Ithra or Jether? That one is easy — they are variant spellings of the same Hebrew name (yeter / yitra), and this kind of variation is normal in Hebrew transmission. Not a real contradiction at the name level.

The ethnicity is the real problem. Samuel says yisre'eli, "Israelite." Chronicles says yishme'eli, "Ishmaelite." The Hebrew words differ by a single letter and a vowel pattern, so a scribal error in one direction or the other is mechanically plausible. But which is the corruption? The Septuagint of 2 Samuel 17:25 reads "Jezreelite" (yizre'eli) in some manuscripts and "Ishmaelite" in others. McCarter and most critical commentators reconstruct the original as "Ishmaelite," matching Chronicles — partly because identifying David's nephew's father as a plain "Israelite" is uninformative (everyone in the narrative is Israelite, so calling Ithra one tells the reader nothing), and partly because Chronicles tends to preserve older readings against MT Samuel in many cases.

The harmonization is to say Ithra was an Ishmaelite by birth who resided among Israelites and adopted Israelite identity, or that the two terms designate different things — birth versus residency. That's not impossible. But it's a story neither text actually tells. Neither narrator says "He was born Ishmaelite but lived as Israelite." Each gives one designation flatly.

The simplest reading is that the Samuel text suffered a single-letter corruption from yishme'eli to yisre'eli — the kind of mistake medieval scribes made constantly — and Chronicles preserves the older reading. That makes Amasa half-Ishmaelite, which is actually theologically interesting given that he becomes David's army commander. A non-Israelite at the top of the Davidic military hierarchy is the kind of detail the Chronicler had little motivation to invent.

answers.answer: Amasa's father was Ithra an Israelite.
answers.answer_explanation: Amasa was a man's son, whose name was Ithra an Israelite. 2 Samuel 17:25

answers.answer: Amasa's father was Jether an Ishmaelite.
answers.answer_explanation: And the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite. 1 Chronicles 2:17

contradictions.question: How many sons did Absalom have?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 14:27 says three sons were born to Absalom. 2 Samuel 18:18 has Absalom himself saying he has no son to keep his name in remembrance, which is why he set up a memorial pillar. Both statements appear in the same book about the same person.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in Samuel. Chapter 14 reports three sons by name (well, by number — only the daughter Tamar is named). Chapter 18 has Absalom explaining the existence of his memorial pillar by saying he has no son to keep his name alive. Both can't be straightforwardly true of the same man at the same time.

The traditional harmonization is that Absalom's three sons died young. Childhood mortality in the ancient Near East was brutal, the argument goes — three boys could easily have died before reaching the age where they'd carry on a father's name. The pillar in 2 Samuel 18:18 is then explained as something Absalom set up after the deaths of his sons, when he realized his name would die with him. The explicit "sons died young" reading is a rabbinic harmonization; Josephus in Antiquities 7.243 simply records Absalom's stated motivation for the pillar ("if his children should perish, his name would remain by that pillar") without asserting that the sons actually died.

The problem with that reading is that the text never says it. 2 Samuel 14:27 reports the births as a piece of straightforward biographical data, no death notice attached. 2 Samuel 18:18 doesn't say "after his sons died." The harmonization works by importing a death event neither narrator mentioned and which the chronology of Absalom's relatively short adult life makes tight to fit.

The other harmonization is that 14:27 refers to sons who would later be born — that is, Absalom's projected future progeny — but the verb is past-tense Hebrew narrative consecutive, not a prediction. The critical reading is that Samuel is composite, drawing on multiple source traditions, and the contradiction reflects the editor's failure to harmonize a notice about Absalom's family in one source with a notice about the pillar in another. The pillar in 18:18 is the older, more weight-bearing tradition — it explains a real monument the original audience would have known. The three-sons notice in 14:27 is biographical fill that doesn't connect to anything else in the narrative.

answers.answer_explanation:
Now Absalom ... said, I have not son to keep my name in
				          remembrance. 2 Samuel 18:18
And unto Absalom there were born three sons. 2 Samuel 14:27

contradictions.question: How many children did Michal (David's first wife) have?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 6:23 states Michal had no child to the day of her death. 2 Samuel 21:8 refers to "the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul" who were handed over to the Gibeonites to be impaled.
contradictions.commentary:
Within the same book of Samuel, Michal is described both as childless to her death and as the mother of five sons who get executed by the Gibeonites. The five sons in 21:8 are usually attributed to Adriel the Meholathite as their father.

The textual situation actually favors the harmonization here, but in a way that makes a different problem visible. A number of Hebrew manuscripts, the Lucianic Greek tradition, the Syriac Peshitta, and a substantial chunk of critical scholarship read "Merab" rather than "Michal" at 2 Samuel 21:8. Merab was Michal's older sister, and 1 Samuel 18:19 explicitly says Merab was given to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife. So the five sons of Adriel the Meholathite are Merab's sons, not Michal's, and the MT "Michal" at 21:8 is widely treated as a scribal error — probably a copyist's mind slipping from the more famous sister to the less famous one.

This is the rare case where the apologetic move (it's a scribal slip, the text originally said Merab) lines up cleanly with the critical conclusion. McCarter, Klein, Tsumura, and most modern translations note this in their apparatus. The NRSV and NIV emend to Merab in the text or footnote. The KJV preserves the MT "Michal," which is why the SAB and other contradiction lists pick this one up — they're working from the received Masoretic Hebrew.

What the harmonization concedes, again, is that the canonical Hebrew text has an error here that all the modern scholarly editions have to fix from the versions. The contradiction is real at the level of the MT. It dissolves only by acknowledging textual corruption. That's a perfectly defensible scholarly position, but it's not consistent with strong preservation-of-the-Hebrew-text inerrancy claims.

Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death. 2 Samuel 6:20-23

And the king said, I will give them. ... And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the LORD. ... And after that God was intreated for the land. 2 Samuel 21:1-14

contradictions.question: Who did Elhanan kill?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim killed Goliath the Gittite — the same Goliath whom 1 Samuel 17 credits David with killing. 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath. The KJV inserts "the brother of" into 2 Samuel 21:19 to harmonize, but the Hebrew has no such phrase.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the most famous and embarrassing harmonizations in the entire King James tradition. The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19 says, in word-for-word literal translation: "And Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam." Not "the brother of Goliath." Just Goliath. The KJV translators added "the brother of" in italics — they at least had the integrity to mark it as not in the text — but the Hebrew Bible says Elhanan killed Goliath.

This directly contradicts 1 Samuel 17, where David kills Goliath in the celebrated duel. Two different killers, same victim, both narratives presented as historical fact. The most parsimonious historical reconstruction is that the older tradition, preserved in 2 Samuel 21:19, credits Elhanan — a relatively obscure warrior — with killing Goliath. The later, more famous David-and-Goliath story in 1 Samuel 17 is a literary expansion that transfers the kill from the obscure soldier to the rising king. Many critical scholars treat the David version as theologically motivated reattribution.

The Chronicler, working with both Samuel narratives in front of him, sees the contradiction and fixes it. 1 Chronicles 20:5 reads: "Elhanan son of Jair struck down Lahmi, brother of Goliath the Gittite." The Chronicler invents (or preserves a tradition of) a previously unmentioned brother Lahmi to absorb Elhanan's kill, leaving David as the unique slayer of Goliath. The Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles 20:5 even gives this brother the name Lahmi (lakhmi), which looks suspiciously like a fragment of beth-hallakhmi ("the Bethlehemite") from 2 Samuel 21:19 that the Chronicler reanalyzed as a personal name.

The critical consensus, including McCarter, Klein, and Tsumura, is that 2 Samuel 21:19 is the older, embarrassing tradition, and that both the KJV's italicized insertion and the Chronicler's "Lahmi the brother" are scribal/editorial attempts to rescue David's exclusive claim to the Goliath kill. This is a textbook case of how harmonization gets baked into the canonical text itself.

answers.answer_explanation:
And there was again a battle in Gob with the Philistines, where Elhanan the 
				  son of Jaareoregim, a Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a
				    weaver's beam. 2 Samuel 21:19
				    
				    [The words "the brother of" were inserted by the KJV translators to avoid the obvious contradiction with 
				    1 Samuel 17:49-51.]

And there was war again with the Philistines; and Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose 
				        spear staff was like a weaver's beam. 1 Chronicles 20:5

contradictions.question: Did David sin?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 22:21-25 has David claiming the LORD rewarded him according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands. 1 Kings 15:5 says David did right "all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah." 2 Samuel 24:10 and 1 Chronicles 21:8 have David confessing he sinned greatly in numbering the people. So at least three answers exist within the canon: none, one (Uriah), and at least two (Uriah plus the census).
contradictions.commentary:
The three texts answer the same question — did David sin? — in three incompatible ways. 2 Samuel 22, paralleled in Psalm 18, is a victory psalm where David sings about his own righteousness in absolute terms: clean hands, righteousness, no departure from God's statutes. Read at face value, this is David saying he hasn't sinned. 1 Kings 15:5 is a deuteronomistic editorial summary that gives the qualified answer — David was righteous except in the Uriah affair. 2 Samuel 24:10 and 1 Chronicles 21:8 introduce a second confessed sin, the census.

The standard harmonization is that 2 Samuel 22 is a piece of liturgical poetry written before the Bathsheba and census incidents, or that David is speaking comparatively (righteous compared to Saul), or that "cleanness of hands" refers to specific contexts (his treatment of Saul) rather than his entire moral record. There is something to the comparative-righteousness reading — the psalm is set in the context of David's deliverance from his enemies, and the immediate referent is probably his behavior toward Saul. But the language is unqualified: "according to my righteousness ... according to the cleanness of my hands ... in his eye sight." Not "compared to Saul." Not "in this matter." The psalmist's voice is making a categorical claim.

1 Kings 15:5 then explicitly carves out the Uriah exception — which means the Deuteronomist who wrote that summary considered the Uriah affair David's only sin. He didn't say "except for Uriah and the census." He said only Uriah. So either the Deuteronomist didn't know the census story, didn't count it as a sin, or considered Uriah categorically worse. 2 Samuel 24 and 1 Chronicles 21 both treat the census as a confessed sin, so the canon as a whole records at least two sins, but 1 Kings 15:5 reports only one.

The critical reading is that these texts come from different hands with different agendas. The Deuteronomistic Historian's summary in 1 Kings 15:5 is designed to make David the standard against which later Judean kings are measured, and the Uriah affair is the only stain he allows on the standard. Different authors, different evaluations, no editorial coordination.

The SAB also lists the second reference as "2 Samuel:22:21" with an extra colon — that's a formatting artifact in the scrape, not a real verse citation problem; the verse exists and the language is as quoted.

				    cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me. 2 Samuel:22:21

				  2 Samuel 22:25

contradictions.question: What were David's last words?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 23:1-7 explicitly introduces a poetic oracle as "the last words of David," a Spirit-inspired psalm of righteous kingship. 1 Kings 2:1-9 records David's deathbed instructions to Solomon, which are largely a list of people to settle scores with — Joab, Shimei — sometimes called the "hit list." Both texts present themselves as David's final pronouncements.
contradictions.commentary:
2 Samuel 23 frames the oracle with the explicit superscription, "These are the last words of David," and gives the king an inspired meditation on the just ruler under God. 1 Kings 2 then opens with David charging Solomon at the threshold of death and works through a series of unfinished business items, ending with Joab and Shimei. Both can't literally be the last words.

The harmonization is that 2 Samuel 23:1 means "David's last inspired poetic utterance" rather than "the last words he spoke before dying." That's not implausible. The Hebrew phrase divre david ha-akharonim can be read as "David's later words" or "David's last poetic words," especially since 2 Samuel 23 is clearly a literary unit of inspired speech rather than a deathbed scene. 1 Kings 2 then provides the historical-narrative deathbed and there is no contradiction at the level of strict chronology.

Fine. But notice what gets lost in that move. 2 Samuel 23:2 says "The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue." The chapter is presented as the prophetically inspired David, full stop, in a position of climactic moral and theological summation. 1 Kings 2 then has the same David, at the actual end of his life, telling Solomon to make sure Joab's gray head goes down to the grave with blood. The two pictures of David are in significant tension even if they aren't literally the same speech-event. The Deuteronomistic Historian who edited 1 Kings 2 is presenting a David who dies giving Solomon a kill order. The compiler of 2 Samuel 23 is presenting a David whose inspired finale is a meditation on the righteous king.

Most critical scholars treat 2 Samuel 23:1-7 as a late insertion into the Samuel scroll — an editorial addition placed near the end of David's narrative to give him a final poetic-prophetic word. 1 Kings 2 is the older, harder-edged tradition of David's actual deathbed. The contradiction isn't only chronological. It's about which David the canon wants you to remember: the inspired psalmist or the dying king settling scores. The canon preserves both, side by side, without choosing.

The hit list he gave to Solomon just before he died
