contradictions.question: Did the Samaritans receive Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Luke 9:52-53 says a Samaritan village refused to receive Jesus because his face was set toward Jerusalem. John 4:39-40 says many Samaritans in the city of Sychar believed in him and asked him to stay, and he stayed two days. The Lukan and Johannine portraits of Samaritan response to Jesus directly contradict each other.
contradictions.commentary:
Luke 9:52-53 and John 4:39-40 are describing different specific incidents, so a flat contradiction reading needs to be careful. Luke's text says "a village of the Samaritans" — singular, one specific place — refused him. John says Sychar — a different specific place — welcomed him. So in a strict reading, two different Samaritan villages had two different responses. That's the obvious apologetic harmonization, and it's not stupid.

The deeper problem is that these aren't isolated narrative facts — they're stand-ins for broader theological characterizations of Samaritans in Luke and John. Luke's Gospel is famously the gospel that rehabilitates Samaritans — the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:25-37), the grateful Samaritan leper (Luke 17:11-19) — but Luke 9:52-53 starts the journey to Jerusalem with Samaritan rejection. John 4 is even more emphatically pro-Samaritan: Jesus has an extended theological dialogue with a Samaritan woman, declares himself Messiah to her, and the Samaritans of Sychar declare him "the Saviour of the world" in John 4:42. The two gospels are working different angles on the Samaritan question.

The historical Samaritans, as Mark Smith and Reinhard Pummer document, had real religious tensions with Jewish pilgrims passing through Samaria on the way to Jerusalem — they didn't accept the Jerusalem temple's centrality and considered Mount Gerizim the true holy mountain. So Luke 9:52-53's depiction of a village refusing a Jerusalem-bound traveler reflects plausible historical hostility. But John 4 isn't drawing on the same hostility-tradition; it's drawing on a Johannine tradition where Jesus' mission crosses ethnic and religious boundaries.

The contradiction at the literal level of "did the Samaritans receive Jesus" can be papered over by saying "some did, some didn't." The contradiction at the level of how each gospel frames Samaritan response is real and reflects different community memories, different theological agendas, and probably different historical roots in the Samaritan mission of early Christianity that Acts 8 also references.

contradictions.question: Was Mary blessed?
contradictions.summary: Luke 1:28 has Gabriel greet Mary as "blessed... among women," and Luke 1:42 has Elisabeth repeat the blessing. Luke 11:27-28 has a woman pronounce blessed the womb that bore Jesus, and Jesus replies, "Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it," redirecting the blessing away from his mother specifically.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a softer contradiction than most because Jesus' "yea rather" — Greek menounge — doesn't flatly deny Mary's blessedness so much as redirect it. The harmonization is actually credible here: Jesus isn't saying Mary isn't blessed; he's saying that biological motherhood isn't what makes anyone blessed, hearing-and-keeping the word is. Luke himself almost certainly didn't see a contradiction, since he wrote both passages.

That said, there's a real tension in how Luke treats the relationship between Jesus and his family. Luke 8:19-21 has Jesus' mother and brothers come to see him and Jesus says, "My mother and my brethren are these which hear the word of God, and do it" — a redefinition of family along non-biological lines. Mark 3:31-35 has an even sharper version of the same scene. The Lukan Jesus, despite the soaring infancy narratives that present Mary as a model disciple, repeatedly de-centers biological family in favor of obedience-based discipleship.

The Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions have done extensive work harmonizing this — Mary is the supreme example of hearing and keeping the word, so she's blessed on both counts. That's a theologically coherent move and it's textually defensible from Luke 1:38 and Luke 1:45. But Jesus' actual words in Luke 11:28 explicitly shift the basis of blessing away from "the womb that bare thee" — biological maternity — toward something anyone can do. The shift is real even if the contradiction isn't absolute.

The critical-scholarly read, going back to Brown's Mary in the New Testament collaborative volume, is that Luke is preserving two strata: an infancy-narrative tradition that celebrates Mary's unique role, and a sayings tradition shared with Mark that subordinates biological kinship to spiritual kinship. Luke harmonizes them by making Mary the exemplar of both, but the seams show.

contradictions.question: Who are wiser, the children of this world or the children of light?
contradictions.summary: Luke 16:8 has Jesus declare, in the parable of the unjust steward, that "the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light." James 3:15-17 contrasts earthly, sensual, devilish wisdom with the wisdom from above, valorizing the wisdom of those aligned with God. The Lukan saying gives the wisdom-edge to worldly people; James gives it to the heavenly-minded.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction depends almost entirely on flattening context, and the apologetic harmonization here is unusually strong. Luke 16:8 is a parable. Jesus is praising the unjust steward's shrewdness as a model for the disciples — not saying that worldly people are categorically wiser, but that they're wiser in pursuing their worldly goals than disciples often are in pursuing kingdom goals. The point is rhetorical: if scoundrels work this hard for money, why don't you work this hard for the kingdom?

James 3:15-17 isn't making a competing claim about which group is shrewder at strategic action. James is distinguishing two types of wisdom — earthly wisdom characterized by envy and strife, heavenly wisdom characterized by purity and peaceableness — and saying the latter is genuinely wise while the former just looks wise. They're not contradicting; they're using "wisdom" in different senses.

Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible treatment of Luke 16:1-13 makes the rhetorical-not-categorical reading explicit: Jesus' "wiser" in 16:8 is phronimōteroi in the Greek (comparative of phronimos) — practically shrewder, not morally wiser. The Lukan Jesus isn't ranking groups by ultimate wisdom; he's noting an asymmetry of effort. James, working in a Hellenistic-Jewish wisdom tradition closer to Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon, is making a much more standard wisdom-versus-folly distinction.

That said, the SAB framing has a point at the populist level: someone reading the King James and stopping at the surface would see Luke saying worldly people are wiser, James saying spiritual people are wiser, and call it a contradiction. The deeper exegetical answer is that the two passages are operating on different axes — practical shrewdness versus moral-spiritual wisdom — and don't actually contradict. This is one of the weaker contradictions in the SAB list. It survives as a contradiction only on a flat, decontextualized reading.

contradictions.question: When was the blind man (or men) healed?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 20:29-30 and Mark 10:46 say Jesus healed blind men as he was departing Jericho. Luke 18:35 says Jesus healed a blind man as he approached Jericho. Matthew has two blind men, Mark and Luke have one. The three Synoptic gospels disagree on both the number of those healed and the geographic timing of the miracle.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a textbook Synoptic Problem case. Mark 10:46 has one blind man, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, healed as Jesus leaves Jericho. Matthew 20:29-30 keeps the post-Jericho timing but turns one blind man into two and drops the name. Luke 18:35 keeps a single anonymous blind man but moves the healing to before Jericho — "as he was come nigh unto Jericho."

The standard apologetic harmonization runs along two tracks. Gleason Archer argues that there were actually three blind men — one Jesus encountered approaching Jericho (Luke), and two more on the way out (Matthew/Mark) — and the gospels each report partial overlapping incidents. Craig Blomberg offers a variant where Luke is describing Jesus entering the new Roman Jericho while Matthew and Mark describe him leaving the old Jewish Jericho a mile away. Both are clever and both are ad-hoc.

The Synoptic Problem solution from Joel Marcus, Ulrich Luz, and the broader two-source-hypothesis consensus is much simpler. Mark wrote first with one named blind man at the exit from Jericho. Matthew, working from Mark, doubled the figure — Matthew has a recurring pattern of doubling Mark's figures (compare Matthew 8:28's two demoniacs against Mark 5:2's one). Luke, also working from Mark, kept the single blind man but relocated the scene from the exit to the entrance because Luke 19:1-10 immediately follows with the Zacchaeus story inside Jericho — Luke needed Jesus to enter Jericho after the healing, so he moved the healing to before the entrance.

Luz's Hermeneia commentary on Matthew documents the doubling pattern, and Marcus's Mark commentary lays out the priority of Mark's account. The harmonizations require either an implausible three-blind-men coincidence or a geographic shell game involving twin Jerichos. The redactional explanation is dramatically more parsimonious: each evangelist adjusted the Markan scene for their own narrative purposes.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus go to heaven after he died but before his ascension?
contradictions.summary: Luke 23:43 has Jesus promise the criminal on the cross, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." John 20:17 has the resurrected Jesus tell Mary Magdalene, "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." The Lukan promise puts Jesus in paradise the day of his death; the Johannine statement keeps him from ascending until after the resurrection.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a clean contradiction at the surface, and the harmonizations require theological footwork. Luke 23:43 has Jesus and the repentant criminal in paradise on the day of the crucifixion — Friday. John 20:17, set on Easter Sunday or shortly after, has Jesus telling Mary not to touch him because he hasn't yet ascended to the Father.

The most common harmonization, developed across the patristic tradition and adopted by modern apologists like Norman Geisler, is that "paradise" and "the Father" are different locations. Paradise in this scheme is an intermediate state — sometimes identified with the "Abraham's bosom" of Luke 16:22, sometimes with the "prison" Christ preaches to in 1 Peter 3:19 — distinct from the heavenly throne room of the Father. Jesus could be in paradise Friday and still not have ascended to the Father by Sunday morning. That harmonization has internal logic but it's reading a complex eschatological geography into texts that don't develop one.

Another apologetic move, going back to the Greek punctuation problem, repositions the comma in Luke 23:43: "Verily I say unto thee today, shalt thou be with me in paradise." That reading saves Jesus from being in paradise Friday by making "today" modify the speech-act rather than the destination. The problem is that this is a violation of Luke's standard phrasing — Luke uses "verily I say unto thee" or "verily I say unto you" 27 times without ever pairing it with a redundant "today." The repositioned-comma reading is grammatically possible but stylistically alien to Luke.

Fitzmyer takes Luke 23:43 at its surface meaning: Jesus tells the criminal he will be with him in paradise that very day. Brown's treatment in the Death of the Messiah agrees. The most economical reading is that Luke and John have different and incompatible post-mortem itineraries for Jesus — Luke's is paradise-then-resurrection-then-ascension, John's is somewhere-not-the-Father-yet until after the resurrection. The harmonizations need to import categories not in the texts.

answers.answer: Yes, Jesus went to heaven on the day of his death.

contradictions.question: When did Satan enter Judas?
contradictions.summary: Luke 22:3 places Satan's entering Judas before the Passover, before the Last Supper. John 13:27 places it during the Last Supper itself, immediately after Jesus hands Judas the morsel of bread. The two gospels put the satanic possession on opposite sides of the meal.
contradictions.commentary:
Luke 22:3-7 makes the chronology explicit: Satan enters Judas, then Judas goes to the chief priests to negotiate the betrayal, then the day of unleavened bread arrives, then the Passover meal is prepared. So in Luke, the satanic entry happens days before the Last Supper. John 13:27 is unambiguous in the other direction: at the Last Supper, after Jesus passes the sop to Judas, "Satan entered into him," and Judas immediately leaves to do the betrayal. Same event, two different times.

The standard apologetic harmonization is that Satan entered Judas twice — once initially to plant the betrayal idea (Luke 22:3), and a second time at the Supper to seal the act (John 13:27). Gleason Archer makes this move. The problem is that it's an ad-hoc duplication that neither text supports. Luke doesn't say "Satan first entered Judas"; John doesn't say "Satan again entered Judas." Both texts present the entry as a singular, definitive event.

The critical-scholarly reading, in Brown's Death of the Messiah and Fitzmyer's Anchor commentary on Luke, is that Luke and John independently developed satanic-possession traditions to explain Judas's betrayal — early Christianity had a theological problem of how a chosen disciple could betray Jesus, and demonic possession was one explanatory move. Luke front-loads the possession to make Judas's entire trajectory toward the betrayal demonically driven. John retrojects it into the Supper itself, where it produces the dramatic moment of Judas leaving into the night (John 13:30).

Both evangelists are working with the same theological tool — "the devil made him do it" — but they deploy it at different narrative moments because they're constructing different theological narratives. Luke wants the betrayal to be cosmically predetermined from the start; John wants the Supper to be the moment of cosmic confrontation. The harmonization that there were two distinct satanic entries is the textbook apologist playbook move of multiplying events to dissolve a contradiction.

contradictions.question: Can thieves go to heaven?
contradictions.summary: Luke 23:32-43 has Jesus promise paradise to the repentant thief crucified beside him. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 has Paul list thieves among those who shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Luke shows a thief admitted to heaven; Paul says thieves are excluded.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction collapses under exegetical pressure pretty quickly, but it's worth working through why. Luke 23:42-43 has the repentant criminal — Greek kakourgos, literally "evildoer," not specifically a thief — confess Jesus' lordship and Jesus promise him paradise. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 has Paul list categories of unrighteous people who won't inherit the kingdom, then in 6:11 says "and such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified."

The key move is 1 Corinthians 6:11. Paul isn't saying former thieves can't be saved; he's saying that ongoing unrepentant identification with these categories excludes someone from the kingdom. The Corinthian believers were thieves and fornicators and idolaters before they were washed. The kakourgos at the cross in Luke 23 confessed and was washed in the same moment — Lukan repentance is paradigmatic, and the criminal becomes a model of last-minute salvation.

So the harmonization here works: Paul and Luke aren't disagreeing on whether a repentant thief can be saved. They're addressing different questions. Luke is showing what salvation through repentance looks like at the cross. Paul is warning Corinthians against returning to or normalizing unrighteous behavior.

That said, there's a residual tension worth flagging. Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 reads like a categorical exclusion before 6:11 walks it back. A SAB reader pulling 6:9-10 in isolation has a reasonable case that thieves are excluded full stop. The exclusion is real at the verse level; the rehabilitation is in the next verse. This is a contradiction created by atomized prooftexting — pulling verses out of their immediate Pauline context. The contradiction is genuine on the surface but dissolves with even one additional verse of context. It's one of the weaker entries in the SAB list, and the critical-scholarly literature mostly doesn't treat this as a real tension because the verses are so close together that they belong to the same argument.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus drink on the cross?
contradictions.summary: John 19:29-30 has Jesus receive the vinegar from the sponge and then declare "It is finished." Mark 15:23 has Jesus refuse the wine mingled with myrrh. Matthew 27:34 has Jesus taste the vinegar mingled with gall and refuse to drink. The Synoptic Jesus refuses the offered drink; the Johannine Jesus drinks it.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction is partly resolvable by distinguishing two separate drink-offers in the crucifixion sequence, but only partly. Mark 15:23 and Matthew 27:34 describe an offer of drugged wine before crucifixion — Mark calls it wine mingled with myrrh, Matthew shifts the substance to vinegar mingled with gall (apparently echoing Psalm 69:21). This pre-crucifixion offer was likely a Jewish custom of providing an analgesic to the condemned, and Jesus refuses to dull his suffering.

Mark 15:36 and Matthew 27:48 then describe a second, later offer near the moment of death — a sponge of vinegar (sour wine, oxos in Greek, the cheap wine of Roman soldiers) lifted to Jesus' lips. Mark and Matthew don't specify whether Jesus drank this second offering. John 19:28-30 jumps directly to this second offer and has Jesus actively receive the vinegar.

So the partial harmonization works: there are two distinct offers, and the Synoptic refusal applies to the first while the Johannine acceptance applies to the second. Carson, Morris, and Blomberg all make this move and it holds up textually.

Where the harmonization gets thin is the question of whether Jesus drinks the second offering in the Synoptics. Mark and Matthew don't explicitly say. John says yes. So strictly speaking, only John makes a positive claim about Jesus drinking. The Synoptics neither confirm nor deny the second drink. The contradiction at the SAB level — "did Jesus drink on the cross" — yields a Synoptic "no" only if you fold the first offer (clearly refused) into the question, and ignore that the second offer is silent in the Synoptics on whether he drank.

The more interesting critical-scholarly point, in Brown's Death of the Messiah, is that John has reshaped the vinegar scene to fulfill Psalm 69:21 explicitly — "in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink" — by adding the hyssop branch and the "I thirst" cry, neither of which appears in the Synoptics. John's account is theologically elaborated. The contradiction is real if you read the question as "did Jesus consume the drink offered to him," with the Synoptic answer being ambiguous to negative and the Johannine answer being affirmative.

contradictions.question: Where did Jesus go when he died?
contradictions.summary: Luke 23:43 has Jesus promise the repentant criminal that they will be together in paradise that very day, implying Jesus went to paradise. The Apostles' Creed has Jesus descend into hell, a tradition grounded in 1 Peter 3:18-20 and 1 Peter 4:6. The biblical and creedal traditions point in opposite directions on where Jesus went between Friday and Sunday.
contradictions.commentary:
This is contradiction id=510 viewed from a different angle, with the added wrinkle that the "hell" answer leads with the Apostles' Creed rather than scripture. The Apostles' Creed is a fourth-century-or-later confessional document, not biblical text. The actual biblical basis for the descent-into-hell tradition is 1 Peter 3:18-20 ("by which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison") and 1 Peter 4:6 ("the gospel preached also to them that are dead"), now added to this answer's references so the contradiction rests on scripture and not just the creedal summary.

With those passages added, the contradiction is real but narrower than "heaven versus hell" suggests. The Greek of 1 Peter 3:19 doesn't use the word for hell (hades or geenna) — it says "prison" (phylake), and the spirits there are usually identified, following the Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 traditions, with the disobedient angels of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch. So Jesus going to the "prison of the spirits" is a specifically apocalyptic-Jewish geography rather than the medieval Christian hell.

Luke 23:43's paradise (paradeisos) is also a specifically apocalyptic-Jewish term — used in 2 Corinthians 12:4 and Revelation 2:7 for the heavenly garden, and in Second Temple texts like 1 Enoch 60:8 and 2 Enoch 8 for the dwelling of the righteous dead.

So at the technical level, Luke's Jesus goes to the heavenly paradise of the righteous, while 1 Peter's Jesus goes to the prison of the disobedient spirits. Both could in principle be true on a complex post-mortem itinerary — Augustine and Aquinas worked out elaborate schemes where Jesus visited multiple post-mortem locations — but the texts themselves don't develop such a scheme. They're two independent traditions about what Jesus did between his death and resurrection.

The critical-scholarly read is that 1 Peter is using a Jewish apocalyptic tradition (the descent to the Watchers) to give Jesus' death cosmic significance, while Luke is using a different apocalyptic tradition (paradise as righteous reward) to highlight individual salvation through the cross. The Apostles' Creed pulls 1 Peter into its summary and creates the "descended into hell" formulation that medieval Latin Christianity then elaborated. This contradiction is real but the SAB framing obscures more than it reveals.

contradictions.question: When did Jesus ascend into heaven?
contradictions.summary: Luke 24:51 has Jesus ascend on the day of resurrection itself, after a single day of post-resurrection appearances. Mark 16:19 has the ascension at the close of a sequence of appearances. John 20:26 has Jesus still on earth eight days after the resurrection, appearing to Thomas. Acts 13:31 has him appearing for many days before ascending. Acts 1:3 specifies forty days. The New Testament gives at least four different timelines for the ascension.
contradictions.commentary:
Acts 1:3 explicitly says Jesus was seen "forty days" before his ascension. Luke 24, written by the same author as Acts, narratively compresses the same period into what reads like a single day — Easter morning at the tomb, the Emmaus road, the appearance to the eleven, and the ascension all flow together in 24:1-51 with no narrative break for the forty days. The two Lukan works contradict each other.

The standard harmonization, developed in detail by F. F. Bruce, is that Luke 24:50-51 is a compressed summary that doesn't explicitly say the ascension happened on the same day as the resurrection — Luke just narrates events in sequence without time markers. The narrative gap between Luke 24:43 and 24:50 could accommodate the forty days. That's textually defensible but it requires the reader to import the Acts timeline into the Lukan narrative, which on its own surface reads as a single-day sequence.

John 20:26's eight-days-after-resurrection appearance to Thomas is a direct problem for any reading that compresses the ascension into the resurrection day. If Jesus is still appearing in his pre-ascension state eight days after Easter, the resurrection-day ascension reading collapses. Most apologists therefore prefer the Acts 1:3 forty-day timeline as the master schema and read Luke 24 as compressed narrative.

The Mark 16:19 reference is from the Longer Ending — Mark 16:9-20 — which Metzger and the critical-text consensus identify as a second-century addition not in Mark's earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus). So one of the four ascension timelines comes from a secondary text.

The critical-scholarly position, articulated by Mikeal Parsons in The Departure of Jesus in Luke-Acts, is that Luke had a problem: he wanted to end his gospel with the ascension as climactic closure (Luke 24), but he also wanted to begin Acts with the ascension as the bridge to Pentecost (Acts 1). He solved it by narrating the ascension twice, with two different timelines, because the rhetorical needs of the two volumes were different. The forty-day figure in Acts probably echoes the Jewish forty-day periods of Moses on Sinai and Elijah at Horeb — a theological number, not a historical datum. The contradiction is real and reflects Lukan compositional priorities, not historical witness.

contradictions.question: Were the disciples frightened or gladdened when they saw Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Luke 24:37 has the disciples terrified and affrighted, supposing they had seen a spirit when Jesus appeared. John 20:20 has the disciples glad when they saw the Lord. The two evangelists describe diametrically opposed emotional responses to the same kind of post-resurrection appearance.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner contradictions in the SAB list because both verses describe the same scene type — Jesus appearing to the assembled disciples on Easter evening — and they give opposite emotional reactions.

The standard apologetic harmonization is sequential: the disciples were first terrified (Luke 24:37), then Jesus calmed them, showed them his hands and feet, and then they became glad (John 20:20). The two reactions are stages of the same emotional arc. Norman Geisler runs this argument. It's textually defensible — Luke 24:41 actually says "they yet believed not for joy, and wondered," which captures the transition from fear to joy that the apologetic reading needs.

But the John 20:20 "then were the disciples glad, when they saw the LORD" reads as the immediate response to seeing him, not as a delayed response after initial terror. John doesn't narrate any fear phase. He has Jesus appear, say "Peace be unto you," show his hands and side, and the disciples respond with gladness. There's no Lukan terror in the Johannine telling.

The critical-scholarly read, in Brown's Death of the Messiah and the Anchor John commentary, is that Luke and John are drawing on different traditions of the Easter appearances with different emphases. Luke emphasizes the physicality of the resurrected Jesus — he shows hands and feet, eats fish, proves he's not a ghost — and the initial terror serves that emphasis by setting up the demonstration. John emphasizes the bestowal of peace and the missio of the disciples — Jesus appears, brings peace, breathes the Spirit, sends them out — and gladness serves that purpose.

The scenes aren't easily harmonized into a single chronological sequence because they're doing different theological work. The most parsimonious reading is that we have two different traditions of the Easter evening appearance, edited by two different evangelists for two different purposes. The fear-then-joy sequencing solution works at the level of "both could in principle be true" but doesn't explain why John would omit the terror that Luke makes central.

contradictions.question: Was it OK to touch the risen Jesus before his ascension?
contradictions.summary: John 20:17 has Jesus tell Mary Magdalene, "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." Matthew 28:9 has the women hold Jesus by the feet and worship him. Luke 24:39 has Jesus invite the disciples to handle him. John 20:26-27 has Jesus, still pre-ascension by John's chronology, invite Thomas to thrust his hand into his side. The Johannine prohibition to Mary directly contradicts the Synoptic and even later Johannine permissions.
contradictions.commentary:
This is an internal Johannine problem before it's a Synoptic-versus-John problem. John 20:17 has Jesus tell Mary not to touch him because he hasn't ascended. John 20:26-27, in the same chapter and apparently on the same temporal side of the ascension, has Jesus invite Thomas to thrust his hand into his side. Same Johannine narrative, opposite instructions.

The standard harmonization runs through the Greek. The verb in John 20:17 is haptou (present imperative middle of haptomai), which can mean "stop touching me" or "do not cling to me" rather than "do not touch me at all." Brown in the Anchor John commentary translates it "stop clinging to me" — Mary has already grabbed Jesus and won't let go, and he's telling her to release him so he can complete his return to the Father. On that reading, John 20:17 isn't forbidding touch in general but forbidding clinging, which is consistent with Thomas being invited to touch later.

That harmonization works for the Johannine internal tension. It still leaves the Matthew 28:9 conflict — there the women "held him by the feet and worshipped him," exactly the kind of grabbing behavior John 20:17 forbids Mary from doing. The Greek verb in Matthew 28:9 is ekratesan from krateo, "to grasp firmly" — the very behavior Mary is told not to do in John.

Matthew Henry and the older apologetic tradition tried to harmonize by sequencing — Matthew 28:9 happened after Jesus had "ascended" in some technical sense, John 20:17 happened before. That requires an unwarranted assumption of multiple ascensions or some technical distinction between "the" ascension and intermediate ascensions, neither of which the texts develop.

The critical-scholarly read in Brown and Davies-Allison is that Matthew and John are working from independent appearance traditions with different theological frames. Matthew's tradition emphasizes embodied recognition and worship; John's emphasizes spiritual recognition and mission. The grasping-the-feet of Matthew 28:9 and the touch-me-not of John 20:17 reflect different framings of the same kind of moment. The contradiction is real but softer than the SAB framing suggests, because John 20:17 is plausibly about clinging, not touch.

contradictions.question: Does Jesus judge people?
contradictions.summary: John 5:22, John 5:26-27, John 9:39, Acts 17:31, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and Revelation 19:11 say Jesus judges everyone, with the Father committing all judgment to the Son. John 8:15 and John 12:47 have Jesus himself say "I judge no man" and "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world." The Johannine Jesus both claims and denies the role of judge within the same gospel.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a Johannine internal contradiction more than a cross-canonical one. The same gospel that gives Jesus universal judicial authority in 5:22 and 5:27 has him denying that authority in 8:15 and 12:47. You can't dissolve this by appealing to authorial diversity — the same author wrote both.

The standard harmonization, in Carson's Pillar commentary and Keener's two-volume John, distinguishes between Jesus' first coming and his second coming. In the first coming Jesus' mission is salvific — "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world" (John 12:47). At the eschatological return Jesus exercises the judicial authority delegated by the Father (John 5:27). On this reading, Jesus judges no one *now*, but will judge everyone at the end. The two-mission framing is theologically coherent and it tracks how the early church developed the Christological doctrine of the first and second advents.

Brown in the Anchor John commentary makes a related but subtler move. The Johannine concept of judgment, krisis, is bivalent — judgment is simultaneously a separation and a verdict. In John 3:18-19 and 9:39, Jesus' very presence in the world functions as krisis whether or not Jesus actively pronounces verdicts — his light reveals what people are. So Jesus "judges no man" in the sense of not actively pronouncing condemnation, while simultaneously functioning as the locus of judgment by his presence. Brown calls this realized judgment.

That's elegant exegesis, but it does require the reader to hold two senses of "judge" in tension and recognize that John uses krino across both. The flat surface contradiction — "Jesus judges everyone" versus "Jesus judges no one" — is real at the verse level. The harmonization works, but it requires importing a doctrine of realized eschatology and a careful disambiguation of Greek krisis. The SAB reader pulling John 5:22 against John 12:47 isn't wrong that the words contradict; the resolution is in the conceptual framework, not the surface text.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus bears witness of himself?
contradictions.summary: John 5:31 has Jesus say, "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true." John 8:14 and 8:18 have Jesus say, "Though I bear record of myself, yet my record is true" and "I am one that bear witness of myself." Within the same gospel, three chapters apart, the Johannine Jesus both denies and affirms that his self-witness is valid.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a near-identical pair of statements making opposite claims, separated by three chapters in the same gospel. The flat-surface contradiction is stark. Note also the question text has a grammatical issue — "Did Jesus bears witness of himself?" — that should be "bear" in the underlying database.

The standard harmonization, going back to the patristic commentators and developed by Carson and Keener, reads John 5:31 as a rhetorical concession to Jewish legal standards. Deuteronomy 19:15 requires two or three witnesses for a valid testimony. Jesus in John 5:31 is acknowledging that *by that standard alone* his self-testimony wouldn't count, and then immediately marshaling additional witnesses — John the Baptist (5:33), his works (5:36), and the Father (5:37). So 5:31 is hypothetical, not a flat denial.

Then in John 8:14, Jesus shifts the argumentative frame. The Pharisees in 8:13 are appealing to the Deuteronomy 19:15 two-witness rule to dismiss Jesus' testimony, and Jesus responds that his witness *is* valid because he knows his origin and destination — he has unique epistemic access that ordinary human testimony doesn't have. In 8:18 he then adds the Father as the second witness, satisfying the legal standard.

So the harmonization runs: 5:31 concedes the two-witness rule as a baseline; 8:14 challenges the rule by appealing to Jesus' unique status; both passages then invoke the Father as the corroborating witness. That's coherent exegesis and it's how Brown reads it in the Anchor commentary.

The critical-scholarly view is that John's Jesus is constructed as a forensic figure who can both submit to and transcend Jewish legal categories depending on rhetorical context — Jesus is on trial in John, and the trial motif organizes the whole gospel. The contradiction between 5:31 and 8:14 is real at the surface level but functions as a deliberate rhetorical move in John's trial-narrative structure. The Johannine Jesus tests legal frameworks, doesn't simply submit to them. The contradiction is genuine on the surface and the harmonization requires recognizing John's literary technique. Most critical scholars don't treat this as a serious doctrinal problem because the rhetorical structure of John makes the apparent self-contradiction intelligible — but it remains a flat textual contradiction at the verse level.

contradictions.question: Was Jesus's witness of himself true?
contradictions.summary: John 8:14 has Jesus say his record of himself is true. John 5:31 has Jesus say that if he bears witness of himself, his witness is not true. John 8:18 has Jesus affirm that he is one who bears witness of himself. The same gospel both affirms and denies the validity of Jesus' self-witness.
contradictions.commentary:
This is functionally the same contradiction as id=519, with the question reframed from "did Jesus bear witness of himself" to "was Jesus' witness of himself true." The textual data is the same — John 5:31 versus John 8:14 — and the harmonization arguments are the same.

The harmonization, again following Carson, Keener, and the broader patristic-to-modern Johannine commentary tradition, reads John 5:31 as a rhetorical concession to the Deuteronomy 19:15 two-witness standard, not as a categorical denial of the truth of Jesus' self-testimony. Jesus is conceding that by ordinary legal standards a person's self-witness doesn't count, then marshaling additional witnesses — John the Baptist, his works, the Father, and scripture itself — to meet the legal standard. John 8:14 then claims Jesus' self-witness *is* true because Jesus has unique epistemic access to his own origin and destination, transcending the ordinary legal frame.

So the resolution depends on recognizing that John 5:31 operates within a hypothetical legal frame ("if I were the only witness, then...") while John 8:14 operates from Jesus' actual epistemic and ontological position ("because I know whence I came..."). That's the way Brown, Barrett, Keener, and Lincoln all read it.

Where this gets thin is that the SAB framing is doing something legitimate — pointing out that the surface text of John 5:31 says self-witness is not true, and the surface text of John 8:14 says it is. A flat literalist reading of either verse without the rhetorical frame produces a contradiction. The frame dissolves the contradiction only if you grant that John is constructing a complex forensic argument where Jesus tests and transcends Jewish legal categories.

This is also a duplicate of id=519 in the SAB database — the same textual data is being framed two different ways. From a database-curation perspective, IDs 519 and 520 should probably be consolidated, because they're functionally the same contradiction with cosmetic question-text variation. The Johannine evidence and harmonization arguments are identical.

contradictions.question: Who makes people blind?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 4:11 has Yahweh personally claim authorship over blindness, deafness, and muteness — they are direct acts of God. Mark 9:17-25, by contrast, treats deafness and muteness as the work of a foul spirit that Jesus exorcises, and John 9:1-3 treats congenital blindness as a setup for a divine demonstration rather than a curse to be undone. The Hebrew Bible's strict monotheistic etiology of disability collides with the Synoptic demonology that develops in the Second Temple period.
contradictions.commentary:
Here's the thing — Exodus 4:11 is unambiguous. Yahweh is asserting sole agency over sensory disability as part of his self-justification to Moses. The verb is qal active: "Who makes (sam) a person mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?" There's no demonic intermediary in the picture. The text reflects what John Collins calls the radically monistic theology of the priestly and Deuteronomistic traditions — Yahweh is the sole causal agent for both prosperity and calamity (cf. Isaiah 45:7, Amos 3:6).

By the time you get to Mark, the entire causal universe has been repopulated. Mark 9:25 explicitly names the spirit "deaf and dumb" (to alalon kai kophon pneuma) and commands it to leave — the disability is the spirit. This is straight Second Temple demonology, the kind you find in 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and the Qumran exorcism fragments. The apologist move here is to say these are separate cases — God causes some disabilities, demons cause others, and there's no contradiction. The apologist playbook, page one. The problem is that Exodus 4:11 is framed as a universal etiological claim, not a case-by-case attribution. Yahweh isn't saying "I make some blind people" — he's making a sweeping claim of authorship to ground Moses' commission.

The John 9:1-3 passage adds a third theological layer: blindness as a setup for divine theater. Raymond Brown notes that John pointedly rejects both Deuteronomic retributive justice (this man didn't sin, his parents didn't sin) and the Synoptic demonological frame — instead, blindness exists "so that the works of God might be revealed in him." That's a third etiology, not a harmonization. Three different theological universes, three different causal agents.

contradictions.question: How did Jesus cure the blind man?
contradictions.summary: Mark 8:22-25 has Jesus heal a blind man at Bethsaida by spitting directly on his eyes and laying hands on him — twice, because the first attempt only half-worked. John 9:1-7 has Jesus heal a blind man in Jerusalem by spitting on the ground, mixing clay, anointing the man's eyes, and sending him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. Different cities, different methods, different timeline, and a different number of steps. Apologists treat them as separate events; the literary parallels suggest John has reworked the Markan tradition into something more dignified.
contradictions.commentary:
At face value these are two different healings — different settings, different protagonists, different outcomes. Apologists like Craig Blomberg lean on this hard: no contradiction because no overlap. Fair enough as a first pass. But here's where it falls apart under scrutiny. The Mark 8 healing is the one synoptic miracle that John 9 is most plausibly transforming. Joel Marcus and Raymond Brown both note the structural parallels: spittle, hands, a two-stage process, a confession of sight. Mark's version is also the one healing the other synoptics conspicuously drop — Matthew and Luke both omit Mark 8:22-26, almost certainly because the two-stage failure and the saliva are theologically awkward. Jesus needing a second try is not a good look.

The parsimonious reading is that John 9 represents a Johannine reworking of the same tradition that produced Mark 8 — saliva is kept (it was too embedded to drop), but the messy two-stage healing is replaced with a single competent act mediated through the Pool of Siloam, which John then helpfully glosses as "Sent" (apestalmenos) — a symbol for Jesus himself. The apologist response — these are simply distinct miracles — has to explain why Jesus used the unusual saliva-and-mud technique twice, in two different cities, with no other healing in the Gospels resembling it. That's not impossible. It's just less parsimonious than the redactional explanation.

Even if you grant the two-event harmonization, the contradiction the SAB is pointing at is still there at the level of method: the Mark version cures by direct spittle on eyes, John cures by mud-paste and a pool washing. Same question — how does Jesus heal blindness? — and two non-overlapping answers. That is of course only a contradiction if you assume one consistent method, which the text never claims.

contradictions.question: Is it possible to fall from grace?
contradictions.summary: Galatians 5:4, Hebrews 6:4-6, and 2 Peter 2:20-21 all explicitly treat falling away from saving grace as possible — Hebrews even pronounces it irrevocable. John 10:28 and Romans 8:38-39 just as explicitly insist that nothing can separate believers from Christ's hand or God's love. This is the classic Reformed-vs-Arminian seam in the New Testament itself: two streams of soteriology that the canon never reconciles.
contradictions.commentary:
The two New Testament streams here aren't subtle. Hebrews 6:4-6 is some of the most explicit apostasy language in the canon: those once enlightened, who tasted the heavenly gift and shared in the Holy Spirit, who then fall away — adynaton, impossible to restore them. Galatians 5:4 uses the unambiguous exepesate — "you have fallen out of grace." 2 Peter 2:20-21 piles on with the line that it would have been better not to have known the way of righteousness than to know it and turn back. On the other side, John 10:28 has Jesus declaring no one can snatch his sheep from his hand, and Romans 8:38-39 stacks negation after negation: nothing in creation can separate us from God's love in Christ.

The apologist harmonization runs through two main moves. First — the Calvinist move (Schreiner, Grudem) — argue that the apostates in Hebrews and 2 Peter were never genuinely saved in the first place. They merely "tasted" without consuming. The problem is that the language Hebrews uses for these people (enlightened, partakers of the Holy Spirit, tasted the powers of the age to come) is precisely the language Hebrews uses elsewhere for true believers. The phrase phōtisthentas (enlightened) is technical baptismal vocabulary in early Christian usage. Second — the Arminian-leaning move (Witherington) — accept that apostasy is real and read John 10 and Romans 8 as referring to external threats, not internal defection. That's plausible for Romans 8 (the list is all external agents), but John 10:28's "they shall never perish" is unconditional on its face.

The parsimonious read is that the New Testament contains multiple soteriological traditions that don't fully cohere. Hebrews and 2 Peter come out of a community concerned with maintaining commitment under persecution; Johannine and Pauline assurance texts come out of communities emphasizing security in Christ. Both are real; neither is dominant. Take your pick on which to weight — the canon doesn't.

contradictions.question: Who sent the Holy Ghost?
contradictions.summary: In John 15:26 Jesus says he himself will send the Paraclete from the Father. In John 14:16 and 14:26 the Father is the one who gives or sends the Spirit, with Jesus only asking. The same Farewell Discourse, two chapters apart, gives two different agents for the same act — a tension that drove the *Filioque* controversy that split Eastern and Western Christianity for a thousand years.
contradictions.commentary:
This one isn't even cross-document — it's the same author, the same discourse, two chapters apart. John 14:16: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete." John 14:26: "the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name." John 15:26: "the Paraclete, whom I will send to you from the Father." The subject of the sending verb (pempso vs. pempsei) literally changes between verses.

The orthodox harmonization is Trinitarian: the Father is the ultimate source, the Son is the mediating sender, and there's no real conflict because the persons of the Trinity act inseparably (the doctrine of *opera trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt*). That's a perfectly coherent dogmatic position — but it's a fifth-century answer to a first-century problem. Raymond Brown, who was a Catholic priest and absolutely no anti-Trinitarian, still acknowledged in his Anchor Bible commentary that John's Spirit-language is ambiguous about agency and that the Farewell Discourse may reflect two stages of composition — chapters 15-17 likely being a later expansion of the original chapter 14 discourse.

The more interesting historical point is what this contradiction did downstream. The question of whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone (John 14:26) or from the Father and the Son (John 15:26) is exactly the *Filioque* clause — the Latin addition to the Nicene Creed that the Eastern Church rejected and that became the formal theological cause of the 1054 Great Schism. The contradiction is real enough that an entire half of Christendom built its identity on one reading and the other half on the other. You can call that a harmonized doctrine of Trinitarian co-agency, or you can call it two competing source layers in a composite discourse. The text itself does not adjudicate.

contradictions.question: Did any of the apostles ask Jesus where he was going?
contradictions.summary: In John 13:36 Peter explicitly asks Jesus, "Lord, where are you going?" Thomas asks essentially the same question in John 14:5. Then in John 16:5, Jesus says, "none of you asks me, where are you going?" — within the same Farewell Discourse. The Johannine author has Jesus deny that anyone has just asked him the question that two named disciples just asked him.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in the Gospel of John, and it's a major piece of evidence for the source-critical view that John 13-17 is a stitched-together composite. Peter in 13:36: *Kyrie, pou hypageis?* — "Lord, where are you going?" Thomas in 14:5: *Kyrie, ouk oidamen pou hypageis* — "Lord, we do not know where you are going." Jesus in 16:5: *oudeis ex hymōn erōta me, Pou hypageis?* — "none of you is asking me, where are you going?" The exact same phrase, *pou hypageis*, is the issue across all three.

The traditional apologetic harmonization (Carson, Morris) is to translate 16:5 as a present-tense observation — "none of you is asking *now*, in this moment," implying that the earlier questions were superficial and they've stopped asking because they're sad about the leaving. That reading is grammatically possible but contextually strained. Why would Jesus complain that they're not asking the question they did ask, while ignoring the fact that they asked it twice?

The parsimonious explanation is the one Raymond Brown, Rudolf Bultmann, and a broad swath of Johannine scholarship landed on: the Farewell Discourse is composite. The original discourse probably ended around 14:31 ("Rise, let us go from here") and chapters 15-17 are a later supplement by the Johannene community or redactor. Chapter 16 was likely composed without 13:36-14:5 in view, which is why it contradicts them. This is the same problem that produces the disconnect between 14:31's "let's leave" and the fact that they don't actually leave until 18:1. The apologist treats these as theological deepening; the critical reader treats them as seams. Take your pick — but the seams hypothesis explains the data without making Jesus contradict himself.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus tell his disciples everything?
contradictions.summary: In John 15:15 Jesus declares he has made known to his disciples "all things" he heard from the Father — the word is *panta*, everything. One chapter later, in John 16:12, he tells them he still has many things to say to them that they cannot bear right now. Same discourse, same audience, two flatly opposed claims about how much Jesus has communicated.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction lives in the same neighborhood as the previous one — the seams of the Johannine Farewell Discourse. John 15:15: *panta ha ēkousa para tou patros mou egnōrisa hymin* — "all things that I heard from my Father I have made known to you." That's a comprehensive claim. The Greek *panta* doesn't admit easy qualification — it means everything, the totality. Then John 16:12: *eti polla echō hymin legein, all' ou dynasthe bastazein arti* — "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now." The same speaker, two chapters later, says the opposite.

The standard apologetic move (Carson, Köstenberger) is to read *panta* in 15:15 as comprehensive only with respect to what Jesus has revealed about his identity and mission — everything *relevant*, not everything *possible*. Then 16:12 covers the additional revelation that will come through the Paraclete. That reading rescues the harmony at the cost of inserting a qualifier the text doesn't have. "All things" gets quietly converted into "all things in the relevant category," with the category supplied by the interpreter.

The critical reading, again, is compositional. C. K. Barrett and Raymond Brown both treated chapters 15-17 as a secondary expansion of an earlier discourse, with 16:12 written in a context where the focus had shifted to ongoing revelation through the Spirit — a Johannine community theologumenon about the Paraclete's continuing teaching role (cf. 16:13, "he will guide you into all truth"). The point of 16:12 in its own context isn't to undermine 15:15 — it's to legitimate the community's later teachings as Spirit-mediated extensions of what Jesus didn't get around to saying directly. That works just fine as a Johannine theological move, but it does contradict the prior claim in 15:15. The contradiction is the cost of stitching the two layers together.

contradictions.question: Was Mary Magdalene happy or sad when she saw the risen Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:1-9 has the women — including Mary Magdalene — leave the empty tomb with "fear and great joy," meet Jesus on the way, grab his feet, and worship. John 20:11-15 has Mary Magdalene weeping at the tomb, talking to angels through tears, and failing even to recognize Jesus when he stands in front of her, mistaking him for the gardener. The emotional state, the location of the encounter, and her ability to recognize him are all different.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologist move (Wenham, Licona) is sequential reconstruction: Mary Magdalene came to the tomb, ran to tell the disciples (John 20:1-2), then came back and had the weeping encounter (John 20:11-15), while in between or simultaneously the other women had the joyful Matthew 28 encounter. That can be made to work if you assume two trips and split the women up, but it requires importing scaffolding that none of the Gospels supply.

The real problem isn't the emotional state by itself — people can shift moods — but the recognition failure in John. *dokousa hoti ho kēpouros estin* — "thinking that he is the gardener." This is theologically loaded in John: Mary recognizes Jesus only when he speaks her name (John 20:16, *Mariam*), which is John's payoff of the shepherd-knows-his-sheep-by-name theme from chapter 10. The recognition failure is not incidental. It's doing theological work in John's narrative. Matthew's version, where the women immediately recognize him and grab his feet, doesn't need any such moment because Matthew is doing different theological work — vindicating Jesus' messianic authority through the women's worship.

Dale Allison's three-volume Matthew commentary points out that the resurrection appearances are the area of greatest divergence across the Gospels and the most likely candidates for late, theologically-shaped additions. The Markan account in its original ending (16:8) has the women fleeing in fear and saying nothing to anyone. Matthew adds Jesus' actual appearance; John adds an entire scene with angels, weeping, gardener-confusion, and the noli me tangere moment. These aren't supplementary details fitting into one timeline — they're competing narrative theologies. The honest critical read is that the resurrection traditions diversified rapidly in the first generation and the Gospels preserved different versions without successful harmonization.

contradictions.question: Should we believe in unseen things?
contradictions.books_in_tension: John, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Colossians, Hebrews
contradictions.summary: Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as the evidence of things not seen; 2 Corinthians 4:18 says we look at things unseen rather than seen; 2 Corinthians 5:7 — "we walk by faith, not by sight"; John 20:29 has Jesus pronouncing those who believe without seeing as blessed. Colossians 2:18, by contrast, warns against being beguiled by people "intruding into those things which they have not seen, vainly puffed up by their fleshly mind." The same New Testament both commands and condemns belief in the unseen, depending on whose visions are being weighed.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a contradiction that mostly evaporates with a careful look at Colossians 2:18 — but only partly. The Greek of Colossians 2:18 is famously contested. The phrase *ha heoraken embateuōn* is variously translated "intruding into things he has seen" (taking the manuscript reading without the negative) or "intruding into things he has not seen" (with the negative *mē*, attested in some manuscripts and reflected in the KJV). The earlier and better attested reading is *without* the negative — so the verse is actually criticizing people who claim to have seen visions during their initiation into some Colossian mystery cult and then puff themselves up about it. The KJV's negative reading flips the meaning and is what creates the surface contradiction the SAB is pointing to.

So if you grant that the modern critical text wins on Colossians 2:18, the contradiction with Hebrews 11 dissolves in one direction — Colossians isn't actually condemning belief in unseen things; it's criticizing people who claim privileged visionary access. That's a textual-criticism point, not a theological one.

But the deeper tension is still real and worth flagging. The New Testament does treat "faith without sight" as the higher virtue (John 20:29, Hebrews 11) while at the same time grounding apostolic authority in eyewitness claims (1 John 1:1, Luke 1:2, 1 Corinthians 15:5-8, 2 Peter 1:16). Bart Ehrman has pointed out that this is the structural irony of early Christianity — eyewitnesses are normative for the apostles, and lack of sight is normative for everyone after them. The contradiction here is between the early-stage epistemology (visions, appearances) and the later-stage epistemology (faith without sight). The SAB pairing is too narrow to catch the full tension, but it's pointing at a real seam. That is of course only a contradiction if you read these as competing universal claims, which the texts arguably don't.

contradictions.question: Did Luke include everything that Jesus did?
contradictions.summary: Acts 1:1-2 opens with Luke telling Theophilus that his "former treatise" (the Gospel of Luke) covered "all that Jesus began both to do and teach" up to the ascension. John 21:25 ends by claiming the things Jesus did were so many that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written. The contradiction is a soft one — Luke's *panta* (all) versus John's hyperbolic inexhaustibility — and depends on whether you read Acts 1:1 as a literal completeness claim or as a conventional preface.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the weaker contradictions in the SAB collection, and it's worth saying so plainly. Acts 1:1 reads: *peri pantōn, ō Theophile, hōn ērxato ho Iēsous poiein te kai didaskein* — "concerning all the things, O Theophilus, that Jesus began both to do and to teach." The key word is *ērxato* (began). Luke is signaling that the Gospel covers what Jesus *began* doing, and that Acts will narrate the continuation through the Spirit and the apostles. The grammar already softens the totality claim. Joseph Fitzmyer in his Anchor Bible Acts commentary takes this as a standard hellenistic preface convention, comparable to Josephus and Lucian — not a literal claim of exhaustiveness.

John 21:25 is doing different work entirely. It's a literary peroration, hyperbole built into the closing of the Gospel: "if every one of them were written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books." Raymond Brown points out this is a standard Hellenistic literary topos — Philo, Quintilian, and various rabbinic sources use the same "the world could not contain it" trope. It's signaling literary closure, not making a claim that competes with Luke's preface.

So here's the honest assessment. If you read Acts 1:1's *peri pantōn* maximally and John 21:25 literally, you get a surface contradiction. If you read both verses in their actual literary register — Luke as preface convention, John as closing hyperbole — they're not really claiming the same kind of thing. This entry is closer to a translation-driven artifact than a genuine doctrinal collision. That is of course a subjective call, but the weight of Acts and Johannine scholarship leans toward both phrases being literary rather than catalog claims. Keep the entry, but flag it as one where the harmonization is genuinely strong on textual grounds.

answers.answer_explanation:

contradictions.question: How many believers were there at the time of the ascension?
contradictions.summary: Acts 1:15 reports the number of names "together" right after the ascension as "about one hundred and twenty." Paul, writing decades earlier in 1 Corinthians 15:6, says the risen Jesus appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom were still alive when he wrote. If both numbers are accurate, more than 380 named believers vanished from the Jerusalem community between the resurrection and the post-ascension prayer gathering.
contradictions.commentary:
Here's where the apologetic harmonization actually has some traction — and where it ultimately runs out of road. The standard move (F. F. Bruce, Bock) is geographic and demographic: the 120 in Acts 1:15 are specifically the believers gathered in one room in Jerusalem in the days immediately after the ascension. The 500-plus appearance witnesses of 1 Corinthians 15:6 likely happened in Galilee (cf. Matthew 28:16-20, the Galilean commissioning) and they all went home. So the two numbers refer to different geographic snapshots, and there's no contradiction.

That's plausible as far as it goes. The problem is what it costs to make it work. You have to accept that of more than 500 people who personally saw the risen Jesus — the most extraordinary thing they'd ever experienced — fewer than 120 followed through to join the Jerusalem community at the founding moment of the church. That's a roughly 75% attrition rate among eyewitnesses. The Acts narrative itself doesn't seem aware that there are hundreds of other resurrection witnesses scattered around Galilee; the framing of Pentecost in Acts 2 treats the 120 as the core community, not as a Jerusalem subset of a much larger witness pool.

The parsimonious read, on the critical side (Lüdemann, Ehrman), is that Paul's "500 at once" is either an embellishment, a reference to a mass ecstatic experience after the fact, or simply a number Paul could not have independently verified. Note that the 500 appearance appears nowhere in the Gospels or Acts. If 500 people had seen the risen Jesus, you'd expect at least one of the Gospel writers to know about it. That gap is hard to explain on the harmonization view. The apologist can keep both numbers if they're willing to accept the 75% attrition. The critical scholar reads the gap as evidence that the 500-witness tradition was a Pauline-circulated claim that didn't propagate into the Gospel-Acts stream.

answers.answer: There were 120 believers after the ascension.

				          twenty. Acts 1:15

answers.answer: There were more than 500 believers before the ascension.

contradictions.question: What did Judas do with the silver?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 27:5 has Judas throw the thirty pieces of silver down in the temple and then hang himself; the priests use the money to buy the Potter's Field. Acts 1:18 says Judas himself bought a field with the reward of iniquity and then fell headlong, bursting open with his bowels gushing out. Same character, same money, two incompatible accounts of who bought what field and how Judas died.
contradictions.commentary:
This one is famous, and the harmonization attempts are creative — and inadequate. The Matthew version: Judas regrets, returns the silver, hangs himself; priests buy the Potter's Field with the now-blood-money. Acts version: Judas keeps the money, buys a field himself, and dies by some kind of bodily rupture (*prēnēs genomenos elakēsen mesos*).

The traditional apologist move (Archer, Geisler) tries to fuse the two: Judas bought the field via the priests as proxy, then hanged himself, and the rope broke or the body decomposed and burst open after falling. So both accounts are partially true. The problems here stack up fast. First, Matthew explicitly says the priests bought the field with the money — *agorazein* — there's no agency or proxy language. Second, Acts says Judas "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity" — that's direct action, not posthumous attribution. Third, the burst-open-after-hanging reconciliation requires inventing a chain of events neither text describes. Fourth, even the name of the field differs in implication: Matthew calls it Field of Blood because it was bought with blood money; Acts calls it Field of Blood (Hakeldama) because Judas's blood burst out on it. Same name, different etiology.

Dale Allison and Joseph Fitzmyer both treat this as two independent legendary developments of an early tradition that linked Judas's death to a piece of land near Jerusalem. Matthew is doing fulfillment work — the thirty pieces of silver, the potter's field, the blood money — all dovetailing with Zechariah 11:12-13 and Jeremiah 18-19 (which Matthew misattributes to Jeremiah at 27:9). Acts is doing typological work — Judas as the wicked man whose body explodes is a riff on Wisdom 4:19 and Psalm 69:25 (cited at Acts 1:20). Neither is reporting; both are theologizing. The apologist harmonization fails because it tries to read two competing midrashic etiologies as overlapping eyewitness reports. They are not. Take your pick on which Judas-death tradition you find more compelling — but you cannot have both as straight history.

contradictions.question: Who raised Jesus from the dead?
contradictions.books_in_tension: John, Acts, Romans, Galatians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians
contradictions.summary: John 2:19-21 has Jesus declaring he will raise his own body in three days. Acts 2:24, 2:32, 4:10, 13:30, Galatians 1:1, Colossians 2:12, and 1 Thessalonians 1:10 all attribute the resurrection to God the Father, who raised Jesus. Romans 8:11 attributes it to the Holy Spirit. Three different agents across the New Testament for the same act, with the bulk of attestation going to the Father.
contradictions.commentary:
The orthodox harmonization is straightforward Trinitarian theology: all three persons act inseparably, and the resurrection is the work of the one God in three persons. That's a perfectly fine confessional answer, and it works on the dogmatic level. The historical-critical question is different — namely, what did the earliest Christians actually think happened, and did they think the same thing?

When you sort the verses chronologically you see something interesting. The earliest stratum — Paul's undisputed letters and the speeches in Acts (which preserve early creedal material) — overwhelmingly attribute the resurrection to God the Father acting on Jesus. *Ho theos auton ēgeiren ek nekrōn* ("God raised him from the dead") is one of the most common formulas in the New Testament. Jesus is the patient, God is the agent. This fits the early christological pattern that Bart Ehrman calls "exaltation Christology" — Jesus is a man whom God vindicated and exalted by raising him.

The John 2:19-21 saying — Jesus actively raising himself — is a Johannine theological development that aligns with John's high Christology of the pre-existent Logos. Even there, the narrator has to clarify that Jesus "spoke of the temple of his body," because the saying in its original form (cf. Mark 14:58, where the temple-destruction saying is preserved without the self-raising element) didn't necessarily imply self-resurrection. Romans 8:11 is the Spirit-resurrection tradition, which is rarer and appears to be a Pauline pneumatological emphasis rather than a developed doctrine.

The parsimonious read is developmental: the earliest formula is "God raised Jesus," the Pauline Spirit-formula is a side variant, and the Johannine self-raising formula is the latest theological refinement, made possible only after the Logos Christology was in place. You can call that a Trinitarian harmony retroactively, or you can call it three stages of Christological development. The data is the same; the interpretive frame is what changes.

contradictions.question: Should we obey human or divine law?
contradictions.summary: Acts 5:29 has Peter and the apostles declaring before the Sanhedrin that they must obey God rather than men. 1 Peter 2:13 commands believers to submit to every human ordinance, and Romans 13:1-4 escalates: every governing authority is ordained by God, resisting them resists God, and they bear the sword as God's ministers to execute wrath. The same New Testament endorses both civil disobedience and unconditional submission, depending on which book you're reading.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard harmonization is the so-called "two kingdoms" or hierarchical reading: obey civil authorities in all matters where their commands don't violate divine law; obey God when they do. That's a perfectly coherent ethical framework, and it's the dominant Christian reading from Augustine through the Reformers. The problem is that this framework has to be imported from outside the texts — neither Romans 13 nor 1 Peter 2 carves out exceptions for unjust commands. Romans 13:1-2 is categorical: every soul to the higher powers, no exceptions stated. *Pasa psychē exousiais hyperechousais hypotassesthō* — "let every soul be subject to the governing authorities." Paul gives no "unless they command sin" qualifier.

Acts 5:29, by contrast, is the apostles directly defying a legitimate authority — the Sanhedrin had authority over Jewish religious matters, and Peter is openly refusing to comply. If Romans 13 is the rule, Acts 5:29 is the exception that Romans 13 doesn't acknowledge. The clean reading is that these are different theological streams responding to different situations. Romans was written to a Roman-Christian community in the imperial capital where political quietism was survival strategy. 1 Peter addresses scattered Christians under imperial pressure with similar concerns. Acts 5:29 is hagiographic — Luke is establishing the apostles as figures of conscience who stand up to corrupt authority. Each text is doing different rhetorical work for different audiences.

The contradiction has had massive downstream effects. Romans 13 has been deployed by every authoritarian Christian regime from Constantine to apartheid South Africa to Trump-era evangelicalism (cf. Jeff Sessions' 2018 invocation to justify family separation). Acts 5:29 is the standard text for Christian civil disobedience from the Anabaptists to Martin Luther King Jr. The New Testament hands the ethical question to the reader without giving them the resolution rules. Take your pick on which verse anchors your political theology — both have impeccable apostolic credentials.

contradictions.question: How old was Abraham when he left Haran?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 12:4 says Abram was 75 years old when he departed Haran. Genesis 11:26 says Terah was 70 when he begat Abram; Genesis 11:32 says Terah died at 205. Acts 7:2-4 explicitly says Abraham left Haran only after Terah died. Doing the arithmetic — 205 minus 70 — Terah died when Abram was 135. The Genesis 11 chronology combined with Stephen's speech in Acts is incompatible with Genesis 12:4.
contradictions.commentary:
The arithmetic here is unforgiving and the contradiction is mechanical. Genesis 11:26 — Terah begat Abram at 70. Genesis 11:32 — Terah dies at 205. Subtraction: Abram is 135 when Terah dies. Acts 7:4 — Abram leaves Haran *after* Terah dies. Genesis 12:4 — Abram leaves Haran at 75. 75 does not equal 135.

The standard apologist resolution, which goes back to Augustine and is endorsed by Gleason Archer, takes Genesis 11:26 as a summary statement that doesn't mean Abram was Terah's firstborn. The reasoning: Genesis 11:26 says "Terah lived 70 years and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran" — three sons listed, not all necessarily born when Terah was 70. Abram is listed first because of his theological importance, not birth order. So Abram could actually have been born when Terah was 130, making him 75 when Terah died at 205. The same move is made in Genesis 5 and 10.

This works as a textual maneuver but it's strained. The Hebrew construction of Genesis 11:26 follows the pattern of all the other patriarchal birth notices in chapter 11 — "X lived Y years and begat Z" — and in every other case the begetting age refers to the named child. The apologetic reading has to make Genesis 11:26 uniquely a summary statement while every other case in the chapter is direct. That's special pleading. The harder problem is Acts 7:4 itself. Stephen's speech reflects a tradition (likely from Philo or a similar Second Temple Jewish reading) that explicitly placed Abraham's departure after Terah's death. Stephen and the Genesis 12:4 chronology are operating from different starting assumptions.

The critical consensus, going back to Wellhausen and modern Pentateuchal scholars like Joel Baden, is that the Abraham chronology in Genesis was assembled from P-source genealogies and J-source narrative, and the seams between sources produced the inconsistency. Acts 7 then preserves a separate Hellenistic Jewish tradition that aligned with one possible reading but not with Genesis 12:4 as it stands. Three traditions, no clean fit. Take your pick — but the math is what it is.

contradictions.question: Did Paul go to Jerusalem from Damascus immediately after his conversion?
contradictions.summary: Acts 9:26 says that when Saul came to Jerusalem after his conversion he tried to join the disciples, and the Lukan narrative places this trip very close to the Damascus event. Galatians 1:16-17, written by Paul himself, flatly denies it: he says immediately after his calling he did *not* go up to Jerusalem to confer with anyone, but went into Arabia and back to Damascus first, only going up to Jerusalem three years later (1:18). Luke and Paul tell incompatible stories about the post-conversion trajectory.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest test cases for the historical reliability of Acts versus the autobiographical claims in Paul's own letters — and it's one where most critical scholars side with Paul. Paul writes Galatians under oath, essentially, swearing he's not lying (Gal 1:20). He's making his point precisely because his apostolic legitimacy depends on his not having received his gospel from the Jerusalem pillars. His own credibility on the timeline is staked on the claim that he didn't go up to Jerusalem immediately. He went to Arabia. Then back to Damascus. Then, *meta etē tria* — after three years — he went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, for just fifteen days, and saw no other apostle except James the Lord's brother (Gal 1:18-19).

Acts 9:26 places Saul's arrival in Jerusalem after he escapes Damascus by being lowered in a basket (Acts 9:25), which Acts treats as immediately following the conversion. Acts knows nothing of the Arabian sojourn. The Lukan timeline runs: conversion → Damascus preaching → escape → Jerusalem.

The traditional apologetic harmonization (Bruce, Witherington) inserts the Arabian trip into the gap implied by Acts 9:23 ("after many days") and treats Luke's "many days" as accommodating the three years. That works as a smoothing exercise, but it requires reading Acts 9:23-26 as a heavily compressed summary that silently skips an entire multi-year Arabian and Damascene ministry. The narrative as Luke tells it gives no indication of that compression.

The critical consensus, from Ernst Haenchen forward, is that Luke either didn't know about the Arabian period or chose to omit it because it didn't fit his theological program of presenting Paul as quickly integrated into the apostolic community. Luke is doing the work of harmonizing Paul with the Jerusalem mother church; Paul is doing the work of insisting on his independence from it. Different agendas, different timelines. Paul's first-person account wins on direct evidentiary grounds. Acts is doing apologetic narration. Take your pick on which to trust, but the methodological default in critical scholarship is to weight the primary source over the secondary.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to eat meat sacrificed to other gods?
contradictions.summary: 1 Corinthians 8:4-8 has Paul argue that since an idol is nothing, food sacrificed to it is theologically neutral — eating it neither commends nor condemns you to God. Acts 15:28-29 has the Jerusalem Council decree, as one of a handful of "necessary things" laid on Gentile believers by the Holy Ghost, that they must abstain from meat offered to idols. One text treats idol-meat as a matter of indifference governed only by love for a weaker brother; the other makes abstaining a binding apostolic requirement. They give incompatible answers to the same question.
contradictions.commentary:
A note on the correction first: this entry came in mis-titled as "Is circumcision required?", but the cited verses and the source page (SAB's /contra/meat.html, "Is it OK to eat meat sacrificed to other gods?") are about food offered to idols, not circumcision — a scraper join error. The verses themselves were correct, so the title has been re-aligned to the food-sacrificed-to-idols question the verses actually support, rather than swapping in the circumcision proof-texts. Everything below describes that real Pauline-vs-Lukan seam.

1 Corinthians 8:4-8: Paul argues that since idols are nothing, meat sacrificed to them is theologically neutral; eating it neither commends nor condemns. The only constraint is not to scandalize a weaker brother whose conscience is troubled. Acts 15:28-29: the Jerusalem Council under James decrees that Gentile believers must abstain from meat sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality. These are presented as binding (*epanankes* — "necessary").

Paul's stance in 1 Corinthians 8-10 (cf. Romans 14) treats the idol-meat question as a matter of Christian liberty conditioned only by love for the weaker member. The Jerusalem Council treats it as a categorical prohibition. F. F. Bruce and the conservative tradition try to reconcile these by reading the Acts 15 decree as a temporary local accommodation for Antioch and Asia Minor, not a universal mandate — and noting that Paul might have respected the decree in those areas while teaching liberty elsewhere. But Paul never references the Jerusalem decree in his letters, including in 1 Corinthians, where it would have settled the dispute. Paul's silence on the Apostolic Decree (Acts 15) is one of the most consistent indicators that either Luke composed the decree to harmonize the early church or Paul didn't consider himself bound by it. The critical consensus (Lüdemann, Dunn) is that Luke's Acts 15 is a theological reconstruction; the historical Paul taught liberty on this question without conditions.

The SAB entry, once you correct the question title, is pointing at a real seam between Pauline and Lukan accounts of early church teaching.
