contradictions.question: If a husband believes, is his wife saved also?
contradictions.summary: 1 Corinthians 7:14 says the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the believing one; Acts 16:31 promises the Philippian jailer that he and his household will be saved through his belief. 1 Corinthians 7:16 — written by the same Paul, in the same chapter — asks rhetorically, "How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?" The same author makes two opposite claims about the soteriological reach of one believing spouse, within the span of two verses.
contradictions.commentary:
This one is interesting because the contradiction lives in the same chapter, two verses apart. 1 Corinthians 7:14 — *hēgiastai gar ho anēr ho apistos en tē gynaiki* — "the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the wife." That's a present perfect — already accomplished, already a settled status. Then 7:16 — *ti gar oidas, gynai, ei ton andra sōseis?* — "how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?" Doubt, contingency, uncertainty. Same chapter, same Paul.

The standard exegetical move (Fee, Garland) distinguishes *hagiasmos* (sanctification, ritual/relational holiness) from *sōtēria* (salvation, eschatological deliverance). 7:14 is making the lesser claim — the unbelieving spouse is in some relational sense holy because of the believing spouse, making the marriage and children legitimate within the community. 7:16 is making the larger claim — whether the believing spouse will actually convert the unbeliever to faith remains uncertain. On this reading, sanctification and salvation are two different things, and there's no contradiction.

That distinction works exegetically. The catch is that Paul uses the same word-family elsewhere (*hēgiasmenoi* in 1 Cor 1:2; *hagiazō* throughout) for the soteriological status of believers, not just for relational holiness. The line between sanctification and salvation is blurry in Pauline thought, and 7:14 explicitly extends this status to the children: "else were your children unclean, but now are they holy." If the children are holy on account of one believing parent, that's pretty close to the inherited-salvation claim of Acts 16:31 ("believe and you will be saved, you and your household" — *sōthēsē sy kai ho oikos sou*).

Acts 16:31 is the bigger problem for the apologist. It explicitly promises salvation, not sanctification, to the jailer's household on the strength of his belief. That cuts against the standard Protestant individualist soteriology that requires each person to believe for themselves. The Reformed harmonization is to read "household" as meaning "each member who believes," but that's not what the Greek says. The text says *you and your household will be saved* on the basis of your belief. Compare 1 Cor 7:16 again: how do you know if you'll save your spouse? You don't. Take your pick — sanctification or salvation, household-grace or individual-grace. Paul and Luke aren't fully aligned.

contradictions.question: Can women be church leaders?
contradictions.summary: Acts 18:26 has Priscilla (with her husband Aquila) instructing Apollos in "the way of God" — a clear example of a woman exercising teaching authority in the early church. 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 commands that women keep silent in the churches and not speak; 1 Timothy 2:11-12 prohibits women from teaching or having authority over a man. Pauline-attributed texts both permit and prohibit female leadership in the same canon.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the contradictions where the critical-scholarly explanation is overwhelming and the apologetic explanation is fragile. 1 Timothy is not from Paul — the Pastoral Epistles (1-2 Timothy, Titus) are pseudepigraphic in the mainstream critical consensus, going back through Bauckham, Brown, and Ehrman. The vocabulary, the church-order concerns (overseers, deacons, widow lists), the polemic against "myths and endless genealogies," and the institutional setting all point to a late first or early second century author writing in Paul's name. So when 1 Timothy 2:11-12 prohibits women teaching, it's not Paul making that prohibition — it's a later Pauline-school author trying to constrain a Pauline tradition that had been more egalitarian.

1 Corinthians 14:34-35 is a different problem. Many critical scholars (Fee, Conzelmann, Ehrman) argue these verses are an interpolation. They interrupt the flow of Paul's argument about prophecy, they appear in different positions in some manuscripts (after 14:40 in the Western text tradition), and they directly contradict 1 Corinthians 11:5, where Paul assumes women are prophesying and praying in the assembly — he just wants them to do it with their heads covered. The textual evidence is suggestive enough that NA28 and several major critical commentaries treat 14:34-35 as possibly secondary.

Meanwhile, the egalitarian side of the canon is robust. Romans 16 names Phoebe as a deacon (*diakonos*) and Junia as outstanding among the apostles. Priscilla is consistently named before her husband Aquila — unusual in the ancient world and suggesting her prominence. Galatians 3:28 — neither male nor female in Christ — is a baptismal formula Paul cites approvingly. The apologist (Köstenberger, Schreiner) tries to reconcile by limiting the egalitarian texts to specific contexts and giving the restrictive texts universal force. The critical reading reverses that: the egalitarian practice is original, and the restrictive texts are either interpolations or pseudepigraphic walk-backs. Take your pick on which Paul to follow — but the historical Paul looks a lot more like the one who worked with Priscilla and Junia than the one who silences women in 1 Timothy.

contradictions.question: In whose name is baptism to be performed?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:19 has the risen Jesus command baptism "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" — a Trinitarian formula. Acts 2:38, 8:16, 10:48, and 19:5 all describe actual baptisms being performed in the name of Jesus Christ alone. The Lukan record of early church practice and the Matthean Great Commission disagree about the baptismal formula.
contradictions.commentary:
Here's where the textual history gets interesting. Every actual baptism described in Acts uses a Jesus-only formula — *eis to onoma tou kyriou Iēsou*, "in the name of the Lord Jesus," or variations. Four separate instances, all consistent. Matthew 28:19, by contrast, has the full Trinitarian formula — *eis to onoma tou patros kai tou hyiou kai tou hagiou pneumatos*. If the Great Commission as recorded in Matthew is what Jesus actually said, the apostles in Acts are systematically disobeying it.

The critical-scholarly explanation has two layers. First — and this is a longstanding minority position with serious advocates — there's textual evidence that the Trinitarian formula in Matthew 28:19 may be a later liturgical addition. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing before the Council of Nicaea, repeatedly quotes Matthew 28:19 in a shorter form: "Go and make disciples of all nations in my name." He cites this short form at least 17 times across his works. After Nicaea, Eusebius starts quoting the Trinitarian form. F. C. Conybeare argued in 1901 that the Trinitarian formula was a post-Nicene liturgical insertion. The textual evidence is contested — every Greek manuscript we have includes the Trinitarian formula — but Eusebius is an early and important witness, and his pre-Nicene quotations are weird.

Second — even if Matthew 28:19 is original in the Trinitarian form — the formula reflects the developed liturgical practice of Matthew's community at the time of writing (likely 80s-90s CE), not the historical practice of the earliest church. Acts preserves the older Jesus-only formula because that's what the early Christians actually did. Larry Hurtado and James Dunn both treat the Jesus-only baptism as the original practice; Matthew's Trinitarian formula reflects a later catechetical and liturgical development.

The apologist harmonization (Carson) reads "in the name of" as functionally equivalent across both formulations — the Jesus-only baptism is implicitly Trinitarian because Jesus is the second person of the Trinity. That's anachronistic theology imported into pre-Nicene texts. Take your pick — either Matthew 28:19 is a liturgical anachronism on the lips of Jesus, or the apostles systematically disobeyed his explicit command. Neither answer is comfortable for the harmonization view.

contradictions.question: Did the men with Paul hear the voice?
contradictions.summary: Acts 9:7 says the men traveling with Saul stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Acts 22:9 — in Paul's own retelling of the same event later in Acts — says they saw the light but did *not* hear the voice of the one speaking to him. Same author, same event, two flatly contradictory descriptions of what Saul's companions experienced. The reference "Acts.22:9" in the source uses a non-standard formatting (period instead of space).
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest in-canon contradictions because it's the same author contradicting himself about the same event. Acts 9:7: *akouontes men tēs phōnēs, mēdena de theōrountes* — "hearing the voice but seeing no one." Acts 22:9: *tēn de phōnēn ouk ēkousan tou lalountos moi* — "they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me." Both verses are Luke writing, both verses describe the Damascus road experience, and they directly disagree.

The traditional harmonization, going back to Augustine and championed by Gleason Archer, hinges on the Greek genitive vs. accusative distinction with *akouō*. *Akouō* + genitive (Acts 9:7, *tēs phōnēs*, genitive) supposedly means "hear a sound"; *akouō* + accusative (Acts 22:9, *tēn phōnēn*, accusative) supposedly means "hear with comprehension." So the men heard a sound but didn't understand the words. Problem solved.

This is one of the most repeated apologetic moves on this contradiction, and it doesn't survive scrutiny. The genitive/accusative distinction with *akouō* doesn't consistently work that way in Koine Greek. Daniel Wallace's *Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics* notes that the case distinction with *akouō* is not a reliable marker of comprehension vs. mere hearing. Examples cut both ways — accusative is used for unintelligible sounds, genitive for intelligible speech, and vice versa. F. F. Bruce, who is no friend to skeptical readings, admitted that the case-distinction harmonization "cannot be relied upon."

More importantly, the visual experience also contradicts. Acts 9:7 says they saw no one. Acts 22:9 says they saw the light. Acts 26:13-14 (Paul's third retelling) says everyone fell to the ground; Acts 9:7 says they stood. Three retellings, three different versions of who was standing, who fell, who saw what, who heard what. The critical consensus, from Haenchen forward, is that Luke is composing the three retellings independently for narrative purposes, not preserving a single eyewitness account. The discrepancies are exactly what you'd expect from an author writing dramatic speeches in character without harmonizing them against each other. Take your pick on which retelling counts — but the case-grammar dodge is dead.

Note: The bibleReferences field contains "Acts.22:9" with a period rather than space, which is non-standard formatting and likely a scraper artifact. The reference should display as "Acts 22:9".

contradictions.question: Were the men with Paul knocked to the ground?
contradictions.summary: Acts gives three accounts of Paul's Damascus road encounter and they don't line up. In Acts 26:14 Paul tells Agrippa everyone in the party fell to the ground. In Acts 9:7 the narrator reports that Paul's companions stood speechless. Same author, same event, two physically incompatible postures.
contradictions.commentary: This is a triple-telling problem. Luke narrates the conversion in Acts 9, then has Paul retell it before the Jerusalem mob in Acts 22, then again before Agrippa in Acts 26. The details shift each time. In 9:7 the men stand and hear the voice but see nothing. In 22:9 they see the light but don't hear the voice. In 26:14 they're all knocked down. Apologists like Gleason Archer and Norman Geisler typically run a two-step harmonization here. Step one: maybe everyone fell at first and then got up, so 9:7 is just describing a later moment. Step two: the Greek verb in 9:7 (heistēkeisan, pluperfect of histēmi with stative force) just means "remained" rather than literally "stood," so it doesn't necessarily contradict 26:14. The first move is pure imagination — the text doesn't describe a sequence, it describes a state. The second move strains the lexicon; the perfect/pluperfect of histēmi regularly carries the standing-on-feet meaning (BDAG s.v. ἵστημι), and the contrast with everyone-fell in 26:14 is exactly what makes the tension obvious. Critical scholars including Ernst Haenchen and Hans Conzelmann read the three accounts as Luke's literary reworking, not stenographic transcripts. Luke is a theological storyteller adapting the conversion narrative to fit each rhetorical setting — apology before a Jewish crowd, apology before a Roman king — and the surface details get moved around in the process. The contradiction is real because Luke wasn't writing a court deposition.

contradictions.question: Was Abraham justified by faith or works?
contradictions.summary: Paul and James pick the same proof text — Genesis 15:6 — and push it in opposite directions. Romans 4:2 explicitly says Abraham was not justified by works. James 2:21 explicitly says Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac. Two New Testament writers using one Old Testament figure to make incompatible soteriological claims.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the oldest internal-NT debates in church history and the one that nearly kept James out of the canon. Luther famously called James a "right strawy epistle" precisely because he could not square James 2:21-24 with Romans 3-4. The standard apologetic move, found in everyone from Calvin to Douglas Moo, says Paul and James are using "justify" and "works" in different senses. Paul means initial declaration of righteousness apart from works of Torah; James means demonstration of genuine faith through subsequent action. On this reading, the two are complementary — Paul attacks legalism, James attacks dead orthodoxy. The problem is that both authors quote Genesis 15:6 (Rom 4:3; Jas 2:23) and reach grammatically opposite verdicts on the same Abrahamic episode. Paul's whole argument in Romans 4:2-5 hinges on Abraham *not* being justified by works, full stop, because that's what protects boasting from creeping back in. James 2:24 then states the inverse with equal directness: "a person is justified by works and not by faith alone." Critical scholars including James Dunn, Luke Timothy Johnson, and Dale Allison have argued that James is not just complementing Paul — he is correcting a Paulinist reading, possibly a misreading, that had begun circulating. The two authors come from different streams of early Christianity with different relationships to Jewish-Christian practice, and the redactional history of the canon papered over a genuine theological dispute. The harmonization works only if you assume a coherence the texts themselves resist.

contradictions.question: Who was to blame for original sin?
contradictions.summary: 1 Timothy 2:14 pins the fall on Eve and explicitly says Adam was not deceived. Romans 5:12 puts the entire entry of sin and death into the world on "one man" — Adam. Two Pauline-tradition letters single out two different culprits for the same event, and the 1 Timothy version functions as the basis for restricting women in the assembly.
contradictions.commentary: These two passages have shaped two thousand years of Christian gender theology and they don't agree. Romans 5:12-21 builds a strict Adam-Christ typology where Adam is *the* gateway for sin and death and Christ is the gateway for righteousness — Eve doesn't appear in the argument at all. 1 Timothy 2:13-14 inverts this completely and uses the deception of Eve, not Adam, as the rationale for forbidding women to teach. Traditional harmonizers like Wayne Grudem and Andreas Köstenberger argue that the two texts address different facets of the same event: Adam bears federal-headship responsibility (Romans), Eve bears chronological priority of deception (1 Timothy). The problem is that 1 Timothy 2:14 doesn't just note that Eve was deceived — it explicitly contrasts her with Adam, who "was not deceived," effectively letting him off the deception hook. Critical scholarship has long noted that 1 Timothy is widely regarded as deutero-Pauline; the standard view from Bart Ehrman, Margaret MacDonald, and Raymond Collins is that the Pastorals were written by a later author in Paul's name, in a more rigid ecclesial setting, who is reworking Genesis 3 to bolster a patriarchal church order Paul himself never articulated. The contradiction isn't theological hairsplitting between two complementary truths — it's two different authors, separated by decades, with different agendas, both authorized in scripture. Genesis 3 itself, by the way, doesn't excuse either party.

contradictions.question: Who was God's firstborn son?
contradictions.summary: The Bible designates three different figures as God's firstborn. Exodus 4:22 calls Israel God's firstborn son. Jeremiah 31:9 says it is Ephraim. Romans 8:29 and Colossians 1:15 transfer the title to Jesus. The label is supposed to mark a unique, singular status, but it gets reassigned across the canon.
contradictions.commentary: "Firstborn" (Hebrew *bekor*, Greek *prototokos*) is not a casual title in the Hebrew Bible — it carries legal and theological weight including priority of inheritance and covenantal favor. Exodus 4:22 deploys it nationally; Yahweh's claim on Israel is what justifies the death of Egypt's firstborn. Jeremiah 31:9, written centuries later in a Northern-restoration context, transfers the title to Ephraim — the dominant tribe of the northern kingdom — even though Ephraim was literally the *younger* son of Joseph (Gen 48:14). The New Testament then reassigns the title again to Jesus in Pauline and deutero-Pauline contexts. Apologetic harmonization typically appeals to a non-literal sense: "firstborn" connotes preeminence rather than chronological priority, so multiple figures can hold the title in different aspects (so Murray Harris, F. F. Bruce). That works for some cases — *prototokos* in Col 1:15 plainly invokes status, not chronology — but it doesn't resolve the Israel-versus-Ephraim tension, where both are corporate entities with covenantal claims. Critical scholarship from Jon Levenson and Brevard Childs treats the multiple firstborn designations as evidence of a developing theology that repeatedly recoded chosen-ness for new political and theological situations. The Ephraim claim reflects Northern self-understanding; the Israel claim reflects Exodus-tradition national identity; the Jesus claim represents the early Christian movement reassigning Israel's distinctives to its messianic figure. The harmonization works only if you read "firstborn" as elastic enough to mean almost nothing.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to curse people?
contradictions.summary: Romans 12:14 commands believers to bless and not curse, with no exception clause. Paul himself then breaks that rule. In 1 Corinthians 16:22 he pronounces anathema on anyone who does not love the Lord, and in Galatians 1:8-9 he pronounces it twice on anyone preaching a different gospel — even an angel.
contradictions.commentary: This isn't two authors disagreeing — this is Paul disagreeing with Paul. Romans 12:14 echoes Jesus' Sermon on the Mount teaching: "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse." Paul's language uses *katarasthe* (curse) absolutely, no qualifier. Then in Galatians 1:8-9 he uses *anathema estō* twice — let him be accursed — against rival missionaries. 1 Corinthians 16:22 does the same to anyone who doesn't love Christ. Harmonizers like Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner draw a distinction between personal animosity (forbidden in Rom 12:14) and ecclesial sanction or eschatological judgment (permitted in Gal 1:8 and 1 Cor 16:22). The idea is that Paul is invoking divine judgment, not personal vindictiveness. That distinction is real in later Christian theology, but it isn't textually marked in Romans 12:14 — the verse offers no exception for theological opponents. Critical scholarship from J. Louis Martyn and Hans Dieter Betz has long noted that Galatians is a polemical white-knuckle letter where Paul's emotional register is raw and the rhetoric is closer to first-century juridical curse formulas than to measured pastoral instruction. Paul is a polemicist who, like any polemicist, applies his own principles selectively when his theology is under attack. The contradiction is psychological as much as exegetical: Paul preaches bless-not-curse, then curses anyone who threatens his gospel. The harmonization rescues consistency only by importing categories Paul didn't supply.

contradictions.question: Should we try to please others?
contradictions.summary: Romans 15:2 tells believers each one of us should please his neighbor for his good. 1 Corinthians 10:33 has Paul claiming he himself pleases all people in all things. Galatians 1:10 then has Paul deny this categorically — if he still pleased men, he would not be a servant of Christ. The same author, the same verb (areskō), opposite directives.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction here is internal to Paul and runs across the verb *areskō* in three of his letters. In Galatians 1:10 Paul is defending his apostolic credentials against opponents who apparently accuse him of softening his message to win human approval — and he denies it with the famous "if I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ." Meanwhile in Romans 15:2 and 1 Corinthians 10:33 he is exhorting the same kind of accommodating behavior he repudiates in Galatians. The standard harmonization, articulated by F. F. Bruce and Richard Longenecker, distinguishes motive: please others *for their good* (Rom 15) is altruistic, please others *for your own approval* (Gal 1:10) is self-serving. That distinction is plausible at the level of intent, but it papers over the textual surface — Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:33 says he pleases all people in all things, full stop, and Galatians 1:10 explicitly contrasts pleasing men with serving Christ as if the two were structurally opposed. Hans Dieter Betz and J. Louis Martyn read Galatians 1 as polemical self-defense where Paul is overcorrecting against accusations. The Romans/Corinthians language reflects Paul's pastoral mode in less embattled correspondence. The contradiction isn't fatal to Paul's overall theology, but it does show that his rhetoric on accommodation shifts dramatically depending on whether he is under attack. A consistent ethic of "please your neighbor for their good" cannot survive contact with Galatians 1:10's absolute rejection of people-pleasing without importing a motive distinction the text doesn't supply.

contradictions.question: Is God the author of confusion?
contradictions.summary: 1 Corinthians 14:33 states flatly that God is not the author of confusion. But Genesis 11:7-9 has Yahweh deliberately confounding human language at Babel so the people will not understand one another, and 1 Corinthians 1:27 has God choosing foolish things specifically to confound the wise. The same epistle that denies confusion also describes God deploying it.
contradictions.commentary: The Hebrew verb in Genesis 11:7 is *balal*, "to confuse, mix up" — a divinely engineered cognitive disruption to scatter humanity. The Greek verb in 1 Corinthians 1:27 is *kataischynō*, often translated "shame" but functionally meaning to confound or disgrace the wise — and Paul makes God the subject. Then in 1 Corinthians 14:33 Paul writes *ou gar estin akatastasias ho theos*, "God is not of disorder." The English word "confusion" papers over what are actually distinct Greek and Hebrew concepts. Apologists like Norman Geisler argue the contradiction dissolves once you recognize three different semantic ranges: linguistic scattering in Genesis, rhetorical shaming in 1 Cor 1, and liturgical disorder in 1 Cor 14. That distinction is genuine, and a charitable reading can accommodate it. But the SAB-style question is whether the popular English-Bible reader, encountering the same word "confound/confuse" across these passages in the KJV, ends up with a coherent picture of God's relationship to confusion — and on that surface level, no. Critical scholarship treats Babel as one of the J-source etiologies explaining linguistic diversity through divine intervention (so Speiser, Westermann), and treats 1 Corinthians 1:27 as Paul reworking Isaiah-style reversal motifs. The tension is mostly a translation artifact, but it's also a substantive theological tension: a God who scatters languages and shames the wise is engaged in cognitive disruption, even if the Greek for liturgical disorder in 14:33 is technically a different word. Worth a coherency note that the "confusion" link is partly lexical.

contradictions.question: What is the foundation of the church?
contradictions.summary: 1 Corinthians 3:11 declares Jesus Christ to be the foundation, and adds that no one can lay any other foundation. Ephesians 2:20 says the household of God is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the chief cornerstone — not the foundation itself. The two passages disagree about both what the foundation is and what Christ's relationship to it is.
contradictions.commentary: Both texts come from the Pauline corpus but they use the construction-metaphor language differently. 1 Corinthians 3:10-11 is Paul defending his own foundational ministry against rival teachers in Corinth: I laid the foundation as a wise master builder, and that foundation is Jesus Christ. The grammar is exclusive — *themelion gar allon oudeis dynatai theinai* — no other foundation can be laid. Ephesians 2:19-20 expands the metaphor in a different direction: the household is built *epi tō themeliō tōn apostolōn kai prophētōn*, on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the *akrogōniaiou* (cornerstone). Apologetic harmonizers like Harold Hoehner and Peter O'Brien argue the genitive in Ephesians is appositional or epexegetical (the foundation *which is* the apostles and prophets — but understood as their proclamation of Christ), so Christ remains the substantive foundation in both passages. That's a grammatically possible reading, but it's not the more natural one; the more natural reading is the genitive of source or possession, making the apostles and prophets the foundation themselves. Critical scholarship widely treats Ephesians as deutero-Pauline (Ernest Best, Margaret MacDonald, Andrew Lincoln, with Markus Barth and Hoehner dissenting in favor of Pauline authorship), written by a later author developing Pauline themes into a more institutional ecclesiology where the apostles function as historical pillars. That shift in ecclesiology — from charismatic Pauline congregations where Christ alone is foundational to institutionalized Pauline-tradition churches where the apostles and prophets are constitutive — produces exactly the tension between these two verses. Ephesians is doing church-as-institution; 1 Corinthians 3 is doing Christ-as-sole-foundation.

contradictions.question: Is all Scripture inspired by God?
contradictions.summary: 2 Timothy 3:16 claims all scripture is God-breathed. But Paul himself in 1 Corinthians 7:12 distinguishes his teaching from the Lord's ("to the rest speak I, not the Lord") and in 7:25 admits he has no commandment from the Lord on virgins, only his own judgment. 2 Maccabees 15:39 has its author apologizing for any imperfections in his writing. Three counter-examples where authors disclaim divine inspiration in their own texts.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction has serious implications for any robust doctrine of biblical inerrancy. 2 Timothy 3:16 — *pasa graphē theopneustos* — is the locus classicus for the doctrine of plenary verbal inspiration. But when you cross-reference Paul's own letters, Paul repeatedly distinguishes what he is saying on his own authority from what he is saying on the Lord's authority. 1 Corinthians 7:10-12 explicitly separates the two: "To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord)... To the rest I say (I, not the Lord)." 1 Corinthians 7:25 escalates: "Concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord, but I give my opinion." The author of 2 Maccabees ends his work asking forgiveness if his composition is imperfect — a self-disclaimer hard to reconcile with theopneustic inspiration. Apologetic responses, from B. B. Warfield onward, argue that Paul's distinction between his own judgment and the Lord's reflects which traditions are dominical sayings — sayings from Jesus' earthly ministry — versus Paul's own apostolic ruling, but the latter is still inspired in the canonical sense. That works at a confessional level but it ignores Paul's own surface meaning: he is distinguishing levels of authority precisely because he doesn't think his ruling carries the same weight as a dominical command. Critical scholars including Bart Ehrman and James D. G. Dunn note that 2 Timothy is likely deutero-Pauline, written after Paul's death, and the inspiration claim in 3:16 was made about Jewish scripture (the LXX), not about a New Testament canon that didn't yet exist. The author of 2 Timothy is not making a claim about Paul's own letters, and Paul himself wouldn't have endorsed flat plenary verbal inspiration as later doctrine framed it. The 2 Maccabees citation is also relevant for Catholic and Orthodox canons that include it as scripture.

But to the rest speak I, not the Lord. 1 Corinthians 7:12
			
			        Now concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment....

contradictions.question: Is it OK to marry unbelievers?
contradictions.summary: 1 Corinthians 7:12-14 has Paul instruct believers not to leave unbelieving spouses, and even says the unbelieving partner is sanctified by the believer. 2 Corinthians 6:14-17 forbids being unequally yoked with unbelievers and demands separation. Two letters from the same author to the same congregation produce diametrically opposed verdicts on cross-faith intimacy.
contradictions.commentary: The textual problem here intersects with one of the most contested questions in Pauline scholarship: is 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 even from Paul? In 1 Corinthians 7:12-14 Paul is unambiguous — a believing spouse should not leave the unbelieving partner; in fact, the unbeliever is *hēgiastai* (sanctified) by the believer, and the children are *hagia* (holy). This is a remarkably permissive theology of mixed marriage. Then in 2 Corinthians 6:14-17 the language flips entirely: "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers... come out from among them and be separate." Apologetic harmonization, articulated by writers like Murray Harris, distinguishes scenarios: 1 Corinthians 7 addresses existing marriages that pre-date conversion, while 2 Corinthians 6 prohibits forming new intimate alliances with unbelievers. That scenario distinction is plausible at a pastoral level, but the 2 Corinthians passage extends well beyond marriage to all close partnerships with unbelievers, including the language of "touch not the unclean thing," which is in direct conceptual tension with 1 Corinthians 7:14 where unbelievers are *sanctified* through the marriage relationship. Critical scholarship from Hans Dieter Betz, Victor Furnish, and Margaret Thrall has long argued that 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 is a non-Pauline interpolation — its vocabulary is anomalously Qumran-like, its theology of separation contradicts Paul's surrounding argument in 2 Corinthians, and removing it produces a smoother narrative flow. If that text-critical judgment is correct, the contradiction dissolves at the level of authorship but remains a contradiction within the canonical text. Either way, what canonical readers receive is two incompatible directives.

contradictions.question: Should you speak in tongues?
contradictions.summary: 1 Corinthians 14:5 has Paul saying he wishes all the Corinthians spoke in tongues and that anyone who speaks in tongues edifies himself. A few verses later in 14:8-9 he ridicules unintelligible speech as a trumpet giving an uncertain sound — words spoken into the air. The same chapter both endorses and discourages the practice.
contradictions.commentary: This is actually a softer contradiction than the SAB framing suggests, and is worth a coherency note. Paul's whole argument in 1 Corinthians 14 is not for-or-against tongues but a structured argument for *prophecy over tongues in the public assembly* because intelligibility builds the church. He affirms tongues as private edification (14:2, 14:5, 14:18 — "I thank God I speak in tongues more than all of you"), then argues that in the assembly, prophecy is greater because it builds others up. The 14:8-9 trumpet image isn't a blanket rejection of tongues — it's a rejection of *uninterpreted* tongues in corporate worship. Apologetic and most critical readings agree on this point: Gordon Fee, Anthony Thiselton, and Joseph Fitzmyer all treat the chapter as internally coherent once you respect Paul's public-versus-private distinction. Where the contradiction genuinely lives is in 14:39's command "do not forbid speaking in tongues" versus the broader Pauline silence on tongues outside Corinthians and the apparent decline of the practice in the post-apostolic period. The SAB-style reading flattens Paul's intentional tension into a flat contradiction. The chapter is better read as a regulated endorsement than as a self-contradiction, which means this entry overstates the conflict. There is real tension between Paul's enthusiasm for tongues in 14:5/14:18 and his strong push for intelligible speech, but framing the chapter as yes-vs-no misreads Paul's pastoral strategy.

contradictions.question: Did Paul see Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:1 and 15:8 unambiguously claims to have seen Jesus. Acts 9:8 says that when Paul opened his eyes on the Damascus road he saw no man and had to be led by the hand into Damascus. Paul's first-person testimony and Luke's narrative description of the same event contradict each other on what Paul actually saw.
contradictions.commentary: Paul stakes his apostolic legitimacy on having seen the risen Jesus. In 1 Corinthians 9:1 the rhetorical question "Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?" assumes the answer yes. In 1 Corinthians 15:8 he places himself last in a list of resurrection appearance recipients — *eschaton de pantōn ōphthē kamoi*. Acts 9:8, however, describes the moment Paul rises from the ground and opens his eyes: he saw no one, and his companions had to lead him by the hand into Damascus. Apologists like Gleason Archer and Norman Geisler reconcile by noting that Acts 9:3-7 describes the actual encounter with the light and the voice — and Paul did see something there — while 9:8 describes the *post-encounter* moment of physical blindness. That harmonization is reasonable for Acts itself, but it doesn't fully address the underlying tension. Critical scholarship from John Knox, Hans Conzelmann, and Alan Segal notes that Acts 9 doesn't actually describe Paul *seeing* Jesus — it describes a light, a voice, and a subsequent blindness. Paul's own language in 1 Cor 15:8 (*ōphthē*) is the same passive form used of the other resurrection appearances and connotes a visionary or revelatory seeing rather than ordinary visual perception. Luke and Paul are operating with different conceptions of what the Damascus event was: Paul calls it seeing the risen Lord; Luke describes a Christophany-without-visual-Christ followed by blindness. The deeper contradiction is whether Paul's experience was the same kind of event as the Twelve's encounters with the risen Jesus — a question with major implications for the historicity of the resurrection appearances. Bart Ehrman and Dale Allison both treat Paul's experience as visionary, which would also reframe what the earlier appearances were.

contradictions.question: Who forces non-believers to disbelieve?
contradictions.summary: John 12:40 attributes the blinding of unbelievers' eyes to God, and 2 Thessalonians 2:11-12 has God sending strong delusion so that they will believe a lie and be damned. 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 instead attributes the blinding of unbelievers' minds to the god of this world (Satan). The New Testament cannot agree on whether divine or demonic agency is responsible for unbelief.
contradictions.commentary: The Johannine reading (John 12:40) quotes Isaiah 6:10 and applies the prophet's hardening commission to Jesus' Jewish opponents — God himself is the grammatical subject doing the blinding. 2 Thessalonians 2:11 extends this with God actively sending a *plane* (delusion) so that unbelievers will believe the lie and be judged. 2 Corinthians 4:3-4 attributes the same outcome — blinded minds among the perishing — to *ho theos tou aiōnos toutou*, the god of this age, almost universally understood as Satan. The standard apologetic harmonization, defended by D. A. Carson and Thomas Schreiner, distinguishes ultimate from proximate causation: God ordains the blinding, Satan executes it, and human beings choose unbelief, so all three layers can be true simultaneously. That layered Calvinistic compatibilism does dissolve the formal contradiction — but only by importing a theological framework not present in the texts themselves. Critical scholarship from Raymond Brown on John, Victor Furnish on 2 Corinthians, and Abraham Malherbe on Thessalonians treats these passages as reflecting different theodicies developed independently in different early Christian communities. The Johannine community needed to explain why fellow Jews rejected Jesus and read Isaiah's hardening motif onto them. The Pauline Corinthian context needed to explain why his own gospel was rejected and reached for the Satan-as-blinder image. 2 Thessalonians, generally regarded as deutero-Pauline, develops an eschatological account where God's judgment includes hardening. These are three different etiologies of unbelief stitched into a single canon. The compatibilist harmonization rescues coherence but it isn't what any of the texts is doing on its own terms.

contradictions.question: Did Paul visit all of the disciples when he went to Jerusalem after his conversion?
contradictions.summary: Acts 9:26-28 has Paul, after his conversion, mingling freely with the disciples in Jerusalem, going in and out among them. Paul's own first-person account in Galatians 1:18-19 says he went to Jerusalem only after three years, stayed fifteen days with Peter, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord's brother. Acts and Paul disagree on both the timeline and the breadth of the meeting.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the foundational tensions in critical New Testament scholarship — the disagreement between Acts and Paul's autobiographical statements in Galatians 1-2. Galatians 1 is Paul under oath, defending his apostolic independence by emphasizing how little contact he had with the Jerusalem leadership: *eis Hierosolyma historēsai Kēphan*, to inquire of Cephas, fifteen days, no other apostles except James. Acts 9:26-28 describes the same trip but has Paul joining the disciples broadly, with Barnabas vouching for him to the apostles plural, and Paul moving freely *eis to onoma tou kyriou*. The standard apologetic harmonization, found in F. F. Bruce and Darrell Bock, says Acts gives a general summary while Galatians gives specifics, so when Acts says "the apostles" it really means Peter and James, the only two Paul mentions. That works grammatically — Acts is often loose with collective terms — but it strains plausibility when you stack the divergences. Paul also says the Judean churches did not know him by sight (Gal 1:22), which directly contradicts Luke's picture of Paul moving in and out openly in Jerusalem. Critical scholars including John Knox, Robert Jewett, and Gerd Lüdemann have argued that Luke is constructing a harmonized narrative of early Christian unity that doesn't match Paul's own polemical defense in Galatians. Luke's program is to show continuity and integration between Paul and the Jerusalem apostles; Paul's program in Galatians is to show his independence from them. The contradictions in details flow directly from the different theological projects. Paul, as his own primary source, has priority over Luke writing decades later.

And he was with them coming in and going out at Jerusalem. Acts 9:26-28

contradictions.question: Should we bear each other's burdens?
contradictions.summary: Galatians 6:2 commands believers to bear one another's burdens. Three verses later, Galatians 6:5 says every person shall bear his own burden. The same paragraph from the same author gives diametrically opposite directives about whose burden you carry.
contradictions.commentary: This one rewards lexical attention because Paul uses two different Greek words. In 6:2 the word is *barē* (heavy weights, burdens, troubles); in 6:5 the word is *phortion* (a load, a soldier's pack, sometimes one's own assigned task). The distinction is real and well-documented in BDAG. Apologetic harmonization, articulated by F. F. Bruce, Richard Longenecker, and Ben Witherington, leverages this distinction: *barē* refers to the crushing weights of life that the community helps shoulder, while *phortion* refers to one's own God-given assignment or moral accountability that no one else can carry for you. Read this way, the paragraph is internally coherent — share crises, but own your own responsibilities — and 6:5 may even allude to eschatological judgment ("each will give an account of himself before God," Rom 14:12). Critical scholarship from Hans Dieter Betz and J. Louis Martyn largely agrees this is the correct reading; the verb in 6:5 is future tense (*bastasei*) and points toward the day of judgment, when each person stands alone for their own works. So the apparent contradiction here is largely an artifact of the KJV's translation of both *barē* and *phortion* as "burden." In modern translations the tension visibly softens. This entry should probably be flagged as overstated — the contradiction is more lexical artifact than substantive theological conflict. There remains a genuine pastoral tension between communal solidarity and individual moral accountability, but Paul is making both points deliberately, not contradicting himself.

contradictions.question: Should believers discuss their faith with non-believers?
contradictions.summary: 1 Peter 3:15 commands believers to be ready always to give an answer to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope in them. Colossians 4:5-6 echoes this with speech seasoned with salt toward outsiders. But 2 John 1:10 forbids even receiving anyone who brings a different doctrine into your house, and 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 2:16 command shunning profane and vain babblings. Engage outsiders, or shun them — the New Testament does both.
contradictions.commentary: The texts are talking past each other because they assume different audiences. 1 Peter 3:15 envisions a Christian minority pressed by hostile outsiders demanding to know why these people are different — the *apologia* (defense) is reactive and requires intelligible engagement. Colossians 4:5-6 likewise prescribes outward-facing speech. The Johannine and Pastoral texts envision a different scenario: itinerant teachers carrying heterodox versions of the gospel into believing households, where the rule becomes shun-and-don't-engage. 2 John 1:10's prohibition is specifically about the docetist Christology that the Johannine letters fight throughout (1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 7). The Pastorals' "profane babblings" (*bebēlous kenophōnias*) refers to proto-Gnostic speculation. Apologetic harmonization, articulated by Karen Jobes and George Knight, says these texts address different scenarios: outsiders genuinely seeking get an apologia; insider teachers spreading false doctrine get shunned. That distinction is real and largely correct as exegesis. The contradiction is partially overstated by SAB's framing, but it isn't fully resolved either. The Pastoral epistles deploy *kenophōnias* and the Johannine letters deploy heretic-shunning language in ways that have historically been weaponized against any external engagement, and the texts themselves don't sharply mark the in-group/out-group distinction the harmonization requires. The contradiction is functionally less about whether to discuss faith with non-believers and more about how internally consistent the NT is on doctrinal engagement with dissenters. A coherency note is warranted.

contradictions.question: Is the day of the Lord at hand?
contradictions.summary: 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 has Paul including himself among "we who are alive and remain" until the Lord's coming — assuming an imminent parousia within his own lifetime. 2 Thessalonians 2:2-3 explicitly tells the same community not to think the day of Christ is at hand, because there must first be the apostasy and the revealing of the man of sin. The two letters give incompatible timelines for the eschaton.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction is one of the central reasons critical scholarship overwhelmingly regards 2 Thessalonians as pseudonymous — written in Paul's name by a later author trying to dampen apocalyptic enthusiasm that 1 Thessalonians had stoked. 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 places Paul squarely in the "we who are alive and remain" cohort; he expects to be raptured up to meet the Lord in the air without dying first. By the time you reach 2 Thessalonians 2:2-3, the message has flipped: the day hasn't come, an apostasy must occur first, the man of sin must be revealed, and the present restrainer must be removed. This is precisely the kind of delay-theology you find in late first-century texts that are trying to manage the failure of the imminent parousia (compare 2 Peter 3:8-9). Apologetic harmonizers like F. F. Bruce and Gene Green argue that even in 1 Thessalonians Paul never specifies a date and the "we" is rhetorical, while 2 Thessalonians clarifies the order of events without rejecting imminence. That reading is grammatically possible but minimizes Paul's natural identification with "we who are alive." Critical scholarship from Wolfgang Trilling, Maarten Menken, and Margaret MacDonald has built a strong case that 2 Thessalonians is a deliberate corrective written by a Paulinist after Paul's death, when the parousia hadn't materialized and Paul's authentic letters were generating problematic eschatological excitement. The verbal echoes of 1 Thessalonians in 2 Thessalonians — combined with the theological reversal — fit a forgery designed to defuse the original letter. The contradiction is real, and it has the additional consequence that 2 Thessalonians is best read as evidence of post-apostolic disappointment.

contradictions.question: Can the devil capture us at will?
contradictions.summary: 2 Timothy 2:26 describes the devil holding people captive at his will. James 4:7 says if you resist the devil, he will flee from you. One text portrays the devil as able to take people captive at his own discretion; the other portrays him as easily repelled by ordinary resistance.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction here is partly translation-driven. The Greek of 2 Timothy 2:26 is *ezōgrēmenoi hyp' autou eis to ekeinou thelēma*, which has been read two ways. The KJV-style reading takes both pronouns as referring to the devil: "taken captive by him at his will." An alternative reading, defended by I. Howard Marshall and others, takes the first pronoun as referring to the devil but the second as referring to God: taken captive by the devil to do God's will (since the people are recovering themselves from the devil's snare). On the latter reading the verse no longer claims the devil captures people at his unilateral discretion. James 4:7 is straightforward: resist the devil and he will flee. Apologetic harmonization, articulated by Peter Davids and Douglas Moo, takes the Pastoral verse to mean that those *outside* the believing community are subject to the devil's will, while James addresses those who *are* in the community and can resist effectively. The harmonization holds if you accept the pronoun ambiguity in 2 Timothy and the in-out distinction in application. Critical scholarship from Raymond Collins and Luke Timothy Johnson generally accepts that 2 Timothy is conceptually closer to a deterministic captivity model than James' resistance model, reflecting different anthropologies in different streams of early Christianity. The Pastorals lean toward a more pessimistic view of unaided human ability against demonic power; James is closer to early Jewish wisdom traditions where moral resistance is straightforward. The contradiction is real but soft, and partially mitigated by the pronoun ambiguity in the Greek. A coherency note about the lexical/pronoun issue is warranted.

contradictions.question: Did Enoch die?
contradictions.summary: Hebrews 11:13 lists Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and Sarah and says "these all died." Eight verses earlier the same chapter, Hebrews 11:5, explicitly says Enoch was translated so that he should not see death — echoing Genesis 5:24 where God simply took him. The same author appears to both deny and affirm Enoch's death within one chapter.
contradictions.commentary: This is the rare contradiction where the author actually does seem to trip over himself, but careful reading mitigates the problem. Hebrews 11:5 is unambiguous about Enoch: he was translated (*metetethē*) so that he should not see death. Hebrews 11:13 then says *kata pistin apethanon houtoi pantes* — "according to faith these all died" — within a paragraph that lists Abraham and Sarah, but the immediate antecedent of "these all" is contested. Apologetic harmonization, defended by William Lane and Harold Attridge, takes 11:13 to refer specifically to the patriarchal figures mentioned in 11:8-12 (Abraham, Sarah, and their descendants), not to Abel and Enoch from earlier in the chapter. On this reading, "these all" is restrictive to the immediately preceding cluster, and Enoch is excluded by 11:5. The Greek grammar is genuinely ambiguous, and the immediate-antecedent reading is plausible. Critical scholarship from Attridge, Craig Koester, and Luke Timothy Johnson largely accepts this restrictive reading; the author of Hebrews knew his own claim about Enoch in 11:5 and is unlikely to have contradicted it eight verses later. The contradiction is more apparent than real and depends on reading "these all" maximally. There is still some literary tension because the chapter's opening cluster of figures includes Abel and Enoch, and the average reader hits 11:13 and naturally folds them back in. A coherency note is warranted: the contradiction is grammatically resolvable and probably overstated by the SAB framing.

contradictions.question: Was Rahab saved by faith or works?
contradictions.summary: Hebrews 11:31 says Rahab the harlot did not perish with the disobedient because of her faith when she received the spies. James 2:25 says Rahab was justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way. Same Old Testament figure, same single act (hiding the Israelite spies in Joshua 2), two contradictory verdicts on what saved her.
contradictions.commentary: This is the same Pauline-vs-Jacobean tension that appears around Abraham (see id 542), now applied to Rahab. Hebrews places Rahab in its great roll-call of faith heroes — *pistei Raab hē pornē* — and credits her preservation to faith. James 2:25 zeroes in on the same episode and credits her justification to works (*ex ergōn*). Both texts cite the same act: hospitable concealment of the spies. The harmonization, articulated by Douglas Moo and Peter Davids, runs through the faith-as-demonstrated-by-works framework: Rahab's reception of the spies was the visible expression of her underlying faith, so both authors are describing the same reality from different angles. That harmonization works at the systematic-theology level but it requires importing later categories — the medieval *fides quae* / *fides qua* distinction, or Reformation faith-and-works syntheses — that neither author articulates. Critical scholarship from Luke Timothy Johnson, Dale Allison, and Harold Attridge treats Hebrews 11 as drawing on Jewish-Hellenistic exemplar traditions (Sirach 44, 4 Maccabees) where faith and faithful action are intertwined, while James 2 is explicitly polemicizing against a faith-alone reading — likely a misreading of Paul. The contradiction reflects two early Christian streams disagreeing about how Rahab's salvation works, with both texts authorized as canonical scripture. Whatever harmonization is possible at the doctrinal level, the canonical text places these two verdicts in unresolved juxtaposition. Rahab is the rare figure both authors reach for, and that's exactly why the disagreement is sharpest.

contradictions.question: Do rabbits chew their cud?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 11:6 declares the hare unclean because it "cheweth the cud" but does not divide the hoof. The problem is that rabbits and hares simply do not chew cud. They are not ruminants. They lack the multi-chambered stomach that defines cud-chewing animals like cattle, sheep, and goats. The text places hares in a biological category they don't belong to.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist move here is what Gleason Archer pulls in the Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties — he points at cecotrophy. Rabbits eat their own soft fecal pellets, called cecotropes, to extract more nutrients on a second pass. Archer wants to call this "rumination" because it kind of looks like the animal is reprocessing food. That's the move. The problem is that it's not what rumination means in zoology and it's not what the Hebrew text is doing. The Hebrew phrase is *ma'alat gerah* — literally "bringing up the cud" — and the parallel verses (Leviticus 11:3-7, Deuteronomy 14:6-7) clearly group the hare with the camel and the rock badger as animals that "bring up" what's already been swallowed. Cecotrophy isn't bringing anything up. The pellets come out the back end. Mary Douglas in *Purity and Danger* and Jacob Milgrom in the Anchor Bible Leviticus commentary both treat this as a straightforward classification by the Israelite observer based on visible jaw motion — the constant chewing motion of hares and rock badgers looked like cud-chewing, so they got grouped that way. That is a perfectly reasonable thing for a Bronze Age priestly writer to do. It is not a perfectly reasonable thing for an omniscient deity to dictate. The harmonization only works if you redefine the Hebrew term to fit modern biology, which is the apologist playbook page one — read the text loosely enough and any error disappears. The text says the hare brings up cud. It doesn't.

answers.answer: The Bible claims rabbits chew their cud, but they do not

contradictions.question: Can visual stimuli during conception affect the appearance of offspring?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 30:39 has Jacob's flocks conceiving in front of peeled striped rods and then producing striped and spotted lambs. The text is making a biological claim — that what an animal looks at while mating influences the genetics of its offspring. This is maternal impression theory, and it is not how heredity works. Coat patterns come from alleles, not from what mom was staring at.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic dodge here is to say God supernaturally produced the speckled offspring and Jacob's rods were just incidental — Walton in the IVP Bible Background Commentary leans this way. But that reading is a retrofit. The text gives no indication that the rods are decorative. Genesis 30:37-39 spells out a deliberate procedure: Jacob peels the rods, sets them in the watering troughs where the strongest animals come to drink and mate, and the flocks "conceived before the rods" and produced spotted offspring. The causal logic of the passage is that the visual exposure produced the phenotype. This is precisely the ancient Near Eastern folk belief in maternal impression — the idea that what a pregnant animal or woman saw could imprint on the fetus. It shows up in Pliny the Elder, in Soranus, in medieval bestiaries. Hermann Gunkel in his Genesis commentary identifies the rods explicitly as sympathetic magic, and Claus Westermann in the Continental Commentary treats it the same way. Even John Walton, who wants to preserve the historicity, admits this is operating on "ancient principles of animal husbandry" that are not scientifically valid. So the apologist has to choose: either the text means what it says and the biology is wrong, or the text is doing folklore and we shouldn't expect it to track modern genetics. Either way, the claim that visual stimuli at conception affects offspring is false, and the narrator of Genesis 30 presents it as if it works. That is of course a subjective reading of intent, but the syntax of verses 37-39 makes the causal chain hard to wave away.

answers.answer: The Bible claims striped rods caused striped offspring
answers.answer_explanation: And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted. (Genesis 30:39)

contradictions.question: What is the shape of the earth?
contradictions.summary: Isaiah 40:22 describes God sitting upon the "circle of the earth," which apologists routinely cite as evidence the Bible knew the planet was spherical. Matthew 4:8 then has the devil taking Jesus up a mountain high enough to see "all the kingdoms of the world" — a geometry that only works on a flat earth. The contradiction is between a text apologists read as scientifically prescient and a text that assumes a flat-earth cosmology where altitude provides global visibility.
contradictions.commentary: First the Isaiah verse, because the apologetic case rests entirely on a translation move. The Hebrew word is *chug*, which means "circle" — a flat disc, a horizon line — not *kaddur*, which is the word for a ball or sphere (used in Isaiah 22:18). The standard critical commentaries — Brevard Childs in the OTL, Joseph Blenkinsopp in the Anchor Bible — all treat *chug* as describing a flat circular disc of land surrounded by waters, sitting under a domed firmament (*raqia*). That cosmology is everywhere in the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 1:6-8, Job 22:14, Job 38:13-14, Proverbs 8:27. It maps cleanly onto Mesopotamian flat-earth cosmology documented by Wayne Horowitz in *Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography*. So Isaiah 40:22 is not a spherical-earth verse. It is a flat-disc verse that some translations have made ambiguous in English. Now Matthew 4:8 — the temptation pericope. Davies and Allison in the ICC point out that the visual logic of "all the kingdoms of the world" being visible from a single mountain only makes sense in a worldview where the earth is flat enough that a high enough vantage point would show everything. Ulrich Luz in the Hermeneia volume agrees. The harmonization that the devil showed Jesus a vision is exactly the kind of post-hoc rationalization that has to be invented because the plain text doesn't work on a globe. The mountain in Matthew is a real mountain doing real geometry, and the geometry assumes a flat earth. Take your pick: either Isaiah 40:22 doesn't mean what apologists want it to mean, or Matthew 4:8 contradicts a sphere — most likely both.

answers.answer_explanation: [It is] he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof [are] as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in: (Isaiah 40:22)

answers.answer: All kingdoms can be seen from a high mountain, implying a flat earth
answers.answer_explanation: Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; (Matthew 4:8)

contradictions.question: Do snakes eat dust?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 3:14 has Yahweh cursing the serpent to crawl on its belly and eat dust "all the days of thy life." Snakes do not eat dust. They eat rodents, eggs, birds, frogs, fish, and other snakes. The text makes a factual claim about reptilian diet that is false.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists run two harmonizations here and both fail. The first is the figurative reading — "eating dust" is just a Hebrew idiom for humiliation, like Micah 7:17 or Isaiah 65:25 or Psalm 72:9. That part is true. The phrase does function idiomatically elsewhere. The problem is that Genesis 3:14 is not just deploying a stock idiom. It is an etiology, a just-so story explaining why snakes look and move the way they do. The verse pairs "upon thy belly shalt thou go" — a physical description of legless locomotion — with "dust shalt thou eat," and the parallelism demands that both clauses be doing the same kind of work. If the belly clause is literal (and it has to be, since it explains the snake's anatomy), then the dust clause is too. Hermann Gunkel and Claus Westermann both read this as a classical etiological curse. Snakes flick their tongues to the ground constantly to taste-smell their environment, and an ancient observer easily concluded they were eating dirt. That is good ancient natural history. It is bad biology. The second harmonization, that snakes incidentally ingest some dust while striking prey, is grasping at straws — the text doesn't say snakes get a little dust on their food, it says dust IS their food, every day of their lives. John Walton in the NIVAC concedes that this is folkloric etiology and not zoological description. So the verse is making a factual claim about snake diet that doesn't comport with reality. The idiomatic reading rescues the metaphor at the cost of conceding the etiology — and the etiology is what the text is actually doing.

answers.answer: The Bible claims snakes eat dust, but they do not
answers.answer_explanation: And the LORD God said unto the serpent, Because thou hast done this, thou [art] cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life: (Genesis 3:14)

contradictions.question: How does the water cycle work according to the Bible?
contradictions.summary: This entry pairs Ecclesiastes 1:7 — rivers running to the sea and returning to their source — with Job 38:22, where snow and hail are kept in heavenly "treasuries" or storehouses. The pairing is meant to show the Bible has both a quasi-naturalistic hydrology and a mythological storehouse cosmology side by side, but the two verses are doing different things and aren't strictly contradictory on their own terms.
contradictions.commentary: This one is weaker as a contradiction than the database treats it. Ecclesiastes 1:7 is observational poetry — Qoheleth notes that rivers flow to the sea, the sea never overflows, and the cycle continues. That's not a precise hydrological cycle in the modern sense (no evaporation mechanism is described), but it's not making a false claim either. Job 38:22, by contrast, is straightforwardly mythological cosmology: snow and hail are stored in *otsarot* (storehouses or treasuries), the same kind of celestial reservoirs that show up in Deuteronomy 28:12, Jeremiah 10:13, and Psalm 135:7. Othmar Keel in *The Symbolism of the Biblical World* documents how this storehouse model maps to broader Ancient Near Eastern cosmology — Yahweh has chambers in the sky for rain, snow, hail, and wind. So the real tension is not between the two verses being compatible with each other but between Job's storehouse cosmology and modern meteorology. The Ecclesiastes verse is doing observational naturalism within an ANE worldview; the Job verse is doing mythological storehouse cosmology. They can coexist as different genres of Hebrew thought without strictly contradicting one another. The contradiction would be sharper if both verses were claiming to describe the same mechanism. As phrased, the question would be better recast as "Does the Bible reflect mythological cosmology about weather?" — at which point Job 38:22 alone does the work without needing Ecclesiastes 1:7 as a foil. That is of course a subjective call, but the entry as written conflates a non-contradiction with a real cosmological problem.

answers.answer: Rivers flow to the sea and return to their source (accurate cycle)
answers.answer_explanation: All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea [is] not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again. (Ecclesiastes 1:7)

answers.answer: Snow and hail are stored in treasuries (storehouses)
answers.answer_explanation: Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail, (Job 38:22)

contradictions.question: How many beatitudes are in the Sermon on the Mount?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 5:3-11 lists nine separate "blessed are" statements as part of the Sermon on the Mount. Luke 6:20-23, in the parallel Sermon on the Plain, lists only four. The two accounts diverge sharply both in number and in content — Luke's beatitudes are addressed in the second person to the materially poor and hungry, while Matthew spiritualizes them ("poor in spirit," "hunger and thirst after righteousness") and addresses them in the third person.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonization apologists like Blomberg deploy is that Matthew and Luke are reporting different sermons on different occasions, so the numerical difference doesn't matter. Two sermons, two sets of beatitudes, no contradiction. The Synoptic data does not support this. Both sermons follow the same narrative position in their respective Gospels (after the calling of disciples, before the healing of the centurion's servant), share the same core sayings about the poor, the hungry, and the persecuted, and conclude with the same parable about building on rock versus sand. Critical scholarship from Hans Dieter Betz to Ulrich Luz to Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Luke treats these as two redactional reworkings of a common Q tradition. Matthew has expanded the list by adding the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers, and has spiritualized the social-economic categories — "poor" becomes "poor in spirit," "hungry" becomes "hungering for righteousness." Luke has preserved a sharper, more economically literal version closer to Q. This is the Synoptic Problem at work — the same source material gets reshaped by each evangelist to serve their theological purpose. So the question "how many beatitudes are in the Sermon" only generates a contradiction if you assume the two Gospels are giving independent eyewitness reports of the same event. Once you accept that both are literary compositions drawing on shared earlier tradition, the divergence is exactly what source-critical scholarship predicts. The apologist needs the two-sermon theory to preserve inerrancy, but the parallels are too tight and the redactional fingerprints too obvious. Matthew added beatitudes. Luke kept fewer. Take your pick on which one matches what Jesus actually said.

answers.answer_explanation:

Blessed [are] they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. (Matthew 5:4)

Blessed [are] the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. (Matthew 5:5)

Blessed [are] they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. (Matthew 5:6)

Blessed [are] the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. (Matthew 5:7)

Blessed [are] the pure in heart: for they shall see God. (Matthew 5:8)

Blessed [are] the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God. (Matthew 5:9)

Blessed [are] they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for their's is the kingdom of heaven. (Matthew 5:10)

Blessed are ye, when [men] shall revile you, and persecute [you], and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. (Matthew 5:11)

And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said, Blessed [be ye] poor: for your's is the kingdom of God. (Luke 6:20)

Blessed [are ye] that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed [are ye] that weep now: for ye shall laugh. (Luke 6:21)

contradictions.question: Who prophesied about the thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 27:9 attributes the quotation about the thirty pieces of silver to Jeremiah the prophet. The actual quotation comes from Zechariah 11:12-13, not Jeremiah. Jeremiah has nothing about thirty pieces of silver — the closest material is the potter's house and the field-purchase narrative in Jeremiah 18-19 and 32, but the specific wording Matthew quotes is unambiguously Zecharian.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the most discussed citation problems in the New Testament. The apologetic responses cluster around three moves and none of them hold up cleanly. Move one, from Gleason Archer and others, is that Matthew is conflating Jeremiah and Zechariah and intentionally citing the more prominent prophet — there's a rabbinic convention of citing a composite quote under the better-known name. This is the strongest harmonization, and Davies and Allison in the ICC give it serious attention. The problem is that the Matthean citation doesn't actually fuse two passages — it quotes Zechariah and attaches Jeremiah's name. There's no Jeremiah material in the quoted text. Move two is that Matthew is alluding to Jeremiah 19 (the potter's flask, the bloody field) and Jeremiah 32 (the field purchase for silver) thematically while quoting Zechariah's wording. This works as a typological reading but doesn't explain why Matthew names Jeremiah as the source of the quote, not just the theme. Raymond Brown in *The Death of the Messiah* concludes the most likely explanation is straightforward — Matthew or his source made a mistake. Move three is the textual-variant dodge, citing the few late manuscripts that read "Zechariah" or omit the name, but Bruce Metzger's *Textual Commentary* makes clear that "Jeremiah" is the original reading, and the variants are scribal corrections of the embarrassment. So the apologist is left with: either Matthew made a citation error, or he was using a non-canonical Jeremianic tradition that no longer exists, or he's doing some rabbinic conflation that the text doesn't actually support. The simplest reading — Matthew misattributed Zechariah to Jeremiah — is the parsimonious one.

answers.answer_explanation: Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value; (Matthew 27:9)

answers.answer: The prophecy is actually found in Zechariah
answers.answer_explanation: And I said unto them, If ye think good, give [me] my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty [pieces] of silver. (Zechariah 11:12)

contradictions.question: Should you answer a fool according to his folly?
contradictions.summary: Proverbs 26:4 says do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him. The very next verse, Proverbs 26:5, says answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes. The two verses give directly opposite instructions using nearly identical wording, juxtaposed back-to-back in the same chapter.
contradictions.commentary: This is the classic example of a deliberately paired contradiction in wisdom literature, and the apologetic response is actually pretty good — but it concedes more than apologists usually admit. The standard harmonization, articulated by Bruce Waltke in the NICOT Proverbs commentary and by Michael Fox in the Anchor Bible, is that the two verses are a deliberate juxtaposition meant to signal the situational nature of wisdom. Sometimes engaging a fool drags you down to his level; sometimes refusing to engage leaves him puffed up. The wise person discerns which situation calls for which response. That is a perfectly defensible reading. It's also a reading that admits the surface contradiction is real and intentional — the editors of Proverbs placed these two verses next to each other precisely because they don't agree, and the disagreement itself is the lesson. So this is not really a contradiction in the inerrantist sense; it's a feature of wisdom literature that resists systematization. The problem for apologists is that this same hermeneutic — "the contradiction is the point" — can't easily be transported elsewhere. When Matthew and Mark disagree about the time of the crucifixion or about who Jesus appeared to first, you don't get to say "the contradiction is the point, it teaches us about the situational nature of truth." Proverbs 26:4-5 works because it's an explicit pedagogical pairing. So as a contradiction this entry is technically valid on the surface but rhetorically weak — the resolution is right there in the literary form. The honest verdict: real surface tension, intentional editorial juxtaposition, and the resolution is genre-internal.

answers.answer: No, do not answer a fool or you will be like him
answers.answer_explanation: Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him. (Proverbs 26:4)

answers.answer: Yes, answer a fool or he will think himself wise
answers.answer_explanation: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit. (Proverbs 26:5)

contradictions.question: How many apostles were in office between the resurrection and ascension?
contradictions.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:5 reports that the risen Jesus appeared "to Cephas, then to the twelve." But by the time of the resurrection, Judas Iscariot had already died (Matthew 27:3-5), and Matthew 28:16 explicitly calls the post-resurrection group "the eleven disciples." Acts 1:9 has Jesus ascending while the eleven look on, and Matthias is not selected until Acts 1:26. So between resurrection and ascension the apostolic college numbered eleven, not twelve.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic move here is to say "the twelve" is a titular collective name for the apostolic group — like calling a sports team "the Bulls" even when one player is injured. Anthony Thiselton in the NIGTC 1 Corinthians commentary and Gordon Fee in the NICNT both adopt this reading: "the twelve" functions as a fixed designation for the apostolic body regardless of actual membership. That's a defensible reading and it's probably what Paul means. But it doesn't fully dissolve the tension — Paul is reporting a resurrection appearance, presumably with a specific historical referent, and at the moment of that appearance the group physically present numbered eleven men. The standard critical observation, made by Hans Conzelmann in the Hermeneia 1 Corinthians, is that Paul is quoting an early creedal formula (1 Corinthians 15:3-5) that pre-dates his letter. The formula's use of "the twelve" probably reflects pre-Pauline tradition that hadn't yet been harmonized with the Judas-betrayal narrative. There's an even deeper problem: the textual variants. Some witnesses read "the eleven" instead of "the twelve" in 1 Corinthians 15:5 — Bruce Metzger's *Textual Commentary* discusses this. The fact that scribes felt the need to correct the number to eleven shows that ancient readers also saw the conflict. So either Paul (or his pre-formed creed) is using "the twelve" as a fixed title that doesn't track actual headcount, or there's an unresolved tension between the Pauline tradition and the gospel narratives about Judas. The titular reading is defensible but it concedes that the number is not literal — which means the contradiction is real at the level of arithmetic and only dissolves at the level of conventional usage.

answers.answer_explanation: And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: (1 Corinthians 15:5)

Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, (Matthew 27:3)

Then the eleven disciples went away into Galilee, into a mountain where Jesus had appointed them. (Matthew 28:16)

And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. (Acts 1:9)

contradictions.question: Should Christians judge others?
contradictions.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:15 says the spiritual person "judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man." Two chapters later in the same letter, 1 Corinthians 4:5, he tells the same audience to "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come." The two verses use related Greek verbs from the same root (*anakrinō* in 2:15, *krinō* in 4:5) and address the same community on the same general topic, and they push in opposite directions.
contradictions.commentary: This is the kind of contradiction that actually has a decent contextual resolution, but the resolution requires admitting that Paul is using *krinō* in two different senses, which is fine but undermines the inerrantist insistence on consistent semantic usage. In 1 Corinthians 2:15, the verb *anakrinō* (to examine, discern, evaluate) describes the pneumatic person's capacity to discern spiritual realities — it's the same word used in Acts 17:11 of the Bereans examining the scriptures. In 1 Corinthians 4:5, the verb *krinō* describes premature verdict-rendering, particularly about whether Paul and Apollos are faithful ministers. So Paul is saying: discern things now, but don't pronounce final judgment until the eschaton. Anthony Thiselton and Gordon Fee both handle this in their commentaries by mapping the semantic range of *krinō* across Paul's usage. The harmonization works, but only if you accept that "judge" doesn't mean one consistent thing — and inerrancy as commonly defended depends on the text speaking with semantic precision. The broader Pauline corpus is even messier. Romans 14:4 tells believers not to judge each other's diet practices; 1 Corinthians 5:12 tells believers to judge insiders; 1 Corinthians 6:2-3 says the saints will judge angels. Paul is not operating with a single doctrine of judgment. He's operating contextually, which is fine if you read him as a pastoral letter-writer responding to specific situations, and a problem if you read him as the inspired and consistent author of a unified systematic theology. So the contradiction is real at the lexical surface and softens with contextual analysis — but the harmonization concedes that Paul is using overlapping vocabulary inconsistently across contexts.

answers.answer: Yes, the spiritual person judges all things
answers.answer_explanation: But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man. (1 Corinthians 2:15)

answers.answer: No, judge nothing before the Lord comes
answers.answer_explanation: Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God. (1 Corinthians 4:5)
