contradictions.question: How long was Jesus in the tomb?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 12:40 has Jesus predicting he will be "three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" — a precise duration of 72 hours, paralleling Jonah in the fish. But the passion narratives uniformly have Jesus crucified Friday afternoon (the day of preparation) and discovered risen Sunday morning. That's at most two nights (Friday night, Saturday night) and parts of three days. The arithmetic doesn't get to three nights.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the harder ones for apologists because the numbers just don't work. The standard harmonization, from Gleason Archer and Craig Blomberg, invokes the rabbinic principle of inclusive reckoning — any part of a day counts as a whole day. So Friday (part) + Saturday + Sunday (part) = three days. The Talmud Yerushalmi Shabbat 9:3 is cited in support. The problem is that the principle covers days, not nights. "Three days" with inclusive reckoning gets you Friday-Saturday-Sunday. "Three nights" with inclusive reckoning gets you... Friday night and Saturday night. Two. There is no third night. You can't include Thursday night because Jesus wasn't dead yet, and you can't include Sunday night because he was already risen. Matthew 12:40 specifically pairs days with nights — three of each — and the Jonah parallel makes the parallelism load-bearing. R. T. France in the NICNT Matthew tries to argue that "three days and three nights" is itself an idiom for a span of time including any part of three days, but he admits the case is strained. Some apologists try to rescue the count by moving the crucifixion to Wednesday — the "Wednesday crucifixion" theory — but this requires rewriting the chronology of the entire passion week against the unanimous testimony of the four gospels that the day of preparation was the day before the Sabbath. So the apologist has three options: redefine "three days and three nights" as a non-literal idiom (which deflates Matthew 12:40's deliberate parallel with Jonah), invent a Wednesday crucifixion (which the gospels don't support), or admit that Matthew 12:40 is overshooting the actual chronology. Take your pick. The parsimonious reading is that Matthew is enhancing the Jonah typology and the result doesn't precisely match the synoptic chronology of the passion.

answers.answer_explanation: For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. (Matthew 12:40)

answers.answer: He rose on the third day (Friday evening to Sunday morning is less than three nights)
answers.answer_explanation: And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again. (Mark 10:34)

contradictions.question: Does God give freely or withhold his blessings?
contradictions.summary: James 1:5 and Luke 11:10 present God as giving freely and liberally to all who ask. But John 12:40 (quoting Isaiah 6:10) has God blinding eyes and hardening hearts so people cannot be converted; Joshua 11:20 says it was "of the LORD to harden their hearts" so they would fight Israel and be destroyed; and Isaiah 63:17 has the prophet accusing God of making his people "err from thy ways" and hardening their hearts. The contradiction is between God-as-generous-giver and God-as-active-spoiler-of-salvation.
contradictions.commentary: This is the Calvinist-Arminian fault line written into the canon itself. Apologists usually run two harmonizations. The first is the theodicy move — God hardens hearts only after the recipients have already hardened their own (cf. Romans 9:18 with the Pharaoh narrative as the test case). On this reading, divine hardening is judicial: God ratifies a prior human choice. Walter Brueggemann in the OTL Isaiah 40-66 commentary, and Douglas Moo in the NICNT Romans, both engage this seriously. The problem is that the texts don't actually support the "prior hardening" sequence consistently. Joshua 11:20 has the Canaanites hardened *so that* God can destroy them — the purpose is annihilation, and there's no indication of prior moral choice driving the divine action. Isaiah 63:17 has the prophet accusing God directly: "Why hast thou made us to err?" — this is not a recipient who hardened first. John 12:40, quoting Isaiah 6:10, makes the hardening the cause, not the consequence, of the people's failure to believe — the verse explicitly says God blinded and hardened them "that they should not see... and be converted, and I should heal them." The second harmonization, the Calvinist one, just bites the bullet: God sovereignly chooses to give to some and harden others, and James 1:5 applies only to the elect. This preserves consistency at the cost of making "giveth to all liberally" mean "giveth to the elect liberally," which is a meaningful narrowing the text doesn't perform on its own. So the apologist is stuck: either God's generosity is genuinely universal (in which case the hardening texts contradict it) or it's restricted (in which case James and Luke are speaking imprecisely). The contradiction is real and it runs through the canon's competing soteriologies.

answers.answer: God gives freely to those who ask
answers.answer_explanation:
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all [men] liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.

For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

answers.answer: God withholds his blessings and prevents men from receiving them
answers.answer_explanation:
He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with [their] eyes, nor understand with [their] heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly, [and] that they might have no favour, but that he might destroy them, as the LORD commanded Moses.

O LORD, why hast thou made us to err from thy ways, [and] hardened our heart from thy fear? Return for thy servants' sake, the tribes of thine inheritance.

contradictions.question: Is God to be found by those who seek him?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 7:8 and Proverbs 8:17 both promise that those who seek will find — the seeker-finds-God formula is presented as a universal principle. Proverbs 1:28 directly contradicts it: "Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me." The same wisdom tradition that promises finding also promises non-finding under certain conditions.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic harmonization is straightforward and partially defensible: Proverbs 1:28 is the voice of personified Wisdom rejecting those who previously rejected her — it's a context-specific judgment on those who scorned wisdom when she called. Bruce Waltke and Michael Fox both read it this way. So the contradiction is contextual, not absolute. Fair enough. But this resolution does some work for the apologist and some work against them. It resolves the surface contradiction by saying "seek and you shall find" comes with an implicit time limit — you have to seek before you've definitively rejected wisdom, after which the door closes. That's a coherent doctrine. The problem is that Matthew 7:8 doesn't include the time limit. Jesus's framing is unconditional: "every one that asketh receiveth." *Pas* — every. Not "every one who has not previously rejected," not "every one within the window." If the apologist imports Proverbs 1:28's time-limit qualifier into Matthew 7:8, they're harmonizing by inserting a condition the text doesn't state. If they don't, then Matthew 7:8 and Proverbs 1:28 are making incompatible promises. Dale Allison and W. D. Davies in the ICC point out that Matthew 7:7-8 sits within a sermon that promises confidence in prayer without qualification — and Matthew's larger context, particularly the rejection of the Pharisees in chapters 23 and the apocalyptic discourse, does include conditions for being shut out. So even within Matthew the universal promise gets qualified elsewhere. The real verdict: there is an absolute-sounding promise in Matthew 7:8 and a conditional non-promise in Proverbs 1:28, and the texts achieve consistency only when readers smuggle each verse's qualifications into the other.

answers.answer: God is to be found by those who seek him
answers.answer_explanation:
For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me.

answers.answer: God is not to be found by those who seek him
answers.answer_explanation: Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me:

contradictions.question: Does God destroy man for his wickedness?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 6:5-7 has God resolving to destroy humanity precisely because "the wickedness of man was great" and "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually." After the flood, Genesis 8:21 has the same God promising never again to curse the ground or smite all living things for man's sake — and giving as his reason "for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." The exact same reason that motivated the flood is now cited as a reason NOT to flood again.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleaner contradictions in Genesis because the same Hebrew phrase — *yetser libbo ra* (the inclination of his heart is evil) — appears in both verses, and it functions as the explicit grounds for opposite divine decisions. In Genesis 6:5 the evil inclination triggers destruction; in Genesis 8:21 it triggers forbearance. Apologists like Kenneth Mathews in the NAC Genesis volume try to harmonize by saying that 8:21 reflects God's mercy responding to Noah's sacrifice — the post-flood promise is a new covenantal move that doesn't contradict the pre-flood judgment because circumstances have changed. That works narratively but it doesn't dissolve the contradiction in the divine reasoning. The text doesn't say "because of Noah's sacrifice I will hold back." It says "because man's heart is evil from his youth I will hold back" — using the evil inclination as the *reason for restraint*. This is one of the strongest pieces of source-critical evidence for the JEDP hypothesis. Critical scholars from Hermann Gunkel to Claus Westermann to Joel Baden have noted that Genesis 6 and Genesis 8 carry different sources within the flood narrative — Genesis 6:5-8 is widely assigned to J (the Yahwist), and so is Genesis 8:20-22. So the contradiction is internal to a single source, not just an artifact of redaction. Robert Alter handles this by reading the divine character development across the narrative — God learns that destruction doesn't fix the human condition and resolves on a different strategy. That's a literary reading and it has real merit, but it concedes that God in Genesis 8:21 is not the immutable God of later systematic theology. He's a deity who changes his mind in response to experience. Either the deity learns and changes (which contradicts immutability) or the text contradicts itself about the relationship between human evil and divine destruction. Take your pick.

answers.answer: Because of man's wickedness God destroys him
answers.answer_explanation:
And GOD saw that the wickedness of man [was] great in the earth, and [that] every imagination of the thoughts of his heart [was] only evil continually.

And the LORD said, I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth; both man, and beast, and the creeping thing, and the fowls of the air; for it repenteth me that I have made them.

answers.answer: Because of man's wickedness God will not destroy him
answers.answer_explanation: And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake; for the imagination of man's heart [is] evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done.

contradictions.question: Can God's attributes be known?
contradictions.summary: Paul in Romans 1:20 says God's invisible attributes — his eternal power and divine nature — are "clearly seen" from the creation, so that humans are "without excuse." Job 11:7 has Zophar asking "Canst thou by searching find out God? Canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?" — the implied answer being no. Isaiah 40:28 says of God "there is no searching of his understanding." The contradiction is between Paul's claim that God's nature is plainly accessible through observation of creation and the wisdom-tradition claim that God is fundamentally beyond human search.
contradictions.commentary: This one softens significantly once you parse what each text is actually claiming. Paul in Romans 1:20 is making a specific argument about *general revelation* — the existence of God and his power are evident from creation, which is enough to render Gentiles morally culpable. He's not claiming that the full divine nature is exhaustively knowable. Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Romans points out that Paul's argument has a polemical purpose: stripping Gentiles of the excuse of ignorance. Job 11:7 and Isaiah 40:28 are making a different claim — that God's *full* nature, his unsearchable understanding, his perfect knowability, exceeds human capacity. Both could be true at once: God's existence and power are evident, but his complete nature is unsearchable. Most apologists run this distinction and most critical scholars accept it. So the surface contradiction has a real exegetical resolution. The remaining problem is that Romans 1:20 has been historically deployed by apologists as much more than a minimal-knowability claim — it's used to argue that natural theology can deliver substantive attributes of God (omniscience, omnipotence, eternality, moral character) directly from observation of nature. That stronger reading does conflict with Job and Isaiah. So the contradiction is real if Romans 1:20 is read maximally and dissolves if it's read minimally. The standard exegesis goes minimal. The popular apologetic deployment goes maximal. That is of course a subjective call about the use rather than the text — but as a textual contradiction this entry is weaker than it looks. The verses can be reconciled by carefully delimiting what "knowing God" means in each context.

answers.answer: God's attributes are revealed in his works'
answers.answer_explanation: For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, [even] his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:

Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?

Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, [that] the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? [there is] no searching of his understanding.

contradictions.question: Should the blood-shedder be put to death?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 9:5-6 lays down the Noahide blood-vengeance principle: whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed, because humans are made in God's image. This is presented as a universal post-flood law. Genesis 4:15 has God explicitly protecting Cain — the original murderer — from being killed, marking him so no one will kill him, and threatening sevenfold vengeance on anyone who does. God's policy toward blood-shedders is opposite in the two passages.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization is chronological: Genesis 9:5-6 establishes the death penalty post-flood, while Genesis 4:15 reflects a pre-flood, pre-law dispensation when the formal mandate for capital punishment hadn't yet been given. Kenneth Mathews and Wenham both run this version. That's a coherent narrative reading and it does dissolve the contradiction on a flat-chronological reading of Genesis. The problem is that the canonical-chronological reading is exactly the kind of harmonization that source criticism dismantles. Critical scholars from Gunkel through Westermann through Joel Baden assign Genesis 4:15 to J (the Yahwist) and Genesis 9:5-6 to P (the Priestly source). They reflect different theological visions of how God deals with murderers. The J source preserves an older tradition where Cain is protected even after fratricide — the mark of Cain is apotropaic, designed to keep blood vengeance from spiraling. The P source articulates the later legal principle that bloodshed requires bloodshed because of the image-of-God theology that P develops elsewhere (Genesis 1:26-27). So the contradiction is not just narrative; it's theological, reflecting two different streams of tradition about divine justice. Apologists who run the chronological harmonization implicitly concede that God's policy toward murder changed between Cain and Noah, which raises a separate theological problem — if the death penalty for murder is grounded in the image of God (Genesis 9:6), and humans were made in God's image from the start (Genesis 1:27), then the principle was always operative and Cain's protection was an arbitrary divine exception. The image-grounded reasoning of 9:6 makes the chronological harmonization sit awkwardly with the broader Priestly anthropology. Either policy changed, or two sources disagree, or both. The contradiction is real and the harmonization carries theological costs.

answers.answer_explanation:
And surely your blood of your lives will I require; at the hand of every beast will I require it, and at the hand of man; at the hand of every man's brother will I require the life of man.

Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
And the LORD said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.

contradictions.question: Is improvidence okay?
contradictions.summary: Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount and parallel Lukan material tells his followers to take no thought for tomorrow, to give to everyone who asks, to lend without expecting return, and to consider the lilies of the field who neither toil nor spin. 1 Timothy 5:8 condemns anyone who fails to provide for his own household as "worse than an infidel," and Proverbs 13:22 praises the good man who leaves an inheritance to his children's children. Improvidence is celebrated in Matthew/Luke and condemned in the Pastoral Epistles and Proverbs.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic move here is to spiritualize the synoptic material as eschatological or attitudinal rather than economic. Don Carson and Craig Keener both argue that "take no thought for the morrow" doesn't mean "don't plan" — it means "don't be anxious," the verb *merimnaō* carrying the sense of crippling worry rather than prudent provision. On that reading, Jesus isn't condemning planning, just anxiety, and 1 Timothy 5:8 is perfectly compatible. This is a defensible exegesis and probably catches part of what Matthew is doing. But it concedes a lot. The radical sayings of Jesus in Matthew 6 and Luke 6 are framed in language that goes well beyond "just don't be anxious." "Sell your possessions and give alms" (Luke 12:33), "give to every one that asketh of thee" (Luke 6:30), "lend, hoping for nothing again" (Luke 6:35) — these are not anxiety-management instructions, they are concrete economic practices. Pieter Craffert and other social-scientific NT scholars have documented that the historical Jesus movement appears to have practiced a radical itinerant economic ethic at odds with householder values. The Pastoral Epistles — almost certainly pseudonymous on the consensus of critical scholars from Bart Ehrman to Margaret MacDonald — represent a later, settled Christian community institutionalizing household and inheritance norms. So the contradiction reflects a real diachronic shift: the early radical Jesus tradition demanded improvidence as a form of trust in eschatological provision; the later church needed stable households and economic responsibility. Ehrman in *Forged* and Raymond Collins in the Sacra Pagina Pastorals both treat 1 Timothy as second-generation Christianity adjusting Jesus's economic ethics for ongoing community life. The harmonization works only if you read Jesus's radical sayings as hyperbole and the Pastorals as their plain meaning — at which point you're picking which texts speak literally. The development is real, and reading it as a contradiction is honest historiography.

answers.answer_explanation:
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:

Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?

Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day [is] the evil thereof.

Give to every man that asketh of thee; and of him that taketh away thy goods ask [them] not again.

But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and [to] the evil.

Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.

But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

A good [man] leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner [is] laid up for the just.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to get angry?
contradictions.summary: Ephesians 4:26 says "Be ye angry, and sin not" — anger is permitted, even commanded, as long as it doesn't lead to sin and isn't carried into the next day. Ecclesiastes 7:9 warns against being hasty to anger because "anger resteth in the bosom of fools." Proverbs 22:24 warns against even associating with an angry man. James 1:20 says "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God." The texts pull in opposite directions on the moral status of human anger.
contradictions.commentary: This one has a relatively clean exegetical resolution that works for most of the texts but leaves residual tension. Ephesians 4:26 is quoting Psalm 4:4 (LXX *orgizesthe kai mē hamartanete*) and almost certainly means something like "in your anger, do not sin" — it's not actually commanding anger, it's regulating it. So even at the lexical level, the Ephesians verse is closer to "when you find yourselves angry, don't let it become sin" than to a positive endorsement of anger. Andrew Lincoln in the WBC Ephesians and Harold Hoehner both read it this way. That brings Ephesians 4:26 closer to the Ecclesiastes/Proverbs/James pole than the contradiction suggests. The remaining tension is genuine but smaller — the wisdom tradition and James present anger as basically negative, while Ephesians 4:26 acknowledges anger as a feature of human experience that must be managed rather than purely condemned. That's a difference of emphasis, not a flat contradiction. Where the contradiction sharpens is in the broader biblical treatment of divine anger — Yahweh's wrath is praised throughout the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, while James 1:20 specifically restricts human anger because it doesn't produce God's righteousness. The implicit move is that anger is appropriate to God but not to humans, which is a coherent theological position but does mean that an emotion presented as virtuous in deity is condemned in humanity. As a contradiction in this entry's framing, the case is weak — Ephesians 4:26 reads more as a regulation of anger than an endorsement, and the texts mostly agree that human anger is dangerous. The contradiction would be sharper if the entry pulled in divine-anger texts as a third pole.

answers.answer_explanation: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:

Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.

Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go:

For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus teach physical resistance?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 5:39 has Jesus teaching non-resistance: do not resist evil, turn the other cheek. Matthew 26:52 has him telling Peter to put away his sword because those who take the sword perish by it. But Luke 22:36 has Jesus instructing his disciples to sell their cloaks and buy swords, and John 2:15 has Jesus himself making a whip of cords and physically driving moneychangers out of the temple. The Jesus of the Sermon on the Mount and the Jesus of the temple cleansing don't appear to operate on the same ethic.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic harmonizations on this one are unusually creative because the surface contradiction is so visible. For Luke 22:36 — "he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one" — Joel Green in the NICNT Luke and others read it as ironic or symbolic. Jesus is telling them to gear up rhetorically for opposition, not to literally arm themselves, which is why two swords (Luke 22:38) is somehow enough. The problem is that two swords being "enough" only makes sense if the swords are literal, just sufficient for a small defensive band. If the swords were purely symbolic, the disciples wouldn't have presented physical weapons. For John 2:15 — the temple cleansing — apologists often argue that the whip was only used on the animals, not the people. The Greek is genuinely ambiguous (*pantas exebalen* — "he drove them all out" — with *ta te probata kai tous boas* clarifying "both the sheep and the oxen"). D. A. Carson in the Pillar John commentary argues the whip targeted livestock, not humans. But the action is still physical force, and "drove them all out" most naturally includes the merchants. Raymond Brown in the Anchor Bible John takes the violence as directed at moneychangers and merchants, not just animals. So even on the most charitable reading, Jesus uses physical force to expel humans from a religious space. The non-resistance teaching in Matthew 5:39 is also widely understood by critical scholars (Dale Allison, John Meier) as referring to personal honor-disputes — slaps to the face are insults, not lethal attacks — rather than a comprehensive pacifism. So both ends of the contradiction get qualified: the resistance teaching may be narrower than absolute pacifism, and the swords/whip incidents may be narrower than general endorsements of violence. But the contradiction persists. The Sermon on the Mount Jesus and the temple-cleansing Jesus represent two streams of tradition about how Jesus related to coercive force, and the harmonizations work only if you let each text qualify the other rather than letting either stand at full strength.

answers.answer_explanation:
But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.

answers.answer: Christ taught and practiced physical resistence
answers.answer_explanation:
Then said he unto them, But now, he that hath a purse, let him take [it], and likewise [his] scrip: and he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one.

And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;

contradictions.question: Should you fear death?
contradictions.summary: Luke 12:4 has Jesus telling his disciples not to fear those who can kill the body, because they have no more power beyond that. John 7:1 then describes Jesus himself avoiding Judea "because the Jews sought to kill him." The teacher who tells his followers not to fear death-threats appears to behave as though he himself takes them seriously enough to avoid the region where the threat is greatest.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of those contradictions that depends entirely on the difference between teaching and behavior, and the apologetic response is reasonable but not airtight. Standard harmonizations from D. A. Carson in the Pillar John and Andreas Köstenberger in the BECNT John argue that Jesus's avoidance of Judea was not fear-driven but strategically timed — he wasn't running from death, he was managing the timeline of his own approach to the cross. The Johannine "hour" (cf. John 7:6, 7:8, 7:30) is a recurring motif throughout John's Gospel: Jesus operates on a divinely-ordained schedule, and premature confrontation with Jerusalem would short-circuit the passion narrative. On this reading, John 7:1 isn't reporting fear, it's reporting tactical patience. That's a coherent Johannine theological reading and it preserves the consistency between Jesus's teaching and behavior. But it's also a reading that depends on theological commitments the synoptic Jesus may not share. In Mark, Jesus's approach to Jerusalem reads more as deliberate confrontation than carefully-timed self-preservation, and the Gethsemane prayer ("let this cup pass from me," Mark 14:36) suggests an authentic moment of dread about death — which is itself in tension with Luke 12:4's teaching. Raymond Brown in *The Death of the Messiah* treats Gethsemane as preserving genuine Jesus-tradition about anxiety in the face of death. So the contradiction isn't only between John 7:1 and Luke 12:4 — it runs deeper, between the Lukan teaching of fearlessness and the broader synoptic and Johannine portrayal of a Jesus who is at minimum strategic about death and at moments visibly distressed by it. The harmonization works if you accept the Johannine "hour" theology as the controlling frame; it gets messier if you take the synoptic data alongside. As a contradiction this is real but the resolution is closer than the database wording suggests — John 7:1 isn't necessarily about fear, but the broader question "did Jesus practice what he taught about not fearing death" gets harder when Gethsemane is included.

answers.answer: Christ warned his followers not to fear being killed
answers.answer_explanation: And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do.

answers.answer: Christ himself avoided the Jews for fear of being killed
answers.answer_explanation: After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to ask for things while praying?
contradictions.summary: The contradiction targets importunity — persistent, repetitive petitioning in prayer. Matthew 6:7-8 directly condemns it, with Jesus telling the disciples not to babble like the Gentiles because the Father already knows what they need before they ask. Luke 11:5-13 (the friend at midnight) and Luke 18:1-8 (the persistent widow) run the opposite way, with Jesus explicitly teaching that persistence in asking is exactly what gets rewarded.
contradictions.commentary: The substantive contradiction here is real and well-attested in Synoptic scholarship — Matthew 6:7-8 directly contradicts the importunity teachings in Luke 11 and Luke 18. In Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, Jesus instructs disciples not to heap up empty phrases (battalogeo) like the Gentiles, because the Father already knows what they need before they ask. The whole point of the Lord's Prayer that follows is brevity. Luke, meanwhile, frames Jesus' parables of the friend at midnight (11:5-13) and the persistent widow (18:1-8) around exactly the opposite logic — keep asking, keep knocking, wear God down like a widow harasses an unjust judge. Luke 18:1 explicitly states the parable's lesson: "that they ought always to pray, and not to faint." Apologists like Blomberg and Carson typically harmonize by claiming Matthew condemns only mindless pagan repetition while Luke commends sincere persistence, but this is a distinction without a textual basis — both passages address the question of whether God responds to repeated, persistent asking, and they answer it differently. The deeper source-critical point is that Matthew and Luke are deploying Jesus tradition to make competing rhetorical points about prayer's mechanics.

answers.answer_explanation:
And he said unto them, Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say unto him, Friend, lend me three loaves; For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him? And he from within shall answer and say, Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee. I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.

And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.

But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen [do]: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.

Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.

contradictions.question: Why was the Sabbath instituted?
contradictions.summary: The two versions of the Decalogue give incompatible etiologies for the Sabbath. Exodus 20:11 grounds it in creation — Yahweh rested on the seventh day after making the heavens and earth, and Israel is commanded to keep the Sabbath because God did. Deuteronomy 5:15 grounds it in the Exodus — Israel is to keep the Sabbath because Yahweh brought them out of Egypt with a mighty hand. These are not complementary motives; they are two distinct theological rationales for the same commandment, each presented as the reason God commanded it.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest source-critical fingerprints in the entire Pentateuch. The Priestly redactor of Exodus 20:11 reaches back to Genesis 2:2-3 — also a Priestly text — and grounds the Sabbath in the cosmic rest of God after creation. The Deuteronomist (singular hand or school, traditional D source) has no interest in that creation theology. The Deuteronomic Sabbath is humanitarian and historical — you rest, your slaves rest, your animals rest, because you used to be slaves yourselves. Two rationales, two source streams, one commandment. Apologists like Gleason Archer typically harmonize by claiming both reasons are true and complementary, that God can have multiple motives for a single commandment. That's true in the abstract, but it does not address the textual problem. Each Decalogue presents its rationale as *the* reason ("wherefore," "therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee"), and the rationales reflect distinct theological programs — P's cosmological Sabbath versus D's social-justice Sabbath. The Documentary Hypothesis predicts exactly this kind of doublet. Mark Smith and Jeffrey Tigay treat the divergence as a textbook case of the redactor's failure (or refusal) to harmonize competing traditions. The contradiction isn't a problem unless you assume a single human author writing a unified theology — which is precisely what historical-critical scholarship has not assumed for over a century.

answers.answer: The Sabbath instituted because God rested on the seventh day
answers.answer_explanation: For [in] six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them [is], and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

answers.answer: The Sabbath instituted because God brought the Israelites out of Ebypt
answers.answer_explanation: And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and [that] the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day.

contradictions.question: Should you be baptized?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:19 places baptism at the center of the risen Jesus' Great Commission to the eleven — go, make disciples, baptize them in the triune name. Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:14, 17 says the opposite about his own mission — he thanks God he baptized almost no one in Corinth, and flatly states that Christ did not send him to baptize but to preach the gospel. The contradiction is at the level of mission priority: Matthew's Jesus makes baptism constitutive of the commission; Paul explicitly excludes it from his own.
contradictions.commentary: The tension here is real but more nuanced than a flat yes/no contradiction. Matthew 28:19 is the climactic command of the Gospel — disciples are made by baptizing and teaching, in the triune name. Most critical scholars (Davies-Allison, Luz) treat 28:19 as a late, post-resurrection composition reflecting the practice of Matthew's community c. 80-90 CE, including the developed triune baptismal formula which is otherwise unattested in this form in the rest of the NT. Paul, writing earlier (mid-50s CE) and apparently unaware of any dominical baptismal command, treats baptism as ancillary to his apostolic calling. In 1 Corinthians 1:17 he draws a sharp distinction: "Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel." Apologists like Blomberg harmonize by noting that Paul baptized *some* (Crispus, Gaius, the household of Stephanas) and that his statement is hyperbolic emphasis on preaching, not rejection of the rite. Fair enough — but that harmonization assumes Paul knew of and accepted the Great Commission as a binding command, which the textual evidence doesn't support. If Paul had received a dominical instruction to baptize all nations, his rhetorical disavowal in 1 Corinthians 1:17 would be theologically suicidal. The more parsimonious reading is that the Great Commission in its Matthean form represents a later ecclesiastical development that Paul did not inherit. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but the evidence leans heavily in that direction.

answers.answer_explanation: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:

I thank God that I baptized none of you, but Crispus and Gaius;

For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to marry your brother's widow?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 25:5 not only permits but commands a man to marry his deceased brother's childless widow — the institution of levirate marriage (Hebrew yibbum), with the explicit purpose of raising up offspring to perpetuate the dead brother's name. Leviticus 20:21 flatly prohibits exactly the same act, calling it an "unclean thing" (niddah) that uncovers the brother's nakedness, with the penalty that the couple shall be childless. Same action, opposite rulings.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest Pentateuchal legal contradictions in the entire corpus, and it's been recognized as such since the medieval rabbis. The Levitical prohibition (Holiness Code, H source) treats marriage to a brother's wife as incest — the same logic that prohibits a man from "uncovering the nakedness" of his father's wife or his daughter-in-law. The penalty in Leviticus 20:21 is even thematically barbed: the violators will be childless, which is precisely the opposite outcome from what Deuteronomy 25 commands the levirate to *prevent*. The Deuteronomic law (D source) addresses a different social anxiety entirely — preserving the dead man's lineage and inheritance line. Apologists like Archer and Walton harmonize by claiming Leviticus addresses marriage to a living brother's wife (adultery) while Deuteronomy addresses marriage to a deceased brother's widow. That harmonization is textually plausible for Leviticus 18:16 (which is parallel), but it strains Leviticus 20:21, which doesn't specify the brother's state. More importantly, the rabbinic tradition itself acknowledged the tension — m. Yebamot is one giant attempt to harmonize the laws, ultimately concluding that the Deuteronomic levirate *overrides* the Levitical prohibition only in the specific case of childless widowhood. That's not harmonization; that's legislative arbitration between two laws that conflict on their face. Source criticism explains this cleanly: H and D reflect distinct legal traditions with different priorities — H is preoccupied with priestly purity, D with social and economic preservation of the family line.

answers.answer: A man may marry his brother's widow
answers.answer_explanation: If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her.

answers.answer: A man may not marry his brother's widow
answers.answer_explanation: And if a man shall take his brother's wife, it [is] an unclean thing: he hath uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to hate your relatives?
contradictions.summary: Luke 14:26 has Jesus state baldly that no one can be his disciple without hating father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and his own life. Ephesians, by contrast, commands honoring father and mother as the first commandment with promise (6:2), commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church (5:25), and observes that no one ever hated his own flesh (5:29). The discipleship hatred Jesus demands is exactly what the Pauline household codes forbid.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologist move on Luke 14:26 is to invoke the Semitic-idiom defense — the Greek miseo ("hate") functions as a Semitic comparative meaning "love less," and Matthew's parallel in 10:37 reads "he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me," supposedly clarifying the meaning. That's a real linguistic phenomenon (cf. Genesis 29:31, Malachi 1:2-3 with Romans 9:13), and Joseph Fitzmyer and François Bovon both note it. But the apologist version oversells the case. Luke's wording is sharper than Matthew's, and Luke 14:26 lists "his own life also" — which complicates the simple "love less" reading, because the rest of the saying clearly requires costly self-renunciation, not just relative prioritization. The point of the radical wording is the *break* from natural family loyalty that itinerant discipleship demanded. Luke's Jesus is recruiting wandering charismatics who literally leave family behind, and the rhetoric matches the social practice. Ephesians, written by a later Pauline disciple (most critical scholars treat it as deutero-Pauline) c. 80-95 CE, reflects the second-generation church that had to figure out how to live in households and stay married — hence the Haustafel (household code) at 5:21-6:9 with its careful instructions about loving wives, honoring parents, and managing slaves. The trajectory from itinerant radicalism to settled household ethics is a well-documented sociological development in early Christianity (Theissen). The contradiction is real: the early Jesus tradition commands family-renunciation; the later household codes command family-affirmation.

answers.answer_explanation: If any [man] come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.

contradictions.question: Should you obey your rulers?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Exodus, Daniel, Mark, Luke, Acts, Romans
contradictions.summary: Romans 13:1-6 commands universal submission to governing authorities on the grounds that they are ordained by God, are God's ministers, and punish only evildoers — resistance to them is resistance to God's ordinance and incurs damnation. Multiple narrative threads contradict this directly: the Hebrew midwives are blessed for disobeying Pharaoh (Exodus 1:17, 20), Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego defy Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:16-18), Daniel defies Darius (Daniel 6:7-10), and the New Testament itself describes righteous figures — Jesus, Daniel, the prophets — being executed or persecuted by the very rulers Romans 13 claims punish only the evil.
contradictions.commentary: Romans 13 is the single most theologically embarrassing passage in the Pauline corpus for any reader who has actually noticed how the Bible's own narratives treat rulers. Paul's claim is sweeping and grammatically unconditional — pasa psyche (every soul) is to be subject; there is no exception clause for unjust rulers. The text explicitly says rulers are not a terror to good works but to evil. That claim is empirically false within the biblical canon itself. The midwives obey God by lying to Pharaoh and are blessed for it. Daniel's friends face the fiery furnace for refusing imperial worship. Daniel himself prays in defiance of a royal decree. Acts 4:26-27 explicitly cites Psalm 2 against the rulers who conspired against Jesus. The cross itself is a state execution carried out by Pilate, a ruler Romans 13 would categorize as God's minister punishing evildoers. Apologists like Cranfield and Moo limit Romans 13 to legitimate authority acting within its proper sphere, importing a Lockean exception clause that Paul does not provide. Others (Käsemann, Wright) read Romans 13 against Paul's own apocalyptic framework — the present age is passing away (13:11-12), so submission is provisional and pragmatic, not absolute. Both readings are post-hoc attempts to soften a passage that, read at face value, commands the kind of obedience the Hebrew Bible's heroes are celebrated for refusing. The best critical assessment is that Paul, writing to a vulnerable Roman house-church in the late 50s, wanted to keep his communities off the imperial radar. The text reflects that pastoral situation rather than a universal theology — but Paul does not say that, and the Bible's own narratives consistently celebrate exactly the kind of civil disobedience Paul condemns.

answers.answer: It is our duty to obey our rulers, who are God's ministers and punish evil doers only
answers.answer_explanation:
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.

Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.

For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:

For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing.

answers.answer: It is not our duty to obey rulers, who sometimes punish the good and receive unto themselves damnation therefor
answers.answer_explanation:
But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.

Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty.

Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we [are] not careful to answer thee in this matter.

But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.

All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.

Wherefore king Darius signed the writing and the decree.

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.

The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord, and against his Christ.

For of a truth against thy holy child Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together,

And he said unto them in his doctrine, Beware of the scribes, which love to go in long clothing, and [love] salutations in the marketplaces,

And the chief seats in the synagogues, and the uppermost rooms at feasts:

Which devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayers: these shall receive greater damnation.

And Herod with his men of war set him at nought, and mocked [him], and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe, and sent him again to Pilate.

And Pilate gave sentence that it should be as they required.

And when they were come to the place, which is called Calvary, there they crucified him, and the malefactors, one on the right hand, and the other on the left.

And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided [him], saying, He saved others; let him save himself, if he be Christ, the chosen of God.

contradictions.question: Do women have rights?
contradictions.books_in_tension: Genesis, Judges, Acts, 1 Corinthians, 1 Timothy, 1 Peter
contradictions.summary: The contradiction sets the silencing-and-subordination passages — Genesis 3:16 (the husband rules over the wife as curse), 1 Timothy 2:12 (woman may not teach or have authority), 1 Corinthians 14:34 (women keep silence in the churches), 1 Peter 3:6 (Sarah as model of calling her husband lord) — against texts that show women exercising public religious and political authority: Deborah the prophetess judging Israel (Judges 4:4, 14-15; 5:7), the Joel/Acts 2:18 promise of women prophesying, and Philip's four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:9). The same canon both denies women teaching authority and celebrates women exercising it.
contradictions.commentary: This is a real and recognized contradiction within the canon, and it sits at the heart of contemporary debates over women in ministry. The egalitarian/complementarian fight in evangelical scholarship (Payne, Belleville, Keener vs. Grudem, Schreiner) is fundamentally an attempt to reconcile these texts. The Pastorals (1-2 Timothy, Titus) and the disputed 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 passage are the silencing texts. Most critical scholars consider 1 Timothy pseudonymous, written c. 90-110 CE to address a more institutionalized church where the egalitarian impulse of earliest Christianity was being rolled back. Even more striking: 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 has serious textual problems. Gordon Fee argues it is a post-Pauline interpolation, noting that some Western manuscripts place these verses after 14:40 rather than after 14:33, which Fee takes as evidence of a marginal gloss that migrated into the text. Payne has extended this argument with manuscript evidence. If 14:34-35 is non-Pauline, then Paul's authentic position is reflected in 1 Corinthians 11, where women pray and prophesy in the assembly. The Deborah and Philip's-daughters texts are not isolated outliers — they reflect a real tradition of female prophetic and judicial authority in ancient Israel and the early church (cf. Phoebe the deacon in Romans 16:1, Junia the apostle in Romans 16:7, Priscilla teaching Apollos in Acts 18:26). The apologist harmonization typically restricts women's authority to extraordinary or domestic contexts while preserving male leadership in the institutional church. That harmonization works only by treating the silencing texts as normative and the agency texts as exceptional — a hermeneutical choice, not a textual one. Reverse the priority and the canon supports women's ministry; keep the priority and it forbids it. The contradiction is real, and the resolution is a question of which texts you privilege.

answers.answer_explanation:
Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire [shall be] to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.

But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.

Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but [they are commanded] to be under obedience, as also saith the law.

Even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord: whose daughters ye are, as long as ye do well, and are not afraid with any amazement.

And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time.

And Deborah said unto Barak, Up; for this [is] the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the LORD gone out before thee? So Barak went down from mount Tabor, and ten thousand men after him.

And the LORD discomfited Sisera, and all [his] chariots, and all [his] host, with the edge of the sword before Barak; so that Sisera lighted down off [his] chariot, and fled away on his feet.

[The inhabitants of] the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel.

And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy:

And the same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy.

contradictions.question: Should you obey both God and your masters?
contradictions.summary: Colossians 3:22-23 and 1 Peter 2:18 command slaves to obey their earthly masters in all things, with fear and sincerity of heart, including "froward" (harsh) masters. Matthew 4:10 cites Deuteronomy that worship and service are owed to God alone. 1 Corinthians 7:23 tells believers, "Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men." Matthew 23:10 forbids anyone being called master (kathegetes) because Christ is the only master. The household codes' command to serve human masters with fear contradicts Jesus' and Paul's direct statements that service belongs to God alone.
contradictions.commentary: The household codes (Haustafeln) in Colossians 3:18-4:1, Ephesians 5:21-6:9, 1 Peter 2:13-3:7, and the Pastorals reflect the post-Pauline church's attempt to make Christianity socially respectable in the Greco-Roman world. The slave-master code in Colossians 3:22 and 1 Peter 2:18 is theologically jarring next to texts like 1 Corinthians 7:23 ("be not ye the servants of men") and Galatians 3:28 ("there is neither slave nor free"). Critical scholarship generally treats Colossians as deutero-Pauline and 1 Peter as pseudonymous, with the Haustafeln representing a second-generation Christian accommodation to Roman social norms. The contradiction with Jesus' teaching in Matthew 23:8-10 — "call no man your father upon the earth... neither be ye called masters" — is sharp. Jesus there forbids the very titles of hierarchical authority that the household codes inscribe. Apologists harmonize by distinguishing categories: slaves obey masters in a limited social sphere; ultimate worship and allegiance go to God alone; therefore there is no conflict. That distinction works rhetorically but founders on 1 Peter 2:18's specific command to obey *harsh* masters and on the household codes' demand for *fear* — a religiously loaded term in the LXX (phobos) that elsewhere is reserved for God. The deeper issue is the Bible's overall failure to condemn slavery as an institution. The household codes don't just permit slavery; they baptize the slave-master relationship into Christian theology by making slave-obedience a religious duty. The contradiction with Jesus' "call no man master" tradition is one of the canon's clearest indicators that the post-Pauline church traded the radical egalitarian gospel of earliest Christianity for institutional respectability. That is of course a judgment call on the evidence, but the textual evidence points in that direction.

answers.answer_explanation:
Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.

Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men.

Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, [even] Christ.

contradictions.question: Do seed time and harvest ever cease?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 8:22, the Noahic covenant, declares that while the earth remains, "seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease." The Joseph cycle then narrates seven years of famine so severe that famine extends "in all lands" and "over all the face of the earth" (Genesis 41:54, 41:56, 45:11). The same book records a global agricultural failure that the same book had just promised would never occur.
contradictions.commentary: Read at face value, the contradiction is direct. The Genesis 8:22 covenant uses universal language — while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest will not cease. The Joseph narrative then describes a seven-year famine that the text repeatedly characterizes as global ("all lands," "all the face of the earth"). The Hebrew kol ha'aretz can be read locally ("all the land") or universally ("all the earth"), and apologists like Archer leverage that ambiguity to limit the famine to the Near East — Egypt, Canaan, and surrounding territories. That's textually plausible for the Joseph narrative; the Hebrew Bible regularly uses kol ha'aretz hyperbolically. The problem is that Genesis 41:57 says "all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn," reinforcing the global framing. More importantly, even granting the localized reading, the question of "cessation" turns on whether seedtime and harvest in the affected region actually stopped. Genesis 41:54 says "the dearth was in all lands" and 41:56 says "the famine waxed sore in the land of Egypt" — meaning the agricultural cycle had functionally ceased for the duration of the famine in the regions described. So either (a) the Noahic covenant is universal and the Joseph famine is local, in which case the contradiction softens to a hyperbolic-language dispute, or (b) one of the two passages is using kol ha'aretz with a different scope than the other. Source-critically, Genesis 8:22 is generally assigned to J (the Yahwist) and the Joseph narrative is a complex composite (J/E with later P insertions). The contradiction is the result of the redactor folding originally independent traditions into a single narrative without flattening their internal tensions. Documentary Hypothesis predicts exactly this kind of doublet-by-juxtaposition.

answers.answer: Seed time and harvest were never to cease
answers.answer_explanation: While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.

answers.answer: Seed time and harvest did cease for seven years
answers.answer_explanation:
And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.

And the famine was over all the face of the earth: And Joseph opened all the storehouses, and sold unto the Egyptians; and the famine waxed sore in the land of Egypt.

And there will I nourish thee; for yet [there are] five years of famine; lest thou, and thy household, and all that thou hast, come to poverty.

contradictions.question: Which woman besought Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 15:22 identifies the woman who asked Jesus to exorcise her daughter as "a woman of Canaan" (gyne Chananaia). Mark 7:26, the source text Matthew is editing, identifies her as "Greek, a Syrophoenician by nation" (Hellenis, Syrophoinikissa to genei). The two designations describe different ethnic and political categories — Canaanite is a biblical-archaic Hebrew Bible term; Syrophoenician is a contemporary first-century Roman regional designation.
contradictions.commentary: This is a classic case of Matthean redaction of Mark, and the contradiction at the level of identification is genuine even if the underlying historical referent is the same person. Mark, writing first (most critical scholars c. 65-75 CE), calls her Greek (in religion/language) and Syrophoenician (in ethnicity/region) — accurate contemporary first-century terminology for someone from coastal Syria/Phoenicia. Matthew, writing later (c. 80-90 CE) and editing Mark for a more Jewish-Christian audience, replaces Syrophoenician with the archaic biblical term "Canaanite." The change is theologically purposeful. Matthew is reframing the encounter as a meeting between Jesus the Son of David and a representative of Israel's ancient enemies — the Canaanites whom Joshua failed to fully dispossess. The Canaanite designation reactivates Hebrew Bible categories that Mark's neutral ethnographic label does not. Apologists harmonize by noting that the two terms can refer to overlapping populations — Phoenicians were historically descendants of Canaanites, and the LXX sometimes uses Chanaan for the broader region. That's true. But the harmonization concedes the point: Matthew has deliberately replaced Mark's contemporary terminology with biblical-archaic terminology. The two designations aren't synonymous in first-century usage. Davies-Allison treat this as a clear example of Matthean redaction reshaping Mark's narrative for his own theological purposes. The contradiction isn't "Matthew made up a different woman" — it's that Matthew rewrote Mark's identification of the same woman to serve his own theological agenda, and the two designations don't match. That's not error per se; it's evidence that the Gospel writers are theologians, not transcribers.

answers.answer_explanation: And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, [thou] Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.
The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation; and she besought him that he would cast forth the devil out of her daughter.

contradictions.question: Where did Jesus ascend?
contradictions.summary: Acts 1:9-12 places the ascension on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), with the disciples returning to Jerusalem from there "a sabbath day's journey." Luke 24:50-51, written by the same author, places the ascension at Bethany, where Jesus led the disciples out and blessed them before being carried up to heaven. The two-volume Luke-Acts gives two different locations for the same event.
contradictions.commentary: This is a contradiction within a single author's two-volume work, which makes it especially interesting from a redaction-critical standpoint. Luke 24 compresses the entire post-resurrection sequence into what reads like a single Easter day — the appearance on the Emmaus road, the appearance to the eleven, and the ascension all seem to occur the same evening. Acts 1, by contrast, separates the ascension from the resurrection by forty days (1:3) and locates it on the Mount of Olives. Apologists like Marshall and Bock harmonize geographically by noting that Bethany sits on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, so the two locations can refer to roughly the same area — a real point of geography. They also harmonize chronologically by claiming Luke 24 telescopes the timeline without specifying a date. Both moves are textually possible but strained. Luke 24:50 specifies Bethany (eis Bethanian), not the Mount of Olives generally, and Acts 1:12 specifies the Mount of Olives as the return point, not Bethany. More importantly, Luke 24 reads as a complete narrative that does not anticipate a forty-day gap. The narrative friction is best explained as Luke writing his Gospel ending and then, when composing Acts later, rewriting the ascension to serve as the prologue/inciting incident of Acts. Critical scholarship has long recognized that Luke uses the ascension as the literary hinge between the two volumes, and the divergent details reflect his rewriting for different rhetorical purposes — closure for the Gospel, prologue for Acts. The geographical and chronological details get reshaped to fit each volume's narrative function.

answers.answer_explanation:
And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.

Then returned they unto Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a sabbath day's journey.

And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them.

And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven.

contradictions.question: Where did Abraham depart to?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 12:5 reports that Abram took his household from Haran and "they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came" — Abram knew his destination. Hebrews 11:8 reframes the same event as faith-departure: "he went out, not knowing whither he went." Genesis has Abram leaving with Canaan as a known target; Hebrews has him leaving in ignorance of the destination.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is genuine at the level of narrative reporting, but it's softer than the cleaner cases in this batch because Hebrews 11 is doing theological midrash on the Genesis narrative, not historical reporting. Genesis 12:1 records God's command "unto a land that I will shew thee" (el ha'aretz asher ar'ekka) — the destination is not specified in the divine command. But by 12:5, the narrator says they left specifically to go to Canaan, and they arrived. The Hebrew Bible doesn't tell us when or how Abram learned the destination was Canaan; the narrative gap allows the author of Hebrews to read Genesis 12:1's open-ended command as the operative moment, with Abram departing in faith before knowing the destination. Apologists harmonize by treating Hebrews 11:8 as commenting on the moment of departure (when the destination was unspecified) and Genesis 12:5 as describing the journey's outcome (when the destination had been disclosed en route). That's a plausible harmonization if you grant the chronological reading the apologist proposes. The harder problem is that the author of Hebrews is using Abraham as a faith exemplar in a theology of pilgrimage — he wants Abraham to stand for the Christian who departs his earthly home without knowing the heavenly destination. The theological agenda shapes the historical claim. Critical scholarship treats Hebrews 11 as a stylized hall-of-faith reread of biblical narrative for hortatory purposes, not as a transcript of what Genesis actually says. Read that way, the "contradiction" is really a difference in narrative purpose — Genesis tells us where Abraham went; Hebrews tells us what kind of faith departure means. Different aims, overlapping vocabulary, real tension at the propositional level.

answers.answer: Abraham departed to go into Canaan
answers.answer_explanation: And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came.
By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.

contradictions.question: Did Abraham's children require interposition of Providence?
contradictions.summary: Romans 4:19 and Hebrews 11:12 both emphasize that Abraham's body was "as good as dead" and Sarah's womb was barren, so the birth of Isaac required miraculous divine intervention. Genesis 25:1-2 then reports that after Sarah's death, Abraham took Keturah as a wife and fathered six more sons — Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, Shuah — apparently without any supernatural assistance, despite being at least 137 years old (since Sarah died at 127 per Genesis 23:1, when Abraham was 137 per Genesis 17:17 / 25:7-10 reckoning).
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction here is more theological than narrative, and it has been a recognized puzzle since the rabbinic period. The Pauline-Hebrews argument depends on Abraham being reproductively dead to make Isaac's birth a paradigm of resurrection-faith. Romans 4:19 says Abraham "considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara's womb." The Keturah narrative in Genesis 25 — with six additional sons, plus the implication of grandchildren born during Abraham's lifetime — undermines that argument. If Abraham was reproductively functional enough to father six sons after Sarah's death (which occurred when he was 137), then his being "as good as dead" at 100 is exegetically suspect. Apologists like Calvin and Archer harmonize in two main ways. First, they argue that the Keturah marriage chronologically *preceded* Sarah's death — the narrative is non-sequential, and Keturah's children were born before or during the Isaac period, when Abraham was younger. The Genesis text does not support this; 25:1 reads "then again Abraham took a wife," placing Keturah after Sarah. Second, they argue that the Isaac birth involved Sarah's barrenness primarily, not just Abraham's age — so divine intervention was needed to restart Sarah's womb regardless of Abraham's continued fertility. That's textually defensible (Genesis 18:11 explicitly says Sarah was past childbearing). But Romans 4:19 explicitly names both — Abraham's deadness and Sarah's. The Keturah cycle puts pressure on the Pauline-Hebrews reading of Abraham as resurrection-typological. The simplest reading is that the Genesis traditions (which preserve older folkloric elements, including the Keturah line as ethnogenesis of the southern Arab tribes) and the Pauline-Hebrews theological reading are working with different agendas, and the later theological reading flattens the narrative complexity to make its rhetorical point.

answers.answer: Abraham begat a son when he was a hundred years old, by the interposition of providence
answers.answer_explanation:
For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.

And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara's womb:

Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, [so many] as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable.

answers.answer: Abraham begat six children more afterward without help
answers.answer_explanation:
Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name [was] Keturah.

And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah.

contradictions.question: Was Canaan promised and given to Abraham and his seed?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 13:14-17 and Genesis 17:8 record God promising the land of Canaan to Abraham and his seed as an "everlasting possession" (achuzzat olam). Acts 7:5 and Hebrews 11:9, 13 directly state that Abraham received no inheritance in the land — "not so much as to set his foot on" — and that he and the patriarchs died in faith "not having received the promises." The Genesis promise of immediate and everlasting possession contradicts the New Testament's retrospective admission that the promise was never fulfilled to Abraham himself.
contradictions.commentary: This one is straightforward at the narrative level. Genesis 13:15 says "all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever." Genesis 17:8 promises Canaan as an everlasting possession. Acts 7:5, Stephen's speech, flatly states that God "gave him none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on." Hebrews 11:13 says "these all died in faith, not having received the promises." The New Testament texts know the contradiction exists and try to resolve it by spiritualizing the promise — Abraham's true inheritance is the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 11:16), not the earthly land. That's a real harmonization strategy, but it concedes the historical-narrative point. Abraham did not, in his lifetime, possess Canaan. Apologists like Walton and Sailhamer harmonize by distinguishing between the promise (which was given to Abraham) and the fulfillment (which was promised to his descendants). Genesis 15:13-16 explicitly tells Abraham his seed will be afflicted four hundred years before returning to possess the land, so the deferred fulfillment is built into the narrative. That's textually correct — but it makes the "everlasting possession" language strange when applied to the patriarch himself, who never possessed it. Critical scholarship treats the Abrahamic land promise as a post-exilic theological retrojection — the J/E sources may preserve older tribal traditions, but the developed "everlasting possession" language likely reflects P's Second Temple theology of Israel's land claims being grounded in pre-conquest divine promise. Acts 7 and Hebrews 11, written in the post-70 CE diaspora when the land had been lost to Rome, deliberately spiritualize the promise to keep it operative when geopolitical fulfillment had failed. Same promise, two reading strategies — one literal-historical (Genesis), one spiritualized-eschatological (NT). The texts contradict at the propositional level; the NT resolves the contradiction by changing what "inheritance" means.

answers.answer: God promised Abraham and his seed Canaan forever
answers.answer_explanation:
And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:

For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever.

Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it; for I will give it unto thee.

And I will give unto thee, and to thy seed after thee, the land wherein thou art a stranger, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession; and I will be their God.

answers.answer: Abraham and his seed never received the promised land
answers.answer_explanation:
And he gave him none inheritance in it, no, not [so much as] to set his foot on: yet he promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him, when [as yet] he had no child.

By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as [in] a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of [them], and embraced [them], and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.

contradictions.question: How long should David's throne endure?
contradictions.summary: Psalm 89:35-37 records God's oath, sworn by his holiness, that David's seed shall endure forever and his throne be established as the sun and moon — a faithful witness in heaven. Eight verses later, the same psalm — Psalm 89:44 — says God has "made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground." The contradiction is internal to a single psalm: the eternal oath in v. 35-37 is followed by the report of the throne's destruction in v. 44.
contradictions.commentary: Psalm 89 is one of the most theologically explosive texts in the entire Psalter, precisely because the contradiction is internal and intentional. The psalm is a three-part composition. Verses 1-37 rehearse the Davidic covenant in maximalist terms, climaxing in God's unbreakable oath. Verses 38-45 then describe the catastrophic reversal — God has rejected, abhorred, broken, profaned, cast down. Verses 46-51 are the lament's prayer for restoration. The psalm is not contradicting itself by accident. The psalmist is *holding God accountable* for the contradiction. The structure is: here is what you swore; here is what has happened; how long, O Lord. Most critical scholars (Tate, Hossfeld-Zenger, Goldingay) date the psalm's final form to the exilic or early post-exilic period, when the Davidic dynasty had been destroyed and the eternal covenant looked like a broken promise. The psalm preserves the older Davidic theology in vv. 1-37 (likely pre-exilic court material) and then juxtaposes it with the exilic reality in vv. 38-45 to confront God with the breach. Apologists harmonize by appealing to messianic fulfillment — the throne was "cast down" for Israel but "restored" in Christ, the eternal Davidic king. That's the standard New Testament reading (Acts 2:30, Hebrews 1:8), but it's a theological resolution to a textual problem that the psalmist himself does not resolve. The psalm ends in unanswered lament. The contradiction is not just real — it's *deliberate*, used as rhetorical pressure on Yahweh. Treating it as a problem to be harmonized away misses the psalm's own theological move.

answers.answer: David's throne was to endure forever
answers.answer_explanation:
Once have I sworn by my holiness that I will not lie unto David.

His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me.

It shall be established for ever as the moon, and [as] a faithful witness in heaven. Selah.
Thou hast made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus lay down his life for friends or enemies?
contradictions.summary: John 15:13 and 10:11 describe Jesus laying down his life for his friends (philoi) and for the sheep — the in-group, the disciples, those who love him. Romans 5:10 says "when we were enemies (echthroi), we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" — the death was for those who were hostile to God, not those who were loyal. The Johannine and Pauline atonement frameworks identify different beneficiaries of the same death.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is more theological-categorical than narrative, and it tracks a real divergence between Johannine and Pauline soteriology. In John's Gospel, the cross is presented within the discourse community of the disciples — the Farewell Discourse (John 13-17) frames the death as the supreme act of friendship-love. The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep that belong to him; the friend lays down his life for his friends. Pauline soteriology in Romans 5:6-10 deploys the opposite framework: Christ died for the ungodly (asebon), for sinners, for enemies. The point Paul is making is that the death is unmerited and unilateral — it precedes the reconciliation, so the recipients were enemies at the time of the action. Apologists harmonize by noting that the two frameworks address different moments in the narrative. The Romans 5 "enemies" describes the soteriological starting point (before reconciliation); the John 15 "friends" describes the relational status of the disciples within the narrative (they are already Jesus' friends because they have followed him). On that reading, both can be true: Christ died for friends-who-were-formerly-enemies. That harmonization works at the systematic-theological level but flattens the distinct rhetorical aims of the two texts. John wants to elevate the cross as the supreme expression of in-group love — the disciples are friends, not slaves, because Jesus has revealed everything to them.
