Paul wants to magnify grace by emphasizing the moral asymmetry — Christ died for those who hated him. The two emphases serve different pastoral functions and resist easy synthesis. The deeper critical point is that John and Paul are working with different atonement theologies. Paul's reconciliation-of-enemies framework (Romans 5, 2 Corinthians 5:18-21) is forensic and substitutionary. John's friendship-laying-down-life framework is relational and revelatory. The texts contradict at the level of who-the-death-is-for because they're answering different soteriological questions.

answers.answer: Christ laid down his life for his friends
answers.answer_explanation:
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.

I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

answers.answer: Christ laid down his life for his enemies
answers.answer_explanation: For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.

contradictions.question: Was it lawful for the Jews to kill Jesus?
contradictions.summary: John 19:7 has the Jewish authorities declaring that under their own law, Jesus deserves death — "by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God." John 18:31 has the same authorities saying to Pilate, "It is not lawful for us to put any man to death." Same group, same trial scene, two different answers about whether their law permits killing Jesus.
contradictions.commentary: The two verses live within the same trial narrative and reflect the historical-juridical complexity of capital cases under Roman occupation in the late Second Temple period. The apologist harmonization, which has substantial scholarly support, distinguishes between two claims: (1) under Jewish law, Jesus' alleged blasphemy was a capital offense (Leviticus 24:16), so John 19:7 reports the substantive verdict the Jewish authorities had reached; (2) under Roman occupation, the *ius gladii* — the right of capital execution — had been removed from the Sanhedrin and reserved for the Roman governor, so John 18:31 reports the procedural limitation. The two statements describe different categories: substantive law (yes, our law condemns him) and procedural authority (but we can't carry out the execution). That harmonization is historically defensible. Raymond Brown in *The Death of the Messiah* extensively documents the debate over whether the Sanhedrin retained capital jurisdiction in the late Second Temple period. The dominant scholarly view is that they did not — Rome had restricted capital cases to the prefect's court, which is exactly why the Jewish authorities need Pilate to ratify the execution. The tension in John is real but not necessarily contradictory at the legal level. Critically, however, John is using both statements rhetorically. The Fourth Gospel has a strong anti-Jewish polemic and is theologically invested in making the Jewish authorities responsible for Jesus' death while showing Pilate as the reluctant executioner. The two statements together work to assign maximum culpability to "the Jews" (John's hostile term for the religious authorities) while shifting procedural responsibility to Rome. The narrative contradiction at the surface dissolves into a coherent juridical picture, but only if you grant John's tendentious framing. The deeper critical issue isn't the legal mechanics but John's anti-Jewish polemic, which most contemporary scholarship (Reinhartz, Levine, Brown) treats as a serious historical and ethical problem.

answers.answer: It was lawful for the Jews to put Christ to death
answers.answer_explanation: The Jews answered him, We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.

answers.answer: It was not lawful for the Jews to put Christ to death
answers.answer_explanation: Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death:

contradictions.question: Are reward and punishment bestowed in this world?
contradictions.summary: Proverbs 11:31 declares that the righteous are recompensed in the earth — "much more the wicked and the sinner." The traditional Deuteronomic-Wisdom theology underwrites this: divine justice operates within the temporal frame of this life. Revelation 20:12, Matthew 16:27, and 2 Corinthians 5:10 relocate judgment to the eschaton — a final reckoning at the throne of judgment after death, when works are weighed and the book of life is opened. Same canonical question — when is justice administered — two different answers.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the most theologically consequential contradictions in the Bible because it tracks the historical development of Jewish-Christian eschatology. The older Israelite worldview, embedded in the Deuteronomic theology and most of Proverbs, operated on a this-worldly justice model — keep covenant and you'll prosper; break covenant and you'll suffer. Sheol was a shadowy non-existence common to all, not a place of moral differentiation (cf. Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10; Job 3 — both cited in the SAB answer 1316). The post-exilic and Second Temple period developed apocalyptic eschatology — a final resurrection, divine judgment, eternal reward or punishment. Daniel 12:2 is the breakthrough text in the Hebrew Bible, dated by most critical scholars to the Maccabean crisis (c. 165 BCE), when the this-worldly justice model collapsed under the experience of righteous martyrs dying for covenant fidelity. The New Testament inherits and develops the apocalyptic eschatology fully. The contradiction the SAB highlights is historically accurate: the Bible contains two distinct theologies of divine justice — a pre-exilic immanent-justice model and a post-exilic transcendent-eschatological model. Apologists harmonize by claiming both are operative — God rewards some things in this life and reserves final judgment for the next. That's a coherent synthetic theology, and it's how most Christian traditions read the texts. But the synthesis flattens the historical development. The Wisdom tradition (Job, Ecclesiastes) is itself a sustained protest against the simple immanent-justice model — Job's friends recite the Proverbs 11:31 theology, and Job calls bullshit. Ecclesiastes 9 explicitly states that the same fate befalls the righteous and the wicked. The Bible contains an internal debate about whether this-worldly justice works, and the apocalyptic eschatology emerged precisely because the older theology had failed to comport with reality. That is not a contradiction to be harmonized — it is the canon recording its own theological evolution.

answers.answer: Reward and punishment to be bestowed in this world
answers.answer_explanation: Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner.

answers.answer: Reward and punishment to be bestowed in the next world
answers.answer_explanation:
And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is [the book] of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.

For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things [done] in [his] body, according to that he hath done, whether [it be] good or bad.

contradictions.question: Is annihilation or endless misery the portion of manking?
contradictions.summary: Job 3, Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10, and Ecclesiastes 3:19-20 articulate a thoroughgoing annihilationist anthropology — the dead know nothing, all go to dust, man has no preeminence above a beast, the grave is silence. Matthew 25:46, Revelation 20:10, 14:11, 20:15, and Daniel 12:2 articulate eternal conscious torment — everlasting punishment, smoke of torment rising forever, the lake of fire, awakening to everlasting shame. The Hebrew Bible's older anthropology and the apocalyptic-NT eschatology give incompatible answers about what happens after death.
contradictions.commentary: This is a sharper version of the previous contradiction (id 598) and tracks the same historical-theological development. The Hebrew Bible's mainstream anthropology — preserved most clearly in Job and Ecclesiastes — is what biblical scholars call a "holistic" view: human beings are animated bodies (nephesh chayyah), not embodied souls, and death is the cessation of life rather than the separation of soul from body. Ecclesiastes 9:5 ("the dead know not any thing") and 3:19-20 ("all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again") are not poetic exaggerations — they reflect the pre-apocalyptic Israelite consensus that death is real and final. Sheol, in this framework, is not hell; it's just the grave, the realm of non-being where everyone goes regardless of moral status. The transition to apocalyptic eternal-torment theology happens in the Second Temple period under multiple influences — Persian Zoroastrian dualism, Hellenistic body-soul dualism, and the theodicy crisis of the Maccabean martyrdoms (cf. 2 Maccabees 7, 1 Enoch). Daniel 12:2 is the first clear Hebrew Bible text positing differentiated post-mortem fates. The Synoptic Gospels and especially Revelation develop the doctrine fully — eternal conscious torment, the lake of fire, the worm that does not die. Apologists like John Walton and Edward Fudge propose either "progressive revelation" (early texts give partial truth, later texts give fuller truth) or, for Fudge specifically, *conditional immortality* / annihilationism — the wicked are destroyed, not eternally tormented, and texts like Job and Ecclesiastes preserve that older truth. The progressive-revelation move is theologically convenient but historically tendentious — it treats earlier Israelite anthropology as defective rather than as a distinct theological tradition. The annihilationist apologetic (Fudge, Stott in his later work) actually agrees with the SAB's reading that the canon contains conflicting eschatologies and chooses the older one. The contradiction is real, well-documented, and reflects the canon recording its own evolving anthropology of death.

answers.answer_explanation:
Why died I not from the womb? [why] did I [not] give up the ghost when I came out of the belly?

For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest,

With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built desolate places for themselves;

Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver:

Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants [which] never saw light.

There the wicked cease [from] troubling; and there the weary be at rest.

The small and great are there; and the servant [is] free from his master.

Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter [in] soul;

Which long for death, but it [cometh] not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures;

Which rejoice exceedingly, [and] are glad, when they can find the grave?

For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.

Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do [it] with thy might; for [there is] no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.

For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all [is] vanity.

All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.

And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet [are], and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.

And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame [and] everlasting contempt.

contradictions.question: Is the Christian yoke easy?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 11:28-30 has Jesus offering rest to the weary — his yoke is easy (chrestos) and his burden is light (elaphron). John 16:33, 2 Timothy 3:12, and Hebrews 12:6, 8 give the opposite framing: in the world believers will have tribulation, all who live godly will suffer persecution, and those without chastisement are bastards rather than legitimate sons. The Matthean invitation and the persecution-discipleship theology of the rest of the New Testament give competing answers about whether following Christ is easy or hard.
contradictions.commentary: The tension is real but the harmonization is also strong here, so this is a softer contradiction than the cleaner cases in this batch. Matthew 11:28-30 is widely recognized as drawing on Wisdom traditions — Sirach 51:23-27 invites the unlearned to take up Wisdom's yoke and find rest, with closely parallel language. The Matthean Jesus is positioning himself as personified Wisdom, offering a yoke (a rabbinic metaphor for the discipline of Torah-study) that is paradoxically restful compared to the burdens the scribes and Pharisees impose (cf. Matt 23:4 — "they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne"). The "easy" yoke is relative to the burden it replaces, not absolutely easy. Apologists like Carson and France harmonize on exactly this point: the Matthean yoke is easy in the sense that Christ's discipline is restful and life-giving, not in the sense that following Jesus is socially or physically painless. The persecution-discipleship texts (John 16:33, 2 Timothy 3:12, Hebrews 12:6) address the external opposition believers face, not the internal experience of the yoke. The two frames address different dimensions — the internal experience of devotion (easy, restful) and the external experience of persecution (hard, painful). That harmonization works reasonably well, and most critical commentators (Davies-Allison, Luz) note the wisdom-tradition background that frames the "easy yoke" relatively rather than absolutely. The genuine tension remaining is rhetorical rather than logical: Matthew 11:30's blanket statement ("my yoke is easy and my burden is light") doesn't include the qualifier the harmonization requires. Read at face value, alongside Jesus' own predictions of persecution and martyrdom for his followers (Matt 10:16-39), the saying does sit in tension with the broader NT picture. The contradiction softens with context but doesn't fully dissolve.

answers.answer_explanation:
Come unto me, all [ye] that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

For my yoke [is] easy, and my burden is light.

These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.

Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.

For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.

But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons.

contradictions.question: Is a good name a blessing or curse?
contradictions.summary: The wisdom tradition treats a good reputation as one of life's highest goods. Ecclesiastes 7:1 ranks a good name above precious ointment and Proverbs 22:1 ranks it above great riches. Luke 6:26 flips the valuation — Jesus pronounces a woe on those of whom all speak well, on the grounds that the same kind of universal approval was given to the false prophets. The shared term is reputation, but the Hebrew sages prize it and the Lukan Jesus treats it as a danger sign.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is real at the level of how each text evaluates public esteem, but it lives in the gap between two distinct genres and theological programs. Ecclesiastes 7:1 and Proverbs 22:1 belong to the mainstream Israelite wisdom tradition, where shem tov — a good name — is the social capital that signals a life lived in alignment with the moral order. Qoheleth even pushes the idea farther: a good name plus the day of death is preferable to perfume plus the day of birth, because reputation is the only thing that outlasts you. Proverbs 22:1 grounds the same valuation in shame-honor logic — favor and reputation outrank wealth. Luke 6:26 stands in a completely different stream. It is the fourth and final woe in the Lukan Sermon on the Plain, an inversion-of-fortunes counterpart to the beatitude in Luke 6:22-23, where the disciples are blessed when men hate them and cast out their name as evil for the Son of Man's sake. The Lukan logic is prophetic-eschatological: in a corrupt world, universal approval is evidence that you are saying what people want to hear, exactly like the court prophets of Ahab and the false prophets denounced by Jeremiah and Micah. Apologists like Gleason Archer typically harmonize by distinguishing between a good name earned by righteous conduct and a good name earned by sycophancy, and the distinction is genuine — but the harmonization papers over the fact that the wisdom texts make no such qualification. They treat the universal good report as straightforwardly desirable. Luke's Jesus treats it as straightforwardly dangerous. The tension is not nominal; it reflects a real shift from sapiential ethics to apocalyptic-prophetic ethics within the canon.

answers.answer_explanation:
A good name [is] better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth.

A [good] name [is] rather to be chosen than great riches, [and] loving favour rather than silver and gold.
Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets.

contradictions.question: Is there a remedy for foolishness?
contradictions.summary: Proverbs 22:15 and Proverbs 27:22 sit in the same book and give opposite verdicts on whether foolishness can be driven out of a person. 22:15 says foolishness is bound in the heart of a child but the rod of correction will drive it far from him — corporal discipline as the cure. 27:22 says you can grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with wheat and his foolishness still will not depart from him — the fool is incorrigible. Same wisdom collection, two incompatible anthropologies of folly.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in Proverbs and it shows up because Proverbs is not a unified treatise but an anthology of distinct collections — at minimum the Solomonic core in chapters 10-22:16, the Sayings of the Wise in 22:17-24:34, the Hezekian collection in 25-29, and the appendices of Agur and Lemuel in 30-31. Different collections, different sages, different views of human nature. The Solomonic collection (which contains 22:15) is optimistic about the formative power of discipline: the rod of musar drives folly out of the child because folly is acquired, not constitutive. The Hezekian collection (which contains 27:22) is closer to the worldview of Qoheleth — folly is an essence, a kind of fixed disposition that no amount of external pressure can dislodge. The image of grinding a fool in a mortar with a pestle is deliberately absurd, the kind of hyperbole that makes the point that even total bodily violence cannot expel the trait. Apologists like Bruce Waltke harmonize by appealing to age — 22:15 applies to children whose character is still being formed, while 27:22 applies to mature fools whose character is set. That is a defensible reading and it does relieve the surface tension, but it requires you to import age categories that the text itself does not specify. Both verses speak generically of the fool (kesil / 'evil) without restricting the proverb to a developmental stage. The more parsimonious reading is that the redactors of Proverbs preserved competing voices from the wisdom schools — one that believed in the malleability of character through discipline, one that did not — and made no attempt to harmonize them. That is exactly what we should expect from an anthology, and exactly what the form-critical work of Whybray and Fox has been arguing for decades.

answers.answer_explanation: Foolishness [is] bound in the heart of a child; [but] the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.

answers.answer: There is no remedy for foolishness
answers.answer_explanation: Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, [yet] will not his foolishness depart from him.

contradictions.question: Is temptation desired?
contradictions.summary: James 1:2 tells believers to count it all joy when they fall into various peirasmoi — testings or temptations — because the testing of faith produces endurance. Matthew 6:13, the petition embedded in the Lord's Prayer, asks the Father not to lead us into peirasmos but to deliver us from evil. The lexical overlap is exact: the same Greek word peirasmos is the object of celebration in James and the object of avoidance in the Lord's Prayer. One source says embrace it, the other says ask God to spare you from it.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction hinges on the Greek word peirasmos, which spans the semantic range from outward trial to inward solicitation to sin. James 1:2 opens his epistle by reframing peirasmoi as occasions for joy because the dokimion (testing) of pistis works endurance — the trial is instrumental in maturing the believer. Matthew 6:13, embedded in the Lord's Prayer, takes the opposite stance — me eisenenkes hemas eis peirasmon, do not bring us into peirasmos. The petition treats peirasmos as something to be avoided, not embraced. Apologists like Douglas Moo and D. A. Carson typically harmonize by claiming the two passages use peirasmos in different senses — James means external trial (testing of faith) while Matthew means inner enticement to sin. The distinction is grammatically defensible but exegetically thin. James 1:13 in fact switches to the inner sense within the same paragraph, saying God tempts no one to evil, which means James knows the dual sense and uses both. Matthew 6:13 includes no qualifier that would restrict its peirasmos to enticement-only. The petition is general and asks for deliverance from the situation itself, not for strength to resist enticement within it. Pope Francis's 2019 retranslation of the Italian missal (to render it as do not let us fall into temptation rather than lead us not into temptation) is essentially an acknowledgment that the plain reading creates exactly this difficulty — it makes God the agent of leading believers into peirasmos, which is theologically intolerable. The honest reading is that James and Matthew represent different early Christian postures toward suffering and trial: James embraces it as paideia, Matthew prays for exemption from it. Same word, opposite responses.

answers.answer_explanation: My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations;
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

contradictions.question: Is prophecy a sure thing?
contradictions.summary: 2 Peter 1:19 calls the prophetic word more sure (bebaioteron) — a lamp shining in a dark place that the faithful do well to heed. Jeremiah 18:7-10 makes prophecy explicitly conditional: if Yahweh declares destruction against a nation and that nation repents, he will relent; if he declares blessing and that nation does evil, he will withdraw the blessing. 2 Peter treats prophecy as fixed and reliable; Jeremiah treats it as contingent on human response. The two passages disagree on whether prophetic announcements are predictions of fixed outcomes or conditional warnings.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is real but it operates at a slightly different level than the proof-texts suggest. 2 Peter 1:19 is using prophecy in a Christological sense — the prophetic word that points to the parousia, validated for the author by the transfiguration tradition cited in the preceding verses. The author's claim is that this Christological prophetic witness is bebaioteron, more firm or reliable, than even the voice from heaven. Jeremiah 18:7-10, embedded in the potter-and-clay oracle, is making a fundamentally different claim about how prophetic announcements work in the political and moral economy of Israel and the nations. They are not fixed predictions; they are responsive declarations. Yahweh announces, the nation responds, Yahweh adjusts. This is the same theological logic that allows Jonah to complain in 4:2 that he knew all along Yahweh would relent over Nineveh — because that is how prophecy works in the Deuteronomistic and Jeremianic theological streams. Apologists like Walter Kaiser harmonize by distinguishing between unconditional prophecies (the messianic promises, the new covenant) and conditional prophecies (oracles of judgment against nations), and the distinction does have textual support — Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 both insist Yahweh is not a man that he should repent, while Jeremiah 18 and Jonah 3-4 insist that he does. The honest reading is that the Hebrew Bible itself contains two competing views on whether prophetic announcement is fixed or conditional, and Jeremiah 18:7-10 represents the conditional view while later prophetic and apocalyptic texts move toward the fixed view. 2 Peter, working within the fixed view, says prophecy is sure. Jeremiah, working within the conditional view, says prophecy is contingent. Apologists are right that the contradiction is not quite a flat yes/no, but they are wrong to deny that the two streams represent genuinely different prophetic anthropologies. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but the textual data points hard in that direction.

answers.answer_explanation: We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:

contradictions.question: Is every animal afraid of man?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 9:2, embedded in the post-flood Noachic covenant, has Yahweh place the fear and dread (morakem ve-hittekem) of human beings upon every beast of the earth, every bird of the sky, every creeping thing, and every fish of the sea — they are delivered into human hands. Proverbs 30:30 says the lion is strongest among beasts and turns away from no one. The Genesis text is a universal claim about every beast; Proverbs offers a counter-example that explicitly exempts at least one species.
contradictions.commentary: This is the kind of contradiction that exists mainly at the level of rhetorical scope rather than narrative substance, and it pays to be honest about that. Genesis 9:2 belongs to the Priestly post-flood narrative and functions theologically — humans are re-authorized after the flood as the dominant ecological force, with carnivory now permitted (9:3) and animal fear of humanity instituted as the means of that dominance. The verse is making a programmatic statement about the post-flood order, not a zoological prediction that no animal will ever attack a human. Proverbs 30:30 sits inside Agur's numerical sayings (30:24-31) and is making a different kind of claim entirely — it is observational wisdom literature cataloging examples of stately or fearless creatures (the lion, the strutting rooster, the male goat, the king with his army), with the lion as exhibit A of an animal that does not retreat. Apologists like Gleason Archer typically harmonize by noting that morakem in Genesis 9:2 expresses a general principle of the post-flood order rather than an absolute exemption from any animal aggression, and that Proverbs 30:30 is poetic observation, not a denial of the Genesis principle. That is fair as far as it goes — the Genesis text is using totalizing language for theological emphasis. But it is also true that the totalizing language of Genesis 9:2 (every beast, every bird, every creeping thing) sets up an expectation that Proverbs 30:30 specifically refuses. Apologetically, the harmonization works. Textually, the two passages stand in tension. The more parsimonious reading is that Genesis 9:2 is a theological-mythic claim about cosmic order while Proverbs 30:30 is empirical observation, and the Israelite canon preserves both without trying to reconcile them. Whether that constitutes a contradiction depends on how literally you want to take the language of Genesis 9:2 — and the inerrantist position requires you to take it very literally indeed.

answers.answer: The fear of man was to be upon every beast
answers.answer_explanation: And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth, and upon every fowl of the air, upon all that moveth [upon] the earth, and upon all the fishes of the sea; into your hand are they delivered.

answers.answer: The fear of man is not upon the lion
answers.answer_explanation: A lion [which is] strongest among beasts, and turneth not away for any;

contradictions.question: Are miracles proof of divine mission?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 11:2-5 has Jesus point to his miracles — blind seeing, lame walking, lepers cleansed, deaf hearing, dead raised — as the answer to John the Baptist's question whether he is the coming one. John 3:2 has Nicodemus reason backward from Jesus' signs to the conclusion that no one could do them unless God were with him. Exodus 14:31 grounds Israelite faith in Moses in the great work at the Red Sea. The opposing side cites Exodus 7:10-12, where Pharaoh's magicians replicate Aaron's serpent-rod sign with their enchantments, Deuteronomy 13:1-3, which explicitly commands Israel to reject a prophet whose sign or wonder comes to pass if he calls them to other gods, and Luke 11:19, where Jesus concedes that Jewish exorcists also cast out demons. Miracles are evidentiary in the first set; the second set says miracles do not settle the question of divine authorization.
contradictions.commentary: This contradiction operates at the level of evidentiary epistemology and it is one of the more interesting ones in the canon because both sides are right about something. The pro-miracle stream — Matthew 11, John 3, Exodus 14 — treats sign-events as warrants for prophetic or messianic identity. The Matthean Jesus deflects John's question by reciting a list of healings that echoes Isaiah 35:5-6 and 61:1, framing the miracles as the fulfillment of messianic prophecy. The Johannine semeia theology is even more explicit — the signs are the basis on which the reader is asked to believe (John 20:30-31). Exodus 14:31 turns the Red Sea event into the foundation of Israel's covenant faith in Yahweh and Moses. But the counter-stream is just as clear. Exodus 7:10-12 puts the Egyptian magicians on the same evidentiary footing as Aaron — they too can produce serpents — which means the sign-event alone does not establish whose god is real. Deuteronomy 13:1-3 makes this explicit at the level of legal principle: even a fulfilled sign or wonder does not authenticate a prophet if his message contradicts covenant fidelity. Luke 11:19 has Jesus himself concede that Jewish exorcists who are not his disciples also perform exorcisms, which means exorcistic power is not by itself proof of his unique authorization. Apologists like Norman Geisler and Craig Blomberg harmonize by distinguishing between genuine and counterfeit miracles, arguing that Pharaoh's magicians performed lesser or demonic signs while Aaron's was true divine power, and that Deuteronomy 13 only applies when the prophet's message is heretical. The distinction is theologically convenient but exegetically strained — the Exodus narrative does not say the magicians' serpents were illusions or demonic; it says they did so as Aaron did, in like manner. The more parsimonious reading is that the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament both contain a more sophisticated epistemology than the pro-miracle proof-texts suggest. Miracles function as evidence in some contexts and are explicitly disqualified as standalone evidence in others. The contradiction is real at the level of any flat claim that miracles prove divine mission — Deuteronomy 13:1-3 is the smoking gun against that thesis, and it is in the same Torah that grounds Mosaic authority in the Red Sea sign.

answers.answer: Miracles are proof of divine missions
